V4-001.q: Describe how consolidation looks on lung ultrasound, and how you tell pneumonia from atelectasis.
a: Consolidated lung has lost its air, so ultrasound can now see into it: it looks like liver (tissue-like pattern, 'hepatisation').
Shred sign: the deep edge, where consolidated lung meets aerated lung, is irregular and fractal (C-profile = anterior consolidation).
Air bronchograms: bright dots or lines of air inside the consolidation.
Dynamic air bronchogram (air moves in and out with breathing) = the airway is open, so it is pneumonia, not resorptive atelectasis (high specificity).
Static air bronchogram: either pneumonia or atelectasis; atelectasis also shows a lung pulse (heartbeat transmitted, no sliding) and volume loss.
Fluid-filled bronchograms suggest an obstructed airway behind the consolidation.
In BLUE terms, posterolateral consolidation or effusion = PLAPS.
V4-001.src: Lichtenstein D, Chest 2009 (dynamic air bronchogram); Lichtenstein BLUE protocol, Chest 2008

V4-002.topic: Lung ultrasound score (LUS): grades and use
V4-002.q: Spotter: lung ultrasound score. How is it built, and how do you use it?
a: 12 regions: anterior, lateral and posterior × upper and lower, on each side.
Each region scored 0–3: 0 = A-lines (≤2 B-lines); 1 = ≥3 well-separated B-lines; 2 = coalescent B-lines; 3 = consolidation.
Total 0–36: more water, less air, higher score.
Uses: ARDS severity and follow-up; weaning (on WEAN-17: <13 success, >17 failure); fluid tolerance (rising B-lines).
PEEP: a falling score shows re-aeration (recruitment), but ultrasound cannot see over-distension, so check driving pressure as well.
Worked example: 4 regions of 1, 4 of 2, 2 of 3, 2 of 0 = 4 + 8 + 6 = 18 → predicts weaning failure.
V4-002.src: Bouhemad B, AJRCCM 2011 (LUS reaeration score); Soummer A, Crit Care Med 2012 (LUS and post-extubation distress)

V4-003.q: Spotter: pleural effusion with consolidated lung. Describe what you see and what it means.
a: Effusion: anechoic (black) space above the diaphragm, bounded by the pleural line, the lung line and two rib shadows (quad sign); on M-mode the lung swings toward the pleural line with breathing (sinusoid sign).
Septations, debris or swirling echoes suggest an exudate or empyema; uniform black can be either transudate or exudate.
Lung floating in a large effusion, flapping with each breath, with no air bronchograms = compressive (passive) atelectasis; it re-aerates once drained.
Consolidated lung with dynamic air bronchograms = pneumonia, so think parapneumonic effusion: sample it.
Measure: the interpleural distance at the base estimates volume (formulas on PLEU-16).
V4-003.src: Lichtenstein D, Chest 2009; Volpicelli G, Intensive Care Med 2012 (international LUS recommendations)

V4-004.q: How do you do diaphragm ultrasound, and what do the numbers mean for weaning?
a: Excursion: low-frequency curved probe, below the right costal margin between the midclavicular and anterior axillary lines, liver as the window, beam aimed at the back of the dome; M-mode; measure the height of the inspiratory wave.
Excursion <10 mm on quiet breathing = diaphragm dysfunction and predicts weaning failure.
Thickening: high-frequency linear probe at the zone of apposition (mid-axillary line, about the 8th–10th intercostal space); B- or M-mode; measure the muscle between the pleural and peritoneal lines.
Thickening fraction (TF) = (end-inspiratory − end-expiratory thickness) ÷ end-expiratory thickness × 100.
TF ≥30–36% predicts success; <about 30% means a weak diaphragm.
Measure on the breathing trial or very low support: ventilator assistance makes the diaphragm move without working.
V4-004.src: Kim WY, Crit Care Med 2011 (excursion <10 mm); DiNino E, Thorax 2014 (thickening fraction); Matamis D, Intensive Care Med 2013 (technique)

V4-005.topic: Light vs deep sedation: the evidence
V4-005.q: Why does PADIS recommend light sedation? Give the evidence and the ABCDEF bundle.
a: Deep sedation early (first 48 h) is linked to later extubation and higher mortality in cohort studies.
Daily sedation interruption (Kress 2000): shorter ventilation and ICU stay.
Paired awakening and breathing trials (ABC trial, Girard 2008): more ventilator-free days and lower 1-year mortality.
SLEAP 2012: adding daily interruption to a nurse protocol gave no faster extubation, only more sedative and more nursing work; one approach is enough.
PADIS 2018: light over deep sedation (target RASS −2 to +1), analgesia first, propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines.
Deep sedation still has a place: severe ARDS early, paralysis, raised ICP, status epilepticus.

ABCDEF bundle: Assess, prevent and manage pain · Both awakening and breathing trials · Choice of analgesia and sedation · Delirium: assess, prevent, manage · Early mobility and exercise · Family engagement.
V4-005.src: Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS); Kress JP, NEJM 2000; Girard TD, Lancet 2008 (ABC); Mehta S, JAMA 2012 (SLEAP); Shehabi Y, AJRCCM 2012

V4-006.q: Dexmedetomidine or propofol? What do the trials show?
a: MIDEX/PRODEX (2012): dexmedetomidine kept light sedation as well as midazolam or propofol; shorter ventilation than midazolam, better communication.

SPICE III (2019, n ≈ 4,000): early dexmedetomidine as main sedative vs usual care: 90-day mortality the same (29.1% each); more bradycardia and hypotension. Subgroup: possible harm at ≤65 years, possible benefit in older patients.
MENDS2 (2021, sepsis): dexmedetomidine vs propofol: no difference in days alive without delirium or coma, ventilator-free days, 90-day death or cognition.
A2B (JAMA 2025, n = 1,404): dexmedetomidine or clonidine vs propofol: no faster extubation; more agitation and more severe bradycardia; same 180-day mortality.
So: propofol remains the default; dexmedetomidine suits light sedation, agitated delirium preventing extubation, and non-intubated patients.
Avoid dexmedetomidine when deep sedation is needed or with bradycardia or heart block.
V4-006.src: Jakob SM, JAMA 2012 (MIDEX/PRODEX); Shehabi Y, NEJM 2019 (SPICE III); Hughes CG, NEJM 2021 (MENDS2); Walsh TS, JAMA 2025 (A2B)

V4-007.q: How do you diagnose and manage delirium in the ICU? What did AID-ICU show?
a: Screen every shift with a tool: CAM-ICU (acute change or fluctuation + inattention + either altered consciousness or disorganised thinking) or ICDSC (≥4 of 8 = delirium).
Types: hypoactive (commonest, missed), hyperactive, mixed.
Look for the cause: hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic, withdrawal, drugs (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics), urinary retention, pain, sleep loss.
Prevent and treat without drugs first: reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation, family, light sedation.

Drugs: haloperidol does not shorten delirium. MIND-USA (2018): haloperidol or ziprasidone = placebo. AID-ICU (2022, n = 1,000): haloperidol vs placebo, no difference in days alive out of hospital at 90 days.
PADIS: no routine antipsychotics, statins or prophylactic haloperidol (REDUCE 2018 neutral); dexmedetomidine for agitated delirium that is stopping extubation (DahLIA 2016).
Short-term antipsychotic only for distress or danger to self.
V4-007.src: Devlin JW, Crit Care Med 2018 (PADIS); Girard TD, NEJM 2018 (MIND-USA); Andersen-Ranberg NC, NEJM 2022 (AID-ICU); van den Boogaard M, JAMA 2018 (REDUCE); Reade MC, JAMA 2016 (DahLIA)

V4-008.topic: Inhaled volatile sedation in the ICU
V4-008.q: What is the role of inhaled volatile sedation in the ICU? Which device, and what are the limits?
a: Agents: isoflurane or sevoflurane given through the ventilator circuit.

Device: AnaConDa (anaesthetic-conserving device), a reflector between the Y-piece and the patient that returns most of the exhaled agent; or MIRUS. A syringe pump feeds the agent; gas monitoring is needed.
Advantages: fast on and off, little accumulation, bronchodilation (refractory bronchospasm), less opioid use; isoflurane is licensed for ICU sedation in Europe.

Limits: added dead space (CO₂ rises with small tidal volumes), scavenging, cost, malignant hyperthermia, sevoflurane fluoride → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria, high sodium) with prolonged use.

SESAR (JAMA 2025, n = 687, ARDS, deep sedation): sevoflurane vs propofol → fewer ventilator-free days and higher 7-day mortality (19.4 vs 13.5%); more hypercapnic acidosis and AKI. So not for routine use in ARDS.
Current place: refractory status asthmaticus, sedation that is failing with IV drugs.
V4-008.src: Jabaudon M, JAMA 2025 (SESAR); Meiser A, Lancet Respir Med 2021 (SED001, isoflurane vs propofol)

V4-009.q: What is the WIND classification, and how is it different from ICC 2007?
a: ICC 2007 (Boles): simple = extubated after the first SBT; difficult = up to 3 SBTs or ≤7 days; prolonged = >3 SBTs or >7 days. It left out patients who never had an SBT.
WIND (Béduneau 2017) counts time from the first separation attempt (SBT or extubation).
Short: separated within 1 day. Difficult: 1–7 days. Prolonged: >7 days. Group 0: no separation attempt ever.
Separation = extubation without death or reintubation for 7 days, or ≥7 days off the ventilator with a tracheostomy.
Mortality rises with each group; that is its point: it covers every ventilated patient and predicts outcome.
V4-009.src: Béduneau G, AJRCCM 2017 (WIND); Boles JM, Eur Respir J 2007

V4-010.topic: SBT: PSV or T-piece — the evidence
V4-010.q: How do you do an SBT, and which method is better?
a: Screen daily: cause improving, P/F >150–200 on PEEP ≤8 and FiO₂ ≤0.4–0.5, stable without high-dose pressors, awake, able to cough.
Run it: PSV 5–8 cmH₂O (with zero or low PEEP) for 30 min, or a T-piece for 30–120 min.
Subirà (JAMA 2019, n = 1,153): PSV 8 with zero PEEP for 30 min vs T-piece for 2 h → successful extubation 82.3 vs 74.0%; same reintubation; lower 90-day mortality with PSV (secondary).
T-piece is the harder test and mimics post-extubation effort most closely: prefer it when you suspect cardiac failure on weaning.
Failure signs: RR >35, SpO₂ <90%, HR >140 or rising 20%, SBP >180 or <90, agitation, sweating, accessory muscles.
After a failed SBT: back to a comfortable mode, find the cause, retry in 24 h.
V4-010.src: Subirà C, JAMA 2019;321:2175; Boles JM, Eur Respir J 2007 (ICC weaning)

V4-011.q: Early or late tracheostomy? Percutaneous or surgical?
a: TracMan (JAMA 2013, n = 909): early (day 1–4) vs late (day ≥10): 30-day mortality 30.8 vs 31.5%, no difference; fewer sedation days with early. Only about half of the late group ever needed one.
SETPOINT2 (JAMA 2022, stroke): early (≤5 days) vs late: no better 6-month function.
Meta-analyses: early tracheostomy may cut sedation and ventilator days, not mortality.
So: decide when weaning is clearly prolonged, often around day 7–10; earlier in high cervical cord injury or severe brain injury needing airway protection.

Percutaneous vs surgical: similar mortality; percutaneous is bedside, quicker, fewer wound infections; surgical for difficult anatomy (short fat neck, previous neck surgery, coagulopathy, unstable spine).
V4-011.src: Young D, JAMA 2013 (TracMan); Bösel J, JAMA 2022 (SETPOINT2)

V4-012.q: How do you prevent extubation failure? Who gets high-flow, and who gets NIV?
a: Identify high risk: age >65, heart failure, COPD, BMI >30, APACHE II >12, weak cough or many secretions, failed first SBT, prolonged ventilation, hypercapnia.
Airway: cuff leak <110 mL (or <24% of Vt) → stridor risk; give methylprednisolone 20 mg 4-hourly starting 12 h before extubation in at-risk patients.
Low risk: high-flow nasal oxygen for 24 h beats standard oxygen (Hernández 2016: reintubation 4.9 vs 12.2%).
High risk: prophylactic NIV, or NIV alternating with high-flow (HIGH-WEAN 2019: reintubation 11.8 vs 18.2% vs high-flow alone).
Hypercapnic or COPD patients: NIV straight after extubation.
Established respiratory failure after extubation: do not use NIV to delay reintubation (Esteban 2004: higher mortality).
V4-012.src: Hernández G, JAMA 2016 (low-risk HFNC); Thille AW, JAMA 2019 (HIGH-WEAN); François B, Lancet 2007 (steroids for low cuff leak); Esteban A, NEJM 2004

V4-013.q: What is ICU-acquired weakness? How do you tell CIP from CIM?
a: Definition: diffuse, symmetrical limb weakness arising in the ICU with no other cause; MRC sum score <48/60 in an awake, cooperative patient (handgrip is a quick screen).
Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP): axonal sensorimotor; nerve conduction shows low motor (CMAP) and sensory (SNAP) amplitudes with normal speed; sensory loss distally.
Critical illness myopathy (CIM): low CMAP with normal SNAP; longer CMAP duration; direct muscle stimulation is weak; sensation intact; may have high CK. Often both (CIPNM).
Risk factors: sepsis and multi-organ failure, hyperglycaemia, immobility and long ventilation, corticosteroids, neuromuscular blockers, early parenteral nutrition.
Prevent: avoid hyperglycaemia, light sedation, early mobilisation, avoid early parenteral nutrition.
It explains weaning failure on the capacity side and long-term disability.
V4-013.src: Fan E, AJRCCM 2014 (ATS ICU-acquired weakness statement); Latronico N, Lancet Neurol 2011; Casaer MP, NEJM 2011 (EPaNIC)

V4-014.q: What is the role of steroids in severe community-acquired pneumonia?
a: CAPE COD (NEJM 2023, n = 800, ICU severe CAP): hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 4 or 8 days then tapered, vs placebo → 28-day mortality 6.2 vs 11.9%; fewer intubations and less vasopressor start.
Excluded: influenza, septic shock already on vasopressors.
ESCAPe (2022, methylprednisolone): no significant mortality difference.
SCCM 2024 focused update: recommends corticosteroids for adults hospitalised with severe bacterial CAP (strong, moderate certainty); no recommendation for less severe CAP.
Avoid in influenza pneumonia (more deaths, secondary infection); caution with aspergillosis risk.
Watch: hyperglycaemia, more secondary infection.
V4-014.src: Dequin PF, NEJM 2023 (CAPE COD); Meduri GU, Intensive Care Med 2022 (ESCAPe); Chaudhuri D, Crit Care Med 2024 (SCCM corticosteroid focused update)

V4-015.q: Differentiate pressure control and volume control. Which is better in ARDS?
a: Volume control: you set Vt and flow; pressure is the result. A stiffer lung or a blocked tube shows as a rising peak pressure.
Pressure control: you set the inspiratory pressure and time; flow decelerates; Vt is the result. A stiffer lung shows as a falling Vt.
VC guarantees minute ventilation; PC limits peak pressure and its decelerating flow may suit an active patient better.
Danger in PC: a strong patient effort adds to the set pressure, so Vt and lung stretch can be large while the pressure on screen stays the same.
Dual modes (PRVC): pressure-limited breaths that adjust to deliver a target Vt.
In ARDS: no outcome difference between the two. What matters is the Vt (6 mL/kg PBW), plateau ≤30 and driving pressure ≤15, whichever mode delivers them.
V4-015.src: Rittayamai N, Chest 2015 (PC vs VC review); ARDSNet, NEJM 2000

V4-016.topic: Driving pressure when the patient is breathing
V4-016.q: How do you measure driving pressure on pressure support, and what are the pitfalls?
a: Driving pressure (ΔP) = plateau − PEEP = Vt ÷ compliance: the stretch on the aerated (baby) lung. Keep it ≤15 (Amato 2015).
On pressure support you can still do an end-inspiratory hold, but only if the patient is relaxed at that moment.
Inspiratory effort during the hold makes the plateau read low, so the true stretch is under-read; expiratory muscle activity makes it read high.
Look at the hold: a flat plateau is valid; a sloping or wavy one is not.
LUNG SAFE: ΔP >15 on pressure support was also linked to higher mortality, so the target applies to spontaneous breathing too.
If the plateau can't be trusted, estimate effort another way (occlusion pressure, oesophageal pressure).
V4-016.src: Amato MBP, NEJM 2015; Bellani G, AJRCCM 2016 (plateau on PSV); Bellani G, Anesthesiology 2019 (LUNG SAFE, ΔP in spontaneous breathing)

V4-017.q: What is mechanical power, what are its parts, and how do you lower it?
a: Mechanical power = the energy the ventilator delivers to the lung per minute (J/min). It joins all the injury causes in one number: volume, pressure, flow and rate.
Three parts, each multiplied by the rate: static (from PEEP), dynamic (from ΔP, the tidal stretch) and resistive (from flow through the airways).
Simplified formula (volume control): MP = 0.098 × RR × Vt (L) × (Ppeak − ½ΔP).
Worked example: RR 20, Vt 0.4 L, Ppeak 30, ΔP 14 → 0.098 × 20 × 0.4 × (30 − 7) = 18 J/min.
Above about 17 J/min was linked to higher mortality (Serpa Neto 2018, observational).
First levers: lower the rate and the ΔP (smaller Vt); lower inspiratory flow cuts the resistive part.
Ergotrauma = injury from that delivered energy. No trial has yet targeted MP itself.
V4-017.src: Gattinoni L, Intensive Care Med 2016 (mechanical power); Serpa Neto A, Intensive Care Med 2018

V4-018.q: How do you use oesophageal pressure to set PEEP? Who benefits, and what's the evidence?
a: Transpulmonary pressure (PL) = airway pressure − oesophageal pressure (stand-in for pleural pressure): the pressure that actually stretches the lung.
End-expiratory PL ≥0 (about 0 to +2): enough PEEP to stop the lung collapsing at end-expiration.
End-inspiratory PL (elastance-based) <20–25 cmH₂O: limits over-stretch.
Most useful when the chest wall is stiff or heavy: obesity, intra-abdominal hypertension, chest-wall oedema or deformity. There a high plateau may be safe, and more PEEP may be needed.
Evidence: EPVent-2 (2019, n = 200): Pes-guided PEEP vs high PEEP table, no difference. Post-hoc (Sarge 2021): better outcomes when PEEP brought end-expiratory PL near 0 (±2).
So: a tool for selected patients, not routine.
V4-018.src: Talmor D, NEJM 2008 (EPVent); Beitler JR, JAMA 2019 (EPVent-2); Sarge T, AJRCCM 2021 (post-hoc)

V4-019.q: Spotter: the pressure–time curve in volume control. What is the stress index, and what do you change?
a: Needs constant flow (square-wave volume control) and a passive patient.
Look at the shape of the pressure rise during inspiration: straight line = stress index (SI) 0.9–1.1, compliance constant through the breath.
Curve bending upward (concave up), SI >1.1: compliance falling as the lung fills = over-distension → lower Vt or PEEP.
Curve bending downward (concave down), SI <0.9: compliance rising as the lung fills = tidal recruitment → raise PEEP.
It is the curve's shape, not its height, that matters.
Limits: chest-wall disease changes the shape too; effort and changing flow make it invalid.
V4-019.src: Grasso S, AJRCCM 2007 (stress index); Ranieri VM, Anesthesiology 2000

V4-020.q: What is P-SILI? How do you detect high drive and effort at the bedside, and what do you do?
a: Mechanism: vigorous effort → very negative pleural pressure → high transpulmonary pressure (lung stretch) and high transvascular pressure (more oedema).
Pendelluft: air moves from non-dependent to dependent lung early in inspiration, over-stretching the dependent part locally while Vt looks normal.
Detect drive: P0.1 (pressure drop in the first 100 ms of an occluded breath) >3.5–4 cmH₂O = high drive.
Detect effort: expiratory occlusion ΔPocc; Pmus ≈ 0.75 × ΔPocc. Large oesophageal swings (ΔPes >15). On NIV: Vt >9.5 mL/kg PBW (Carteaux 2016).

Manage the drive: treat its causes (fever, acidosis, pain, anxiety, hypoxaemia); sedation and opioids to lower drive; adjust support; intubate early if failing on NIV; partial or full paralysis in severe cases.
V4-020.src: Brochard L, AJRCCM 2017 (P-SILI); Telias I, AJRCCM 2018 (P0.1); Bertoni M, Crit Care 2019 (Pocc); Carteaux G, Crit Care Med 2016

V4-021.topic: Recruitment manoeuvres: ART and the guidelines
V4-021.q: Tell us about recruitment manoeuvres. What did ART show, and what do the guidelines say?
a: Aim: open collapsed alveoli with a brief high pressure, then hold them open with PEEP.
Types: sustained inflation (e.g. 40 cmH₂O for 40 s) or stepwise (staircase) rise in PEEP.
ART (2017, n = 1,010): stepwise RM plus PEEP titrated to best compliance → 28-day mortality 55.3 vs 49.3% (harm); more barotrauma and hypotension.
Why harm: the lung that doesn't recruit gets over-stretched; high pressure drops venous return and loads the RV.
ESICM 2023: strongly against prolonged high-pressure RMs; weakly against routine brief RMs.
ATS 2024: strongly against prolonged RMs.
V4-021.src: ART investigators, JAMA 2017; Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023 (ESICM); Qadir N, AJRCCM 2024 (ATS)

V4-022.q: Does lung-protective ventilation help patients without ARDS?
a: Rule: 6–8 mL/kg PBW; avoid >10 mL/kg; keep driving pressure low.
Serpa Neto 2012 meta-analysis (mostly RCTs): lower Vt in non-ARDS patients linked to less lung injury and lower mortality.
PReVENT (2018, n = 961): low (4–6, starting at 6) vs intermediate (8–10, starting at 10) mL/kg PBW in ventilated patients without ARDS → ventilator-free days the same; no harm, no benefit.
So: no need to force 6 mL/kg if it causes distress or high sedation needs, but avoid large breaths.
In the OR: lower Vt with PEEP reduces postoperative pulmonary complications (IMPROVE 2013).
V4-022.src: Serpa Neto A, JAMA 2012 (meta-analysis); Simonis FD, JAMA 2018 (PReVENT); Futier E, NEJM 2013 (IMPROVE)

V4-023.q: Explain APRV. Why is it not first-line?
a: Settings: P-high (high pressure most of the cycle), T-high (several seconds), P-low (often 0), T-low (brief release, about 0.4–0.8 s, ended when expiratory flow falls to 50–75% of peak).
Idea: the long high pressure recruits; the patient breathes spontaneously on top; CO₂ leaves during the releases; the short release traps gas to keep alveoli open.
Risks: release volumes are not controlled and can be large; CO₂ can rise; vigorous spontaneous effort on a high pressure adds hidden lung stress.
Evidence: no large trial shows lower mortality; one small single-centre trial was positive and not replicated.
So: a rescue option in experienced hands, not first-line.
V4-023.src: Zhou Y, Intensive Care Med 2017 (single-centre APRV RCT); Habashi NM, Crit Care Med 2005

V4-024.q: What did the 2023 global definition of ARDS change from Berlin?
a: Berlin kept: within 1 week of a known insult; bilateral opacities; not fully explained by heart failure or fluid; P/F ≤300 on PEEP ≥5.
Why PEEP ≥5 in Berlin: PEEP changes P/F, so a floor makes the ratio comparable between patients.
2023 adds non-intubated patients: on HFNO ≥30 L/min or NIV/CPAP ≥5.
SpO₂/FiO₂ ≤315 allowed in place of P/F, when SpO₂ ≤97%.
Lung ultrasound accepted to show bilateral changes.
Resource-limited settings: no PEEP or flow requirement; S/F and ultrasound enough.
Severity in intubated patients unchanged: mild ≤300, moderate ≤200, severe ≤100 (S/F ≤315 / ≤235 / ≤148).
V4-024.src: Matthay MA, AJRCCM 2024 (2023 global definition); ARDS Definition Task Force, JAMA 2012 (Berlin)

V4-025.topic: Setting PEEP in ARDS: methods and evidence
V4-025.q: How do you titrate PEEP in ARDS? What's the evidence?
a: Methods: ARDSNet PEEP–FiO₂ table (higher table for moderate–severe); best compliance (decremental trial: compliance peaks, PEEP 2 above); oesophageal pressure (end-expiratory PL ≥0); EIT; stress index; lung ultrasound.
Trials: ALVEOLI (2004), LOVS and EXPRESS (2008): higher vs lower PEEP, no mortality difference.
Briel 2010 meta-analysis: higher PEEP lowered mortality when P/F ≤200 (moderate–severe), not in mild.
EPVent-2 (2019): Pes-guided, neutral.
Guidelines: ATS 2024 conditional for higher PEEP without prolonged RMs in moderate–severe ARDS; ESICM 2023 no recommendation for any one method.
Bedside check: if raising PEEP lowers driving pressure, lung recruited; if ΔP rises, it over-stretched.
V4-025.src: ARDSNet ALVEOLI, NEJM 2004; Meade MO, JAMA 2008 (LOVS); Mercat A, JAMA 2008 (EXPRESS); Briel M, JAMA 2010; Beitler JR, JAMA 2019 (EPVent-2); Qadir N, AJRCCM 2024 (ATS); Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023 (ESICM)

V4-026.q: What oxygen target do you use in ventilated patients? What do the trials show?
a: Conservative vs liberal: ICU-ROX (2020, n = 1,000), HOT-ICU (2021, PaO₂ 60 vs 90; 90-day mortality 42.9 vs 42.4%), UK-ROX (2025, n ≈ 16,500, SpO₂ 90% vs usual; 35.4 vs 34.9%) → no mortality difference.
ARDS: SpO₂ 88–95% (PaO₂ 55–80). Going lower is not safer: LOCO₂ (2020) stopped early with a harm signal at PaO₂ 55–70.
Avoid hyperoxia: oxygen toxicity, absorption collapse, vasoconstriction.
Exceptions: carbon monoxide (100%), pneumothorax being absorbed, post-arrest (avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia).
V4-026.src: ICU-ROX, NEJM 2020; Schjørring OL, NEJM 2021 (HOT-ICU); UK-ROX, JAMA 2025; Barrot L, NEJM 2020 (LOCO2)

V4-027.q: HFNO vs NIV in hypoxaemic respiratory failure: how does HFNO work, and what's the evidence?
a: Mechanism: high flow (up to 60 L/min) matches the patient's peak inspiratory flow, so FiO₂ is reliable; washes CO₂ out of the upper airway (dead-space washout); small PEEP (about 1 cmH₂O per 10 L/min, mouth closed); warm humid gas, comfortable.
FLORALI (2015, n = 310): intubation 38% (HFNO) vs 47% (O₂) vs 50% (NIV), not significant; 90-day mortality lower with HFNO.
ESICM 2023: HFNO over conventional oxygen (strong); no recommendation for or against NIV over HFNO.
Monitor: ROX index (SpO₂/FiO₂ ÷ RR): ≥4.88 at 2, 6 or 12 h predicts success; <3.85 at 12 h predicts failure.
Delayed intubation harms: decide early if failing.
V4-027.src: Frat JP, NEJM 2015 (FLORALI); Roca O, AJRCCM 2019 (ROX); Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023 (ESICM)

V4-028.q: When will you put this patient on VV-ECMO, and when not?
a: First optimise: Vt 6 mL/kg, plateau ≤30, PEEP, prone, paralysis if needed.
EOLIA criteria despite that: P/F <50 for >3 h, or <80 for >6 h, or pH <7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥60 for >6 h (with RR raised to 35 and plateau ≤32).
Ventilated <7 days (longer = worse outcome, relative contraindication).
Contraindications: irreversible disease with no exit (no transplant option), unable to anticoagulate, severe immunosuppression, moribund, very severe brain injury.
EOLIA (2018, n = 249): 60-day mortality 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09; not significant but supported by Bayesian re-analysis and crossover.
Guidelines: ESICM 2023 strong for VV-ECMO in selected severe ARDS at experienced centres; ATS 2024 conditional.
V4-028.src: Combes A, NEJM 2018 (EOLIA); Goligher EC, JAMA 2018 (Bayesian re-analysis); Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023; Qadir N, AJRCCM 2024

V4-029.q: How do you safely intubate a critically ill hypoxaemic patient?
a: Expect collapse: low oxygen reserve (shunt, small FRC), low blood pressure after induction and positive pressure.
Pre-oxygenate with NIV: PREOXI (2024): hypoxaemia during intubation 9.1 vs 18.5% with facemask oxygen.
Video laryngoscope first: DEVICE (2023): first-pass success 85.1 vs 70.8%.
Haemodynamics: fluid if responsive, pressor drawn up or running, cautious induction dose (ketamine or etomidate).
Bougie, apnoeic oxygenation, the most experienced operator, a failed-airway plan.
After the tube: lung-protective settings from the first breath; check placement with waveform capnography.
V4-029.src: Gibbs KW, NEJM 2024 (PREOXI); Prekker ME, NEJM 2023 (DEVICE)

V4-030.q: How will you ventilate this ARDS patient? Give your starting settings.
a: Calculate PBW: men 50 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4); women 45.5 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4).
Start Vt at 6 mL/kg PBW (range 4–8); plateau ≤30; ΔP ≤15.
PEEP and FiO₂ by the ARDSNet table (higher table if moderate–severe); SpO₂ 88–95%.
Rate up to 35 to hold minute ventilation; accept CO₂ while pH ≥7.20.
Plateau still >30: step Vt down to 4 mL/kg; check for a stiff chest wall (Pes) and auto-PEEP.
ATS 2024: higher PEEP without prolonged RMs (conditional); ESICM 2023 no recommendation on PEEP; both strongly against prolonged high-pressure RMs.
Then: prone if P/F <150; adjuncts; ECMO by criteria.
V4-030.src: ARDSNet, NEJM 2000 (ARMA); Qadir N, AJRCCM 2024 (ATS); Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023 (ESICM)

V4-031.q: Spotter: CT chest of a supine ARDS patient. Describe it.
a: Three zones from front to back: anterior aerated (near normal) lung → middle ground glass → dependent (posterior) dense consolidation.
The aerated front part is the baby lung: small, not stiff.
The back collapses under the weight of the oedematous lung above it: the sponge lung.
Proning turns this: the dorsal lung reopens and the collapse moves to the now-dependent front, where there is less lung.
CT also shows: barotrauma (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum), effusions, the original cause (pneumonia).
V4-031.src: Gattinoni L, Intensive Care Med 2005 (baby lung); Gattinoni L, AJRCCM 2001 (CT and prone)

V4-032.topic: Prone positioning: why, when, when to stop
V4-032.q: Why does prone positioning work? When do you start and stop it?
a: Why: the dorsal lung reopens while perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so V/Q matches better; stretch spreads more evenly (less over-distension); RV afterload falls.
When: P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥5, early (within 36 h), sessions ≥16 h.
PROSEVA (2013, n = 466): 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%.
Stop when, after ≥4 h supine, P/F ≥150 on PEEP ≤10 and FiO₂ ≤0.6.
Contraindications: unstable spine, raised ICP, open abdomen or recent sternotomy, massive haemoptysis.
Complications: pressure sores (face), tube displacement, line loss.
ESICM 2023 strong for (P/F <150, ≥16 h).
V4-032.src: Guérin C, NEJM 2013 (PROSEVA); Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023 (ESICM)

V4-033.q: What is electrical impedance tomography and how is it used?
a: Principle: a belt of 16–32 electrodes round the chest passes small currents; air raises impedance, fluid lowers it; the machine builds a live cross-sectional image of where ventilation goes.
Radiation-free, bedside, continuous, regional (front vs back, left vs right).
PEEP titration: during a decremental PEEP trial, plot collapse (rising as PEEP falls) and over-distension (rising as PEEP rises); choose the PEEP where the two curves cross.
Also shows: pneumothorax (sudden loss of ventilation on one side), pendelluft, the effect of proning, regional ventilation–perfusion with a saline bolus.
Limits: one slice of the chest; no proven outcome benefit; cost.
V4-033.src: Frerichs I, Thorax 2017 (TREND consensus); Costa EL, Intensive Care Med 2009 (EIT PEEP titration)

V4-034.q: What is the non-ventilatory management of severe ARDS? Where do ESICM and ATS differ?
a: Prone: both strong for.
Fluids: conservative once out of shock (FACTT: more ventilator-free days).
Neuromuscular blockade: ATS 2024 conditional for early, in severe ARDS; ESICM 2023 against routine continuous infusion (ROSE 2019: 42.5 vs 42.8%, no benefit).
Steroids: ATS 2024 conditional for. DEXA-ARDS (2020, n = 277): dexamethasone 20 mg daily days 1–5, then 10 mg days 6–10, for P/F ≤200 on PEEP ≥10 and FiO₂ ≥0.5 → 60-day mortality 21 vs 36%.
VV-ECMO: ESICM strong, ATS conditional, by EOLIA criteria.
ECCO₂R: strongly against (ESICM 2023); REST (2021, n = 412): 41.5 vs 39.5%, stopped for futility, more adverse events.
Inhaled nitric oxide: rescue only; improves oxygenation, not survival.
V4-034.src: Wiedemann HP, NEJM 2006 (FACTT); ROSE, NEJM 2019; Villar J, Lancet Respir Med 2020 (DEXA-ARDS); McNamee JJ, JAMA 2021 (REST); Qadir N, AJRCCM 2024; Grasselli G, Intensive Care Med 2023

MV03|ASYN-12: Flow asynchrony has two forms: flow starvation (too little flow, scooped pressure curve) and excess flow (too much, early pressure overshoot).
NEURO06B|PADIS-17: Avoid dexmedetomidine when deep sedation is needed or with bradycardia or heart block (A2B 2025: more severe bradycardia vs propofol).

questions.text: Differentiate pressure control and volume control ventilation.

steps.bridge: The ventilator can fix only one variable at a time; the others follow. Next: what limits and ends each breath →

lesson.text:
Every breath into a relaxed, passive lung obeys one rule. The pressure in the airway is made of three parts added together. The first is the push through the tubes, which is the flow multiplied by the resistance. The second is the stretch, which is the volume divided by the compliance. And the third is the PEEP underneath. This is called the equation of motion. Take a moment with it, because almost everything in this package sits on top of it.

Now notice something. The resistance and the compliance belong to the patient. You don't set them. So pressure, volume and flow are tied together by the lung itself. If you fix one side of that equation, the lung decides the other side.

[[That's why the ventilator can control only one variable at a time. Whatever you fix, the lung decides the rest.]]

That one variable is called the control variable. It's the variable the ventilator manipulates to cause inspiration.

Fix the pressure, and you have pressure control. The pressure waveform is fixed, and the volume and flow are free to vary. If the lung gets stiffer, or the tube gets narrower, the same pressure now buys less volume.

Fix the volume, and you have volume control. And here the flow is fixed too, because flow is simply volume divided by time. So the volume and flow waveforms are fixed, and the pressure varies. The machine pushes whatever pressure it takes. A stiffer lung shows up as a higher pressure.

There is a third kind, time control, where the inspiratory and expiratory times are fixed and both volume and pressure vary. You'll meet it less. Just know that it exists.

Picture squeezing a balloon through a straw. Fix how hard you squeeze, and the straw and the balloon decide how much air goes in. Fix how much air must go in, and the straw and the balloon decide how hard you'll have to squeeze.

You've lived this in theatre. A patient in steep head-down tilt with a pneumoperitoneum, on volume control. The peak pressure climbs. Switch him to pressure control and the pressure stays put, but now watch the tidal volume fall.

[[So in volume control, the pressure is the answer. In pressure control, the volume is the answer.]] Hold on to that sentence. It will explain every difference that follows.

Now, if the machine fixes one thing during the breath, what holds the breath at its ceiling, and what tells it to stop?

steps.bridge: VC is cycled by volume, PC by time. Next: how each looks on the pressure and flow scalars →

lesson.text:
Every breath answers two questions. What is held at a ceiling while the breath goes in? That's the limit. And what ends the breath? That's the cycle.

In volume control, the breath is limited by flow. The flow is held at the value you set. And it's cycled by volume. The moment the set volume is in, the breath ends. Think of a tap that shuts off as soon as the glass is full.

In pressure control, the breath is limited by pressure. And it's cycled by time. When the set inspiratory time is up, the breath ends, whatever volume has gone in. That's a kitchen timer.

And pressure support, which you'll meet every day. It's also limited by pressure. But it's cycled by flow. The breath ends when the patient's own inspiratory flow falls, usually to twenty-five percent of its peak.

[[Volume control ends on volume. Pressure control ends on time. Pressure support ends on flow.]]

Here is the distinction that makes this useful. Ending on pressure, volume or time is machine cycling. Ending on flow is patient cycling. That's why pressure support follows the patient. And it's why, in COPD, where the flow falls slowly, the cycle is often set higher, at forty to fifty percent of the peak flow. The breath ends sooner, and he has more time to breathe out.

And notice the link to the last card. In pressure control, time ends the breath. So if flow hasn't yet fallen to zero when the time runs out, a longer inspiratory time would have given more volume.

Now let's see how all of this looks on the screen.

steps.bridge: Square flow means VC; square pressure with decaying flow means PC. Next: how each behaves in assist-control →

lesson.text:
Picture the two sets of traces side by side, A and B. Pressure on top, flow below. The picture is on your screen if you want it.

{{pic}}

Start with volume control. The machine drives a constant flow. So the flow trace is a square. It jumps up, stays flat, and stops. And while that steady flow fills the lung, the pressure keeps climbing, because the more volume is in, the more stretch there is. So the pressure is a ramp, rising to its peak at the very end of the breath. That's trace A.

Now pressure control. The machine holds one pressure. So the pressure trace is a square, a box. But look at the flow. It's fastest right at the start, and then it falls away. Why?

Because flow is driven by a gap. The gap between the machine's pressure and the pressure inside the alveoli. At the start of the breath, the alveoli are empty, the gap is at its biggest, and gas rushes in. As they fill, their pressure rises, the gap shrinks, and the flow decays. That's trace B.

[[Square flow with a rising pressure ramp is volume control. Square pressure with a decaying flow is pressure control.]]

Volume control is a ramp. Pressure control is a box.

Now the panel's favourite twist. Which one gives the higher mean airway pressure? Most residents say volume control, because its peak is higher. That's the trap.

Mean airway pressure is the area under the pressure curve. The volume control ramp climbs to a high peak, but it spends much of the breath lower down. The pressure control box peaks lower, but stays up for the whole breath. So for the same breath, the box holds more area.

[[Pressure control has the lower peak, but the higher mean airway pressure.]] And mean airway pressure, together with the FiO2, is one of the main drivers of oxygenation. That's why the professor cares about this answer.

One last point about that decaying flow. It suits high airway resistance, and it suits a patient with high demand, because flow follows the gap, and a hungry patient widens that gap himself. We'll come back to that when we talk about asynchrony.

Now let's add the patient. What happens when he starts triggering the breaths himself?
lesson.cap: Trace A is volume control, trace B is pressure control. Pressure on top, flow below.

steps.bridge: In VC the volume is fixed and pressure varies; in PC the reverse. Next: which danger each hides, and which is better in ARDS →

lesson.text:
In assist-control, you set a minimum rate, and that rate is guaranteed. But every time the patient makes an effort and triggers the ventilator, he gets a full set breath. Identical to a controlled one. Not a small breath. A full one.

Now apply the first card. In volume assist-control, every breath delivers the same tidal volume at the same flow, and the inspiratory pressure varies. The inspiratory time simply follows from the flow and the volume. In pressure assist-control, every breath gets the same pressure for the same set time, and the tidal volume and the flow vary.

[[It's the same rule again. In volume assist-control, the volume is fixed and the pressure varies. In pressure assist-control, it's the reverse.]]

The advantage is easy to see. The machine does the work of every breath, so the work of breathing is low, and there's less asynchrony.

But now think of a patient who is anxious, or in pain, or acidotic, triggering fast. Every small effort buys a full-sized breath. His minute ventilation is his own rate multiplied by the machine's full tidal volume. So it overshoots. You get hyperventilation and a respiratory alkalosis.

And there is a second danger. If his effort is strong and lasts longer than the set breath, he can trigger a second breath before the first one is out. That's breath stacking. The lung receives nearly double the volume, and with it comes the risk of barotrauma. And a fast rate also shortens the time to breathe out, so gas is left behind in the lung. That trapped gas is auto-PEEP.

[[So assist-control rests the muscles. But a fast, strong patient can overshoot, stack his breaths, and trap gas.]]

So now you know how each mode behaves, with the patient passive and with the patient triggering. Which danger does each one hide? And which is better in ARDS?

Now let's put it all together, the way the panel wants to hear it.

In volume control, you set the tidal volume and the flow, and pressure is the result. So if the lung stiffens, or the tube blocks, the problem announces itself. The peak pressure rises, and the alarm rings. And volume control guarantees the minute ventilation.

In pressure control, you set the inspiratory pressure and the inspiratory time. The flow decelerates, and the tidal volume is the result. Now if the lung stiffens, nothing on the pressure trace changes at all. The tidal volume just falls. Silently.

Go back to our two patients. Patient A, on volume control, alarmed at four in the morning. Patient B, on pressure control, lost his tidal volume without a sound.

[[So the alarm must watch whatever the mode lets go. In volume control, the pressure alarms. In pressure control, the tidal volume and minute ventilation alarms.]]

So which do you choose? It's a trade-off. Volume control guarantees ventilation. Pressure control caps the peak pressure, and its decelerating flow may suit an active patient better.

And now the danger hidden inside pressure control. This is the one a good panel will push on. Pressure control caps the pressure the machine applies. But the patient can add his own. If he pulls hard during the breath, his effort adds to the set pressure. The pressure on the screen stays exactly where you set it. But the tidal volume grows, and so does the stretch on his lung.

[[The screen looks unchanged, while the lung is being stretched hard.]]

That's why you should not claim that pressure control protects the lung. Pressure control caps the airway pressure. It does not cap the stretch. We'll go much deeper into this when we reach transpulmonary pressure and self-inflicted lung injury.

The manufacturers tried to have it both ways, with dual modes such as pressure-regulated volume control. These give pressure-limited breaths that adjust themselves to deliver a target tidal volume.

And the final question. Which is better in ARDS?

[[Neither. There is no outcome difference between the two modes. What matters is a tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight, a plateau of thirty or below, and a driving pressure of fifteen or below, whichever mode delivers them.]]

The ARMA trial, the one that showed small breaths save lives, used volume control. But what saved lives was the size of the breath, not the mode that delivered it.

spine: What it is: in volume control I set tidal volume and flow, and pressure is the result. In pressure control I set pressure and inspiratory time, and volume is the result.
How to tell: volume control has square flow and a rising pressure ramp; pressure control has square pressure and decelerating flow, with a lower peak but higher mean pressure.
Why it matters: a stiffer lung shows as a rising peak in volume control, but as a silently falling tidal volume in pressure control. Set the alarms to match.
Trade-off: volume control guarantees minute ventilation; pressure control caps peak pressure and its decelerating flow may suit an active patient better.
Caution: in pressure control a strong patient effort adds to the set pressure, so tidal volume and lung stretch can be large while the screen looks unchanged.
In ARDS: no outcome difference between modes. What matters is **6 mL/kg PBW**, plateau **≤30** and driving pressure **≤15**, whichever mode delivers them.

open.text:
Let me start with two patients.

Patient A is on volume control. Through the night, his lungs slowly fill with oedema. At four in the morning the high-pressure alarm goes off, the nurse calls you, and you come and look.

Patient B has exactly the same lungs and exactly the same night. But he is on pressure control. The pressure alarm never sounds. The pressure trace looks calm. And by morning his tidal volume has quietly fallen, and his carbon dioxide has crept up.

Same disease. Same night. Two completely different screens.

Why? That is what this question is really about.

When the panel says differentiate pressure control and volume control, most residents give a list. One sets volume, the other sets pressure. That's true, but it's only the surface. What the professor is really checking is whether you understand one deeper idea. The ventilator can guarantee only one thing. The lung decides the rest. If you hold that idea, every difference follows by itself: the waveforms, the alarms, the hidden dangers, and the answer to which mode is better in ARDS.

So we'll build it in order. First, what a control variable is, and why there can only be one. Then what holds each breath at its ceiling, and what ends it. Then how each mode looks on the screen. Then what happens when the patient starts triggering the breaths himself. And finally, which danger each mode hides, and which one you'd choose in ARDS.

Let's begin with the rule that every breath has to obey.

close.text:
So let's bring it together, slowly.

The ventilator can fix only one thing. [[In volume control I set the tidal volume and the flow, and the pressure is the result. In pressure control I set the pressure and the inspiratory time, and the volume is the result.]]

Volume control ends when the volume is in. Pressure control ends when the time is up.

On the screen, volume control is square flow and a rising pressure ramp. Pressure control is square pressure and decaying flow, with a lower peak but a higher mean pressure.

When the lung stiffens, volume control shows you a rising peak, while pressure control lets the tidal volume fall in silence. So set your alarms to match the mode.

Volume control guarantees ventilation. Pressure control caps the peak pressure, and its flow may suit an active patient better. But in pressure control, a strong effort adds to the set pressure, and the lung can be stretched hard while the screen looks the same.

[[And in ARDS, the mode doesn't matter. Six millilitres per kilo, a plateau of thirty or below, a driving pressure of fifteen or below, whichever mode gets you there.]]

That's your answer to the panel. What each mode fixes, how to tell them apart, what each one hides, and what really matters in ARDS.

Now something to carry into the next lesson. We said that in volume control, the pressure is the answer. But that pressure is made of layers: the push through the tubes, the stretch, and the PEEP. What if you could take it apart, right at the bedside, and read the lung's compliance and the airway's resistance separately?

You can. With one button and half a second. That's where we go next.

questions.text: How do you calculate compliance and resistance at the bedside?

steps.bridge: An inspiratory hold splits peak into a resistance part and a stretch part. Next: what compliance means and its normal values →

lesson.text:
Look at the trace on your screen. A pressure-time curve in volume control, with a pause at the end of the breath. Three levels are marked.

{{pic}}

At the top, the peak inspiratory pressure. Below it, the plateau. At the bottom, the baseline, the PEEP.

Now, why is the peak higher than the plateau? Because during the breath, the ventilator's pressure is doing two jobs at once. Part of it is pushing gas through the tube and the airways. That's the transairway pressure, and it needs flow. The rest is holding the lung stretched open. That's the alveolar pressure, and it needs volume.

[[So the peak is two pressures added together: the push through the airways, and the pressure holding the volume in the lung.]]

Here's the trick. Press an inspiratory hold at the end of the breath. The ventilator pauses for about half a second, with no gas moving. And the moment flow stops, the pushing part falls to zero, because with no flow there is no resistance cost. What's left is the stretch, sitting on top of the PEEP. That's the plateau.

So now the two jobs are separated. The gap from peak to plateau is the airway part. The gap from plateau to PEEP is the lung and chest wall part. Normally, peak minus plateau is about five centimetres of water.

And the formulas simply follow. Resistance is pressure divided by flow. So you take the pushing part, peak minus plateau, and divide it by the flow. Compliance is volume divided by pressure. So you take the tidal volume and divide it by the stretch part, plateau minus PEEP.

[[Resistance is peak minus plateau, divided by flow. Compliance is tidal volume, divided by plateau minus PEEP.]]

You don't have to memorise those as formulas. Peak is push plus stretch. Plateau is stretch alone. Once you see that, the formulas write themselves.

Let's carry one patient through the next few cards. Volume control, a tidal volume of four hundred and fifty millilitres, a constant flow of sixty litres a minute, which is one litre a second. PEEP of ten. Peak of thirty-five. Plateau of twenty-five.

{{**Worked patient:** Vt 450 mL · flow 1 L/s · PEEP 10 · peak 35 · plateau 25
Resistance = (35 − 25) ÷ 1 = **10 cmH₂O/L/s**
Compliance = 450 ÷ (25 − 10) = **30 mL/cmH₂O**}}

Keep those numbers in your head. And in ARDS, remember the plateau has its own ceiling. Keep it at thirty or below.

Now, what does compliance actually mean, and what is normal?
lesson.cap: Peak = resistive + elastic + PEEP. The hold removes the resistive layer and leaves the plateau.

steps.bridge: Compliance is volume per unit pressure; ARDS falls below 20. Next: the resistance formula and its normal values →

lesson.text:
Compliance is the change in volume for each unit change in pressure. How much volume each centimetre of water buys you. Its opposite, its reciprocal, is elastance, the stiffness.

Breathing spontaneously, a normal person's compliance is wide, fifty to one hundred and seventy millilitres per centimetre of water. On a ventilator it's lower. In men about forty to fifty. In women about thirty-five to forty. And in ARDS, below twenty.

Why lower on a ventilator? Because the patient is lying flat and sedated, with some lung already collapsed. Less open lung means less volume for the same pressure.

Now our patient. Four hundred and fifty, divided by twenty-five minus ten, which is fifteen. That gives a compliance of thirty. That's low.

But low what? This is where you show the panel you understand it. Compliance has two parts, the lung and the chest wall, and they are stretched together. Their stiffness adds up, so the total is lower than either one alone. The lung part falls in ARDS. The chest wall part falls in kyphoscoliosis, in obesity, or with a tense abdomen. [[A stiff chest wall lowers the total compliance, even when the lung itself is fine.]] So this one number can't tell you which part is to blame. For that you need the pressure map, which comes in a later lesson.

And here's the deeper point. In early ARDS, the lung that's still open behaves almost normally. There's just far less of it. The same pressure fills a smaller space. It's like the same push going into one balloon instead of three.

[[So in early ARDS, a low compliance mostly means a small lung, not a stiff one.]] In fibrosis, the lung really is stiff. That difference will matter a great deal when we reach driving pressure.

One more distinction, because the panel likes it. Static compliance uses the plateau. Dynamic compliance uses the peak, so it mixes in the airway resistance.

Now the other half of the formula. Resistance.

steps.bridge: Resistance needs the flow stated; about 6 when intubated. Next: why the plateau is best measured in volume control →

lesson.text:
Resistance is peak minus plateau, divided by the flow. Its unit is centimetres of water per litre per second.

And here's the rule most residents forget. [[Resistance is meaningless unless the flow is stated.]] The same peak-to-plateau gap at a different flow means a different resistance.

The normal value breathing spontaneously is about zero point six to two point four. Intubated, about six, because the tube is narrower than the trachea.

Our patient. Thirty-five minus twenty-five is ten, divided by one litre a second. A resistance of ten. That's on the high side.

What changes resistance most during ventilation? The diameter of the airway. In smooth, laminar flow, resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius. Halve the radius and you need about sixteen times the pressure for the same flow. That's why secretions or bronchospasm show up so quickly as a higher peak. The causes of a rise are bronchospasm, secretions, mucosal oedema, and a kinked or narrow tube.

So why do we insist on volume control for all of this?

steps.bridge: Plateau needs zero flow and square-wave flow for a clean drop. Next: how to read peak and plateau together at the bedside →

lesson.text:
The plateau is the airway pressure under static, no-flow conditions. It's the elastic recoil of the volume sitting in the alveoli. That's why it's an index of compliance.

And it's best measured in volume control. Why? Because volume control gives a constant, square flow. So at the end of the breath there is a known flow, and when you hold, the pressure makes a clear drop from peak to plateau. You can see the gap, and you know exactly which flow to divide it by.

In pressure control, the flow has already been decaying throughout the breath. By the end it may be close to zero, and peak and plateau almost merge. The airway part is hidden, and there is no single flow to divide by.

[[Square flow gives a clean drop. That clean drop is what lets you separate the airway from the lung.]]

And if that gap from peak to plateau is wide, it means high airway resistance, as in severe bronchospasm.

One honest caution. The hold only tells the truth if the patient is relaxed. If he's pulling or pushing during the pause, the plateau is wrong.

Now let's use all of this to answer the nurse.

Go back to two in the morning. The peak has jumped from twenty-five to forty. You press the inspiratory hold. And now you look at one thing, the plateau.

Remember, the peak contains both the push and the stretch. The plateau contains only the stretch.

So if the peak has risen and the plateau hasn't moved, the extra pressure is all in the pushing path. [[Peak up, plateau unchanged, is a resistance problem.]] Think of the tube and the airways. Bronchospasm. Secretions. A kinked or bitten tube.

If both the peak and the plateau have risen together, and the gap between them is unchanged, the stretch itself has gone up. [[Peak and plateau up together is a compliance problem.]] The lung or the chest has become stiffer, or smaller. Think of ARDS, pulmonary oedema, a pneumothorax, a tube slipped into one main bronchus, or abdominal distension.

Why are a pneumothorax and a mainstem intubation in that second group? Because both of them shrink the lung available to the same breath. The breath now goes into less lung, so its stretch rises.

And if both fall, gas is escaping. A leak, or a disconnection.

{{Peak | Plateau | Problem
Up | Same | Resistance (tube, airways)
Up | Up (gap same) | Compliance (lung, chest wall)
Down | Down | Leak or disconnection}}

[[The gap is the airway. The plateau is the lung.]]

Now the honest caution that a sharp panel will test. At the end of breathing out, do an expiratory hold as well. If gas is trapped in the lung, that trapped pressure, the auto-PEEP, shows up and adds to the set PEEP. The sum is the total PEEP, and that's the number you must put in the compliance formula. If you use only the set PEEP, the stretch part looks bigger than it really is. Then compliance looks worse than it truly is, and the driving pressure looks higher. And the plateau, as always, is only true in a passive patient.

spine: What I do: in volume control with constant flow, a passive patient and an end-inspiratory hold, I read peak, plateau and PEEP.
Resistance: (peak minus plateau) divided by flow in L/s. Normal is about **6 cmH2O/L/s** when intubated. It is meaningless unless the flow is stated.
Compliance: tidal volume divided by (plateau minus PEEP). Normal on a ventilator is about **40–50 mL/cmH2O** in men; below **20** in ARDS.
Why: peak is the pressure to push gas through the airways plus the pressure to hold the volume in the lung. The hold separates the two.
Reading it: peak up with plateau unchanged is a resistance problem (bronchospasm, secretions, kinked tube). Both up is a compliance problem (ARDS, oedema, pneumothorax).
Caution: do an expiratory hold and use total PEEP. Using set PEEP alone with auto-PEEP present makes compliance look worse and driving pressure higher than they are.

open.text:
Let me start with a call.

It's two in the morning. Your patient's peak pressure has jumped from twenty-five to forty. The nurse is standing at the bedside asking you one question. Is it the tube, or is it the lung?

It matters, because the two need completely different hands. A plug of mucus needs suction, and a bitten tube needs a bite block. Bronchospasm needs a bronchodilator. A pneumothorax needs a drain. And you have one button on the ventilator that will tell you which world you're in, in about half a second.

This question sounds like a formula question. Compliance equals this, resistance equals that. And yes, the panel wants the formulas. But what the professor is really checking is three things. Do you know why the formulas work? Do you know the conditions you need to measure them properly? And do you know what the numbers tell you to do?

A resident who recites the formula, but measures it in a patient who is breathing hard on pressure support, without stating the flow, has produced a number that means nothing. That's the trap this question sets.

In the last lesson, we said that in volume control, the pressure is the answer. Today, we take that answer apart.

So here's the plan. First, the hold that splits the peak pressure into its parts. Then compliance, what it means and its normal values. Then resistance and its values. Then why you measure all this in volume control. And finally, how to read peak and plateau together, so you can answer that nurse at two in the morning.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[In volume control, with constant flow, in a passive patient, I do an end-inspiratory hold and read the peak, the plateau and the PEEP.]]

Why does that work? Because the peak is the pressure to push gas through the airways plus the pressure to hold the volume in the lung. The hold stops the flow and separates the two.

Resistance is peak minus plateau, divided by the flow in litres per second. About six when intubated. And it means nothing unless you state the flow.

Compliance is tidal volume divided by plateau minus PEEP. About forty to fifty on a ventilator in men, and below twenty in ARDS.

Then read the pattern. [[Peak up with the plateau unchanged is a resistance problem. Both up together is a compliance problem.]]

And the caution: do an expiratory hold too, and use the total PEEP, or auto-PEEP will distort your compliance.

That's your answer. What you do, the two formulas with their normal values, why they work, how to read them, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Today we read three numbers from one paused breath. Yet the ventilator is drawing the whole breath for you, every moment, in curves of pressure and flow. And those curves tell you far more than three numbers can. The mode, the airways, trapped gas, and whether the patient and the machine are fighting each other.

So what happens when the examiner turns the screen towards you, points at those curves, and says, interpret? That's next.

questions.text: Spotter - pressure-time and flow-time scalars. Interpret.

steps.bridge: Pressure and flow are measured; volume is calculated from flow. Next: how to tell the mode from the shapes →

lesson.text:
The ventilator shows you three curves against time. Pressure, flow and volume.

But they're not equal. [[Pressure and flow are measured. Volume is calculated.]] The machine measures flow, moment by moment, and adds it up over time. So the volume is the area under the flow curve.

By convention, inspiratory flow is drawn above the baseline, and expiratory flow below it.

Now, why does that matter in a spotter? Because if volume comes from adding up flow, then the volume curve should rise during the breath, and come all the way back to zero by the end of expiration. Everything that went in should come out.

If the volume trace doesn't return to baseline, the expired volume was less than the inspired. [[A volume curve that fails to return to baseline means a leak, or gas trapped in the lung.]]

Now the first real step of every spotter. Name the mode.

steps.bridge: Square flow is volume control; square pressure with decaying flow is pressure control. Next: what obstruction looks like on flow →

lesson.text:
You've met these two shapes already. Square flow with a rising pressure ramp is volume control. A square pressure box with a decaying flow is pressure control, because flow follows the shrinking gap between the machine and the filling alveoli. In a spotter, this is your first sentence, because every other sign is read against the mode.

{{pic}}
lesson.cap: A: volume control, square flow and a pressure ramp. B: pressure control, a pressure box and decaying flow.

steps.bridge: Expiratory flow not reaching zero means air trapping and auto-PEEP. Next: which asynchronies to spot on the traces →

lesson.text:
Now look below the baseline, at expiration.

Here's the key idea. Breathing out is passive. The machine isn't doing it. Gas leaves because the stretched lung recoils, and it travels out through the airways. So the shape of the expiratory flow depends only on two things, the resistance and the compliance. Not on the mode. [[The expiratory limb is the lung telling you about itself, whatever mode you're in.]]

Now narrow the airways, as in asthma or COPD. Two things happen. The gas can't leave fast, so the peak expiratory flow is reduced. The curve is low. And it takes longer to empty, so expiration is prolonged. The curve is long.

And then the most important sign. If the next breath starts before the expiratory flow has come back to zero, the lung hasn't finished emptying. Some gas is still inside. And that trapped gas keeps the pressure in the alveoli above the set PEEP at the end of expiration.

{{pic}}

[[Expiratory flow that doesn't reach zero before the next breath means air trapping, and auto-PEEP.]]

Think of a bath that's still draining when you turn the tap on again. Do that breath after breath, and the water level creeps up.

You've seen this in theatre. The bronchospastic asthmatic, ventilated fast. The trapped gas raises the pressure inside the chest, squeezes the great veins, and cuts the venous return. So his pressures creep up and his blood pressure falls.

How do you confirm it? An expiratory hold. The trapped pressure spreads to the airway and shows up as total PEEP.

And the fix follows from the bath. Give more time to empty, and less water to empty. Lower the rate first. Then shorten the inspiration, or reduce the tidal volume.

Now, the fourth step. The patient himself.
lesson.cap: Normal expiratory flow returns to zero. Obstructed flow is low, long, and cut off by the next breath.

steps.bridge: Three classic patterns: ineffective effort, double trigger, flow starvation. Next: why ineffective effort happens →

lesson.text:
Three classic patterns to name on sight.

{{pic}}

First, on the flow curve. A bump in the expiratory flow, moving towards the baseline, with no breath delivered. The patient tried, and the machine didn't notice. [[That's ineffective effort.]]

Second, also on flow. Two inspirations, one straight after the other, with no real expiration in between. The patient's effort outlasted the set breath, and triggered a second one. [[That's double trigger.]]

Third, on the pressure curve in volume control. Instead of rising smoothly, the curve is concave, scooped, sucked down. [[That's flow starvation.]]

Now let's understand why each happens, starting with ineffective effort.
lesson.cap: Panel 1: ineffective effort. Panel 2: double trigger. Panel 3: flow starvation, a scooped pressure curve.

steps.bridge: Ineffective effort is mostly auto-PEEP or over-assistance, typically in COPD. Next: how to read and fix flow starvation →

lesson.text:
An ineffective effort is an inspiratory effort that fails to trigger the ventilator.

It's best seen on the flow waveform. A sudden bump in the expiratory flow, back towards the baseline. On the pressure trace, there's a small dip at the same moment. That's the patient's diaphragm pulling. And nothing follows.

{{pic}}

Why does it happen? To trigger a breath, the patient has to pull the airway pressure or flow past a threshold. Now add auto-PEEP. The alveoli are already sitting above the set PEEP. So before the ventilator can notice anything, his effort must first cancel out that trapped pressure. A weak effort never gets there.

It's like knocking on a door with a crowd leaning against it. You have to push the crowd back before the door even moves.

[[The classic mechanism of ineffective effort is auto-PEEP. The patient spends his effort cancelling trapped gas.]]

So the causes follow. Intrinsic PEEP, from a high tidal volume, a short expiratory time, or low recoil. Then excess assistance, too much pressure support or too big a tidal volume. Then a low drive, from over-sedation or a low carbon dioxide. And finally, an insensitive trigger.

And in whom? COPD above all. Floppy lungs with high compliance and narrow airways empty slowly, so trapping is commonest there.

Now here's the trap. You see a patient whose efforts are being missed, and the instinct is to give him more support. But too much support is itself a cause. Big breaths lower his drive, and leave less time to empty. So his next efforts are weaker, and start against even more trapped gas.

[[So for ineffective effort, reduce the auto-PEEP and the excess support, and check the sedation. More support often makes it worse.]]

Now the third pattern. The scooped curve.
lesson.cap: Panel 1 shows it: a bump in the expiratory flow towards baseline, and no breath delivered.

lesson.text:
In volume control, the flow is fixed. Now imagine the patient wants more flow than the machine is giving. He's pulling hard. His own pull lowers the pressure in the airway during the breath. So the pressure curve sags. It's scooped, concave, instead of rising smoothly.

{{pic}}

[[A scooped pressure curve in volume control means flow starvation. The patient wants more flow than you're giving.]]

He's working hard against a machine that will not speed up. Like a waiter pouring slowly while you gulp.

The fix comes straight from the mode lesson. Increase the flow. Or switch to pressure control. Why does pressure control help? Because there, flow follows the pressure gap. His pull widens that gap, so the flow rises to meet his demand.

And in pressure modes, look for flow starvation on the flow waveform instead.

Now one more setting that shapes the curves in pressure modes, the rise time. It's the time taken to reach the target pressure at the start of the breath. It sets the slope of inspiration, and its usual range is one hundred to six hundred milliseconds.

Too fast for the patient's demand, and you see an early pressure spike, an overshoot. Too slow, and you see a scooped curve, under-filling early.

[[Rise time shapes the curve too. Too fast gives a spike. Too slow gives a scoop.]]

So who gets which? A fast rise for COPD. It puts the volume in early, and leaves more time to breathe out. A slower rise for restrictive and neuromuscular disease.
lesson.cap: Panel 3 shows it: the pressure curve in volume control is scooped, sucked down by the patient.

spine: First: name the mode. Square flow with a rising pressure ramp is volume control; square pressure with decelerating flow is pressure control.
Why: pressure and flow are measured, and volume is the area under the flow curve. A volume trace that does not return to baseline means a leak or air trapping.
Obstruction: low peak expiratory flow, prolonged expiration, and expiratory flow not reaching zero before the next breath, which means auto-PEEP.
Asynchrony: a bump in expiratory flow with no breath is ineffective effort; two breaths with no expiration is double trigger; a scooped pressure curve is flow starvation.
What I do: for flow starvation, increase flow or switch to pressure control. For ineffective effort, reduce auto-PEEP and excess support, and check sedation.
Caution: rise time (usual **100–600 ms**) shapes the curve too. Too fast gives an early spike; too slow gives a scooped curve.

open.text:
Picture the moment.

The examiner turns a ventilator screen towards you. Or hands you a printout. Two or three wavy lines. No numbers, no settings. And one word. Interpret.

Most residents freeze, or start describing shapes at random. A bump here, a dip there. That's the trap. The panel isn't checking whether you can see a bump. What the professor is really checking is whether you have a system. Whether you read the curves in a fixed order, the way you'd read an ECG, and whether each thing you see leads you to a cause and a fix.

So let me give you that order now, and then we'll build each step.

First, know what you're looking at. Which curves are measured, and which one is calculated. Second, name the mode. Third, look at expiration, because that's where obstruction and trapped gas show themselves. Fourth, look for the patient fighting the machine, the asynchronies. And fifth, say what you'd do.

Here's why these curves are worth so much. In the last lesson, we paused a breath and read three numbers. But the ventilator draws every breath, moment by moment. And the shapes carry the same physics we've been building. The push through the tubes. The stretch of the lung. The PEEP underneath. And now one more player, the patient himself, pulling against the machine.

So once you can read these curves, you're not memorising pictures. You're watching the equation of motion move.

Let's start with what's actually being measured.

close.text:
So let's put your system together.

[[First, name the mode. Square flow with a rising pressure ramp is volume control. Square pressure with decaying flow is pressure control.]]

Remember what you're looking at. Pressure and flow are measured. Volume is the area under the flow curve. And a volume trace that doesn't come back to baseline means a leak, or trapped gas.

Then look at expiration. Obstruction is a low peak expiratory flow, a long expiration, and a flow that doesn't reach zero before the next breath. That last sign means auto-PEEP.

Then look for the patient. [[A bump in expiratory flow with no breath is ineffective effort. Two breaths with no expiration is double trigger. A scooped pressure curve is flow starvation.]]

And say what you'd do. For flow starvation, more flow, or pressure control. For ineffective effort, less auto-PEEP, less excess support, and a look at the sedation.

And the caution. Rise time shapes the curve too. Too fast gives a spike, too slow gives a scoop.

That's a complete spotter answer, in order.

But here's what to carry into the next lesson. Every curve we've read today tells you about the airways, the trapped gas, and the patient. None of them tells you directly how hard each breath is stretching the lung that's actually open.

There is a single number for that. Every ventilator already shows it, hidden in plain sight. And of all the settings, it turned out to be the one most strongly linked to survival. It's called the driving pressure. That's next.

questions.text: What is driving pressure and why does it matter?

steps.bridge: The hold separates the resistive gap from the plateau-to-PEEP gap. Next: what each pressure difference actually reflects →

lesson.text:
So let's begin with the screen.

When you give a breath in volume control, the pressure on the ventilator climbs to a peak. That peak pressure is doing two jobs at once. Part of it is pushing gas through the tube and the airways. That part needs flow. The rest of it is holding the lung and chest wall stretched open. That part needs volume.

Now here's the trick. If you press an inspiratory hold at the end of the breath, the flow stops. And the moment flow stops, the pushing part disappears. [[What's left is only the stretch. That number is the plateau pressure.]]

And under everything, there's the pressure that never leaves, the PEEP, sitting there at the end of every breath.

[[So you have three layers stacked on top of each other. The push through the tubes. The stretch of the lung and chest wall. And the PEEP underneath.]]

Look at the picture on your screen if you'd like to see it. Peak at the top, plateau below it, PEEP at the bottom.

{{pic}}

The gap between peak and plateau tells you about the airways. If only the peak rises, think of the tube, secretions, or bronchospasm. If the peak and the plateau rise together, the problem is in the lung or the chest wall.

And one honest caution. The plateau is only true if the patient is relaxed during the hold. If he's pulling or pushing against the ventilator, the number lies. Keep that in mind. We'll come back to it.

Now, the next question. That plateau pressure, what does it actually stretch?
lesson.cap: Peak = push through the tubes + stretch + PEEP. The hold removes the push and leaves the plateau.

steps.bridge: Plateau minus PEEP is driving pressure: tidal volume over compliance. Next: its target and why it beats mL/kg →

lesson.text:
The ventilator can only see one pressure: the pressure in the airway. But inside the chest, that pressure is shared between two structures. Part of it stretches the lung. The rest of it moves the chest wall.

Think of blowing up a balloon inside a tight glass jar. You have to push harder, but not because the balloon is stiff. You're fighting the jar.

[[Only the lung's share injures the lung. That share is the alveolar pressure minus the pleural pressure, and we call it the transpulmonary pressure.]]

{{pic}}

In most patients, the chest wall takes a modest share, and the airway numbers are a fair guide. But in a patient with a heavy chest wall, with obesity, or with a tense, distended abdomen, the chest wall takes a much bigger share. In him, a plateau of thirty may be putting far less stress on the lung than it seems.

We can't measure pleural pressure directly at the bedside, so we use a balloon in the oesophagus as its stand-in. We'll meet that properly in another lesson.

For now, keep this one idea. [[The airway pressure is not the lung pressure. The chest wall is always taking its cut.]]

And that brings us to the heart of today's lesson. Why does the open lung matter so much?
lesson.cap: The ventilator shows airway pressure; the lung feels airway minus pleural pressure.

steps.bridge: It scales the breath to the baby lung and best predicted survival. Next: does the same hold in the operating room →

lesson.text:
Let's go back to the late nineteen eighties. Luciano Gattinoni put patients with severe ARDS into a CT scanner. And what he saw changed how we think about this disease.

He expected a stiff lung, uniformly damaged. Instead, he saw a lung that was mostly shut. The back was collapsed and flooded. Only a small band at the front was still aerated, and that aerated part behaved almost normally. In the sickest patients, it was the size of a young child's lung. He called it the baby lung.

[[So the ARDS lung is not stiff. It is small.]]

Now think about what that means for compliance. Compliance is how much volume you get for each unit of pressure. If the open lung is small, the same pressure fills a smaller space, and compliance falls. Gattinoni showed that compliance tracks the size of the aerated lung. So in early ARDS, a low compliance is really telling you how small the baby lung is.

Now put the pieces together.

[[Driving pressure is the plateau minus the PEEP. And it's exactly equal to the tidal volume divided by the compliance.]]

{{**Driving pressure = plateau − PEEP = tidal volume ÷ compliance**}}

Read that slowly. Tidal volume divided by compliance. The breath, divided by the size of the open lung.

That's why it's so powerful. Six millilitres per kilo is sized to the patient's height. [[Driving pressure is sized to the lung he actually has left.]]

Go back to our two patients. Patient A has a plateau of thirty and a PEEP of ten. His driving pressure is twenty. Patient B has a plateau of twenty-four and a PEEP of twelve. His driving pressure is twelve. Same tidal volume. But Patient A's breath is landing in a much smaller lung, and stretching it far harder.

And that's what Amato found. Of all the ventilator settings, driving pressure was the one most strongly linked to survival. For every seven centimetres of water higher, the risk of death rose by about forty percent. And here's the striking part. Lowering the tidal volume or raising the PEEP helped only when it brought the driving pressure down.

[[So the practical rule is simple. Keep the driving pressure at fifteen or below.]]

And there's a lovely bedside test hidden in this. When you raise the PEEP, watch the driving pressure. If it falls, the PEEP has opened more lung, and the same breath now spreads into a bigger space. That's recruitment. If it rises, the PEEP has only over-stretched the lung that was already open. Take it back down.

One honest caution, the kind a good panel will test. Amato's analysis showed a strong association, not proof that driving pressure causes the harm. And driving pressure includes the chest wall too, so it's not pure lung stress. It's the best simple number we have, not a perfect one.

Now you might ask: is this only about ARDS?

steps.bridge: In surgery too, PEEP helps only if it lowers driving pressure. Next: how to measure it when the patient is breathing →

lesson.text:
It isn't. The same idea was tested in the operating theatre, in patients with normal lungs having surgery. A meta-analysis of seventeen trials, about two thousand two hundred patients, found that a higher driving pressure during anaesthesia was linked to more lung complications after surgery. Each extra centimetre of water raised the odds by about sixteen percent.

And the PEEP finding held there too. When a change in PEEP pushed the driving pressure up, complications rose.

[[So the stretch on the open lung matters everywhere: in the ICU, in the theatre, in any lung you put a breath into.]] As an anaesthetist, you have been watching this number for years without calling it by name.

And now the last piece. Remember that caution about the plateau? Here it matters.

Many of your patients won't be passive. They'll be on pressure support, breathing for themselves. Can you still measure the driving pressure?

You can try an inspiratory hold. But if the patient is still pulling in during the hold, his own effort lowers the plateau, and the driving pressure reads falsely low. The true stretch is higher than the screen says. If he's pushing out, it reads high.

{{pic}}

[[So look at the shape of the hold. A flat, steady plateau you can trust. A sloping or wavy one, you can't.]]

And does the number matter in breathing patients? It does. In the large LUNG SAFE study, a driving pressure above fifteen on pressure support was also linked to higher mortality. [[The breath stretches the lung whoever generates it, the machine or the patient.]]
lesson.cap: Left: a flat plateau, patient relaxed, trust it. Right: sloping or wavy, patient still breathing, do not.

spine: What it is: driving pressure is plateau minus PEEP. It equals tidal volume divided by compliance: the stretch the breath puts on the open lung.
