The bedside check. [[If raising PEEP lowers the driving pressure, lung was recruited. If it rises, you're over-stretching.]]

The evidence. ALVEOLI, LOVS and EXPRESS, no mortality difference. Briel in twenty ten, benefit only when the P to F was two hundred or less. EPVent-2, guided by the balloon, neutral.

And the caution. ATS in twenty twenty-four suggests higher PEEP without prolonged recruitment manoeuvres. The ART trial showed higher mortality with stepwise recruitment.

That's your answer. What it is, who benefits, how, the bedside check, the evidence, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Patient A's new PEEP has lifted his saturation to ninety-four percent. The nurse asks, shall I push the oxygen up and get him to a hundred? It feels safer. Is it? How much oxygen is the right amount in a ventilated patient?

That's next.

questions.text: What oxygen target do you use in ventilated patients?

steps.bridge: FiO2 and mean airway pressure set oxygen; usual PaO2 goal 60 to 80. Next: is ARDS different →

lesson.text:
Oxygen and CO2 fail in different ways, so they're fixed by different knobs.

Start with CO2. It diffuses easily, so its removal depends almost entirely on how much air moves through the alveoli. That's the minute ventilation, the rate and the tidal volume. [[Ventilation is set by the rate and the tidal volume. Oxygenation is set by the FiO2 and the mean airway pressure.]]

The PaCO2 is roughly inversely proportional to the alveolar ventilation. Halve the ventilation, and the PaCO2 roughly doubles. And a bigger tidal volume does more than a faster rate, for the same proportion, because each breath loses a fixed dead space first.

Two things push the CO2 up from the other side. More CO2 being made, with fever, sepsis or overfeeding. And more dead space, in ARDS, lung injury, or a pulmonary embolism.

Now oxygen. It depends on two things. How much oxygen is in the alveolar gas, which is the FiO2. And how many alveoli are open to receive it. That second part is the mean airway pressure, the average pressure across the whole breath. PEEP raises it. A longer inspiratory time raises it. A higher inspiratory pressure raises it. And what mean airway pressure does is keep alveoli open.

Look at the picture on your screen.

{{pic}}

You saw it in the definition question. Now read it as a treatment chart. With no shunt, oxygen lifts the PaO2 steeply. At thirty percent shunt, the line flattens. And at fifty percent, even a hundred percent oxygen barely lifts it.

[[FiO2 helps poorly ventilated units. Only mean airway pressure, by opening alveoli, treats shunt.]]

Think of it this way. Clearing CO2 is emptying a room by opening the windows. Oxygen is filling the rooms, but only the ones with open doors.

And the usual targets? A PaCO2 of thirty-five to forty-five. A PaO2 of sixty to eighty. Why sixty? Because a PaO2 of sixty sits at a saturation of about ninety percent, the shoulder of the curve. Below it, saturation falls steeply. Above it, every extra unit of PaO2 adds very little.

So when the nurse wants a hundred percent, ask what's on the curve beyond ninety-five. Very little content. And a lot of FiO2.

Is ARDS any different?
lesson.cap: PaO₂ against FiO₂ at 0, 10, 30 and 50% shunt. At 50% shunt, even 100% oxygen barely lifts PaO₂.

steps.bridge: ARDSNet accepted lower: PaO2 55 to 80, SpO2 88 to 95%. Next: what target do we use on ECMO →

lesson.text: You met this card when we set Patient A's PEEP. The ARDSNet target was a PaO2 of fifty-five to eighty, or a saturation of eighty-eight to ninety-five percent. Lower than the usual sixty to eighty, and deliberately so. In ARDS, a higher PaO2 costs more FiO2 and more pressure on an injured lung, for very little extra content. So Patient A, at ninety-four percent, is already inside his band. The nurse can leave the oxygen alone.

steps.bridge: Even on ECMO we aim for about 92 to 96%, not 100%. Next: what about sepsis →

lesson.text:
Now jump ahead, to a version of Patient A's story where the ventilator can't support his lung at all, and he goes on VV-ECMO. We'll meet that decision later in this block. For now, one question. What saturation do you aim for when the circuit is doing the oxygenating?

First, how VV-ECMO oxygenates. Blood is drained from a large vein, passed through the oxygenator, and returned to the venous side. There it mixes with the rest of the venous blood coming back to the heart. So his arterial saturation depends on what share of his cardiac output passes through the oxygenator.

[[On VV-ECMO, the blood flow sets the oxygenation. The sweep gas sets the CO2 removal.]]

Think of a filter on a stream. The bigger the share of the stream that passes through the filter, the cleaner the water downstream. So if his cardiac output is very high, or blood recirculates straight from the return cannula back into the drainage cannula, his saturation falls at the same flow.

How is the flow controlled? By the pump speed. About three thousand revolutions a minute gives roughly three and a half to four litres a minute. But a centrifugal pump doesn't fix the flow. If filling drops, or the cannula sucks against the vessel wall, the flow falls at the same speed. So watch the measured flow, not the pump speed.

You start low, around two litres a minute, and step it up every few minutes, watching drainage, pressures and blood pressure.

And the target? [[The card's target on VV-ECMO is a saturation of about ninety-two to ninety-six percent. Most patients reach it at four to five litres a minute.]] Not a hundred. And many centres accept lower, around eighty-eight to ninety-two, as long as oxygen delivery is adequate.

Why not push higher? Because more flow has costs. Too much means high shear, and red cells break. That's haemolysis. Too little means slow blood in the circuit, and stagnant blood clots. So even with a machine that could drive his saturation to a hundred, we aim for enough.

As the lung recovers, you wean the oxygen fraction in the sweep gas, the flow, and the sweep. The final test is turning the sweep off. With no gas through the oxygenator, the circuit exchanges nothing, and what remains is his own lung's work.

So even on ECMO, enough, not more. What about the septic patient?

steps.bridge: Sepsis guidance is uncertain, with a possible harm signal from going low. Next: what the big trials show →

lesson.text:
Sepsis has its own guidance, from the Surviving Sepsis Campaign, and it's less certain than you'd like.

On oxygen targets, the twenty twenty-one guideline found insufficient evidence to recommend a conservative target. The newer update says to titrate to either a conservative or a liberal target, patient by patient. A saturation of ninety to ninety-six percent is what's usually taught.

Why the hesitation? Because of one analysis. In the ICU-ROX trial, the septic patients were looked at separately, after the fact, and the point estimates suggested possible harm from conservative oxygen. [[In sepsis, a post hoc signal suggests going low may harm. Liberal oxygen may be preferred.]] Post hoc, so not proof. But enough to stop you driving a septic patient down to eighty-eight.

The card's second line is about the device. For sepsis-induced hypoxaemic respiratory failure, the guideline suggests high-flow nasal oxygen over NIV, a weak recommendation. Keep that one. It's the bridge to the high-flow question.

Now the trials that settled the broad question.

Three big trials compared conservative with liberal oxygen in ICU patients.

ICU-ROX, in twenty twenty, a thousand ventilated patients. HOT-ICU, in twenty twenty-one, patients with acute hypoxaemic failure, a PaO2 target of sixty against ninety. And UK-ROX, in twenty twenty-five, about sixteen and a half thousand patients, a saturation of ninety percent against usual care.

The answer was the same in all three. [[No difference in mortality between conservative and liberal oxygen.]] In HOT-ICU, ninety-day mortality was forty-two point nine against forty-two point four percent. In UK-ROX, thirty-five point four against thirty-four point nine.

{{**ICU-ROX** 2020, n = 1,000 · **HOT-ICU** 2021, PaO₂ 60 vs 90: 42.9 vs 42.4% · **UK-ROX** 2025, n ≈ 16,500, SpO₂ 90% vs usual: 35.4 vs 34.9% → no mortality difference
**LOCO₂** 2020 (ARDS), PaO₂ 55–70: stopped early, harm signal}}

Why no difference? Most likely because both arms sat inside the safe band. You're comparing two points where the glass is already nearly full.

Then why not aim high, just in case? Because the extra oxygen isn't free. Oxygen free radicals injure the lung. High FiO2 washes out nitrogen, and behind a blocked airway the oxygen is absorbed into the blood, so the alveolus empties and collapses. That's absorption collapse. And high oxygen constricts arteries in the heart and the brain. [[Avoid hyperoxia: oxygen toxicity, absorption collapse and vasoconstriction, for no gain in content.]]

But here's the trap. If high isn't better, is low safer? In ARDS, no. LOCO2, in twenty twenty, aimed for a PaO2 of fifty-five to seventy in ARDS. It was stopped early, with more deaths in the conservative arm. [[In ARDS, lower is not safer. A PaO2 of fifty-five sits near the steep part of the curve and leaves no margin.]] A harm signal from a stopped trial, not proof. But it's why, in ARDS, you aim inside the band, and don't deliberately sit at its floor.

And then the exceptions, where you break the rule on purpose.

Carbon monoxide. A hundred percent oxygen, because a high PaO2 competes the carbon monoxide off the haemoglobin. Its half-life falls from about five hours on air to about one to one and a half hours on a hundred percent.

A pneumothorax being absorbed. The pleural gas is mostly nitrogen. High FiO2 washes nitrogen out of the blood, so the gradient steepens and the air is absorbed faster.

And after cardiac arrest. Here both ends hurt. Hyperoxia after reperfusion is linked to worse brain outcome, and hypoxia adds injury. So you avoid both.

spine: What I aim for: enough, not more. Roughly SpO2 92 to 96%, or 88 to 95% (PaO2 55 to 80) in ARDS.
Why: too little injures organs. Too much causes oxygen toxicity, absorption collapse and vasoconstriction, and does not fix shunt.
Evidence: ICU-ROX, HOT-ICU (90-day mortality 42.9 vs 42.4%) and UK-ROX (35.4 vs 34.9%) found no mortality difference between conservative and liberal.
Caution: in ARDS, lower is not safer. LOCO2 stopped early with a harm signal at PaO2 55 to 70. In sepsis, a post hoc signal suggested harm from conservative oxygen.
Exceptions: carbon monoxide (100%), a pneumothorax being absorbed, and after cardiac arrest, where both hypoxia and hyperoxia are avoided.

open.text:
Let me start with a question that sounds too simple to ask.

Patient A's saturation is ninety-four percent. The nurse wants to turn the oxygen up and get him to a hundred. Every instinct you have from the operating theatre says yes. A full saturation feels safe.

But think about what oxygen does in his lung. Much of his hypoxaemia is shunt, and extra oxygen barely touches shunt. So turning up the FiO2 buys him very little oxygen content. What it does buy is a higher FiO2 sitting on his injured lung, hour after hour.

[[Oxygen is a drug with a narrow useful band. Below it, organs starve. Above it, the extra adds almost nothing, and brings harm.]]

So where is that band? And here's what makes this a good viva question. Huge trials have now been done, one of them with more than sixteen thousand ICU patients, comparing conservative with liberal oxygen. And they keep giving the same answer, which is not the answer most residents expect.

What is the professor really checking? First, do you know which ventilator settings move oxygen, and which move CO2. Second, do you have a target, with a reason. Third, do you know the trials, especially the one in ARDS that went the other way. And fourth, do you know the patients where the rule is broken on purpose.

So here's the plan. Which settings change oxygenation. The target in ARDS. The target on ECMO. Sepsis. And then the big trials, and the exceptions.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[What I aim for is enough, not more. A saturation of roughly ninety-two to ninety-six percent. In ARDS, eighty-eight to ninety-five, a PaO2 of fifty-five to eighty.]]

Why? Too little injures organs. Too much brings oxygen toxicity, absorption collapse and vasoconstriction. And it doesn't fix shunt anyway.

The evidence. ICU-ROX. HOT-ICU, with ninety-day mortality of forty-two point nine against forty-two point four. And UK-ROX, thirty-five point four against thirty-four point nine. No mortality difference between conservative and liberal.

The caution. In ARDS, lower is not safer. LOCO2 stopped early with a harm signal at a PaO2 of fifty-five to seventy. And in sepsis, a post hoc signal suggested harm from conservative oxygen.

And the exceptions. Carbon monoxide, a hundred percent. A pneumothorax being absorbed. And after cardiac arrest, where you avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia.

That's your answer. What you aim for, why, the evidence, the caution, and the exceptions.

But here's something to carry forward. Let's rewind Patient A's story to the night he arrived, on high-flow oxygen, before anyone had decided on a tube. Was high flow the right choice? Should he have had NIV instead? And how would you have known, hour by hour, that he was failing?

That's next.

questions.text: HFNO vs NIV in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

steps.bridge: HFNO did not cut intubation overall but lowered 90-day mortality. Next: what the sepsis guideline prefers →

lesson.text:
Start with what high flow actually does, because it explains the trial.

A breathless patient pulls in thirty to sixty litres a minute at the peak of each breath. An ordinary face mask delivers far less than that. So with every breath he also sucks in room air around the mask, and the FiO2 he really gets is unknown, and lower than you set.

High flow delivers up to sixty litres a minute. That matches his own demand, so he never has to sip from the room. [[With high flow, the FiO2 he breathes is the FiO2 you set.]]

Then three more effects. The flow flushes the CO2-rich gas out of his nose and throat. That's dead-space washout, so each breath carries less CO2 back in. Flow pushing against his breath out gives a few centimetres of water of PEEP. And the gas is warm and wet, so he isn't spending work warming and humidifying dry air, and he can tolerate it for days.

Now FLORALI, published in twenty fifteen. Three hundred and ten patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure, not hypercapnic. Three arms. High flow, standard oxygen by face mask, and NIV.

The primary outcome was intubation at twenty-eight days. Thirty-eight percent with high flow, forty-seven with standard oxygen, fifty with NIV. [[FLORALI's primary outcome, intubation, did not differ significantly.]] That's the line most residents get wrong. Your own notes said high flow lowered intubation. In the trial, that held only in a post hoc subgroup, the patients with a P to F of two hundred or less.

So what did favour high flow? Ninety-day mortality. Twelve percent with high flow, twenty-three with standard oxygen, twenty-eight with NIV. [[Lower ninety-day mortality with high flow, but as a secondary outcome. It suggests benefit. It doesn't prove it.]]

{{**FLORALI** 2015, n = 310, non-hypercapnic
Intubation at 28 d: HFNO 38% · O₂ 47% · NIV 50% (ns)
90-day mortality: 12% · 23% · 28%
Fewer intubations with HFNO only if P/F ≤200 (post hoc)}}

And notice that NIV did worst on every count. In the large LUNG SAFE study too, NIV in patients with a P to F below one hundred and fifty was linked to higher mortality. We'll see why in a few cards.

So for Patient A, high flow was the right first choice. What does the sepsis guideline say?

steps.bridge: Surviving Sepsis suggests high flow over NIV. Next: how do I know high flow is working →

lesson.text: You met the sepsis card in the oxygen question. Its second line is the one for here. For sepsis-induced hypoxaemic respiratory failure, Surviving Sepsis suggests high-flow nasal oxygen over NIV, as a weak recommendation. Patient A's pneumonia makes him exactly that patient. So FLORALI and the sepsis guideline point the same way. High flow first.

steps.bridge: ROX 4.88 or more predicts success; low values at 2, 6 or 12 h predict failure. Next: the quick version and when to act →

lesson.text:
Once he's on high flow, you need to know early whether it's working. That's the ROX index.

It's the SpO2 over the FiO2, divided by the respiratory rate. The top half is how well he's oxygenating. The bottom half is how hard he's working to do it.

{{**ROX** = (SpO₂ ÷ FiO₂) ÷ RR
Success: **≥4.88** at 2, 6 or 12 h
Failure if below: **2.85** at 2 h · **3.47** at 6 h · **3.85** at 12 h}}

Good oxygenation at a calm rate gives a high ROX. The same saturation, bought with an FiO2 of ninety percent and a rate of forty, gives a low one. [[A lower ROX is worse. Four point eight eight or more, at two, six or twelve hours, predicts high-flow success.]]

And the failure thresholds. Below two point eight five at two hours, three point four seven at six hours, or three point eight five at twelve hours. Your notes printed three point eight five at six hours. The original paper, by Roca, gives three point four seven.

Why do the failure thresholds rise over time? Because a patient who's going to succeed should be getting better. [[A ROX that's acceptable at two hours is worrying at twelve.]]

Now Patient A. Two hours in. Saturation ninety-two, on sixty percent oxygen, rate thirty-two. Ninety-two over nought point six is about one hundred and fifty-three. Divided by thirty-two, about four point eight. Just under four point eight eight. Not reassuring, not yet failing. A grey zone. You watch.

At six hours, his saturation is eighty-nine on eighty percent oxygen, and his rate is thirty-six. Eighty-nine over nought point eight is about one hundred and eleven. Divided by thirty-six, about three point one. Below three point four seven. The ROX is telling you high flow is failing, and it's telling you before he tires.

So the number gives you a decision point. What do you do with it?

steps.bridge: High effort and a rising rate on support mean intubate. Next: how do I judge failure on NIV →

lesson.text: You met this card in the P-SILI lesson, and its last line is the answer to Patient A at six hours. On high flow or NIV, high effort with a rising respiratory rate means intubate. Why not wait? Because every hour he spends pulling hard, he's stretching his own lung, and the mask can't reliably measure it, or limit it. Waiting doesn't rest the lung. It may injure it. A falling ROX and a rising rate are the same warning, read two ways.

steps.bridge: HACOR above 5 at 1 hour means over 80% will fail. Next: why does waiting hurt →

lesson.text:
If he were on NIV instead, you'd use a different score. HACOR. It predicts NIV failure in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

Five components, and the letters give them to you. Heart rate. Acidosis, the pH. Consciousness, the Glasgow coma score. Oxygenation, the P to F ratio. And respiratory rate. Of the five, consciousness carries the most points.

[[A HACOR above five, at one hour of NIV, means a failure rate above eighty percent. Intubate early.]]

Notice the one-hour mark. NIV gets a short trial, and the score is built to tell you early.

And don't mix the two scores up. They point in opposite directions. [[ROX is for high flow, and lower is worse. HACOR is for NIV, and higher is worse.]]

Now, why is waiting so dangerous?

steps.bridge: Strong efforts injure the lung themselves. Next: how HFNO works and what the guideline says →

lesson.text: You learned P-SILI in its own question. A patient breathing hard pulls his pleural pressure deeply negative, so the lung feels far more stretch than the airway pressure shows. The same swing pulls fluid into a leaky lung, and pendelluft over-stretches the dependent units. And on NIV, the machine's pressure adds on top of that huge effort, so tidal volumes can become very large. The answer is not to delay intubation in a patient with high drive.

So let's put the mechanism and the guidelines together, the way you'd say them.

High flow delivers up to sixty litres a minute, matching his peak inspiratory flow, so the FiO2 is reliable. It washes CO2 out of the upper airway. It gives a small PEEP, about one centimetre of water for every ten litres a minute, with the mouth closed. And it's warm, humid and comfortable.

The guideline. ESICM, in twenty twenty-three, made a strong recommendation for high flow over conventional oxygen, to reduce intubation. Not for cardiogenic oedema or COPD. And it made no recommendation for or against NIV over high flow.

[[High flow over ordinary oxygen, strongly. NIV against high flow, no recommendation either way.]]

Then the monitoring. A ROX of four point eight eight or more at two, six or twelve hours predicts success. Below three point eight five at twelve hours predicts failure.

{{**HFNO:** up to 60 L/min · reliable FiO₂ · dead-space washout · PEEP ≈1 cmH₂O per 10 L/min (mouth closed)
**ESICM 2023:** HFNO over conventional O₂ (strong) · no rec on NIV vs HFNO
**Surviving Sepsis:** HFNO over NIV (weak)}}

And the last line is the one that protects your patient. [[Delayed intubation harms. Decide early if he is failing.]]

So back to the puzzle we started with. Why did the weaker tool do better? Because high flow fixes what matters most, a reliable FiO2 and less work of breathing, without adding machine pressure on top of his own huge breaths. And a patient on high flow tells you how he's doing through his ROX, early enough to act.

spine: What HFNO is: heated, humid gas up to 60 L/min, matching his inspiratory flow, so FiO2 is reliable. It washes out dead space and gives a little PEEP.
Evidence: FLORALI (2015, n = 310): intubation 38% with HFNO, 47% with oxygen, 50% with NIV, not significant. 90-day mortality was lower with HFNO.
Guidelines: ESICM 2023 favours HFNO over conventional oxygen (strong), with no recommendation for or against NIV over HFNO. Surviving Sepsis suggests HFNO over NIV.
How I monitor: ROX index, SpO2/FiO2 divided by rate. 4.88 or more at 2, 6 or 12 h predicts success. On NIV, HACOR above 5 at 1 hour predicts failure.
Caution: vigorous effort causes self-inflicted lung injury. Delayed intubation harms, so decide early if he is failing.

open.text:
Let's go back to the first night.

In the emergency department, on a face mask, Patient A's saturation is in the eighties. You have two non-invasive options on the shelf. High-flow nasal oxygen, or NIV through a tight-fitting mask. Both promise to keep him off the ventilator.

Here's the puzzle. NIV gives real pressure, real PEEP, real support for his breathing. High flow gives only a little PEEP. So NIV should be the stronger tool. And yet, when the two were tested side by side in hypoxaemic patients, high flow did at least as well. In the trial that matters most, the patients on NIV did worst.

Why would the weaker tool win? Hold that question. The answer is partly about what each tool really does, and partly about what the patient does to his own lung while he's on it.

[[In hypoxaemic failure, the danger isn't only the low oxygen. It's the hard breathing, and the delay in seeing that support has failed.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, do you know how high flow works, not just that it's high flow. Second, do you know FLORALI, with its numbers and its honest limits. Third, the guidelines. And fourth, how you'd monitor him, and when you'd stop and intubate. The resident who keeps a failing patient on a mask for one more hour, hoping, has walked into the trap.

So here's the plan. FLORALI. The sepsis guideline. The ROX index for high flow. When effort means intubate. The HACOR score for NIV. Why waiting hurts. And then the mechanism and the guidelines together.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[High-flow nasal oxygen is heated, humid gas at up to sixty litres a minute, matching his inspiratory flow, so the FiO2 is reliable. It washes out dead space and gives a little PEEP.]]

The evidence. FLORALI, twenty fifteen, three hundred and ten patients. Intubation thirty-eight percent with high flow, forty-seven with oxygen, fifty with NIV, not significant. But ninety-day mortality was lower with high flow.

The guidelines. ESICM twenty twenty-three, high flow over conventional oxygen, strong, and no recommendation for or against NIV over high flow. Surviving Sepsis suggests high flow over NIV.

How I monitor. The ROX index, four point eight eight or more at two, six or twelve hours predicts success. On NIV, a HACOR above five at one hour predicts failure.

And the caution. [[Vigorous effort causes self-inflicted lung injury. Delayed intubation harms, so decide early if he's failing.]]

That's your answer. What high flow is, the evidence, the guidelines, how you monitor, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Patient A got his tube at six hours. Now jump forward to his second day on the ventilator. He's been proned, his PEEP is high, his FiO2 is ninety percent, and his P to F is still only about seventy. Someone at the bedside says, let's try nitric oxide, it did wonders for the last patient's numbers.

Should you? That's next.

questions.text: What is the role of inhaled nitric oxide in ARDS?

steps.bridge: It dilates vessels only next to ventilated alveoli, so oxygenation rises for 24 to 72 h, but not survival. Next: where it sits among failed therapies →

lesson.text:
Nitric oxide is a molecule your own vessels make. It's the signal the endothelium uses to relax the smooth muscle around it. Now deliver it as a gas, into the airway.

Here's the key. An inhaled gas can only reach alveoli that are ventilated. Flooded or collapsed alveoli get none of it. So the nitric oxide dilates only the vessels beside working alveoli. Blood is drawn towards them, and away from the shunt units. [[Inhaled nitric oxide is selective. It dilates only the vessels beside ventilated alveoli, so blood moves away from shunt and matching improves.]]

Think of opening the gates on the roads that lead somewhere, so the traffic leaves the dead ends.

And there's a second gift. As soon as nitric oxide enters the blood, haemoglobin inactivates it. So very little of it reaches the systemic circulation. [[It lowers the pulmonary artery pressure without systemic hypotension.]] That's why it has a place in acute right-heart failure.

Now compare an intravenous vasodilator. It reaches every vessel in the lung, including the ones beside collapsed alveoli. It dilates the unventilated units, sends more blood into the shunt, and the oxygen gets worse. Inhaled does the opposite. Inhaled prostacyclin works in the same selective way, through a different messenger.

So what happens to the patient? Oxygenation improves for twenty-four to seventy-two hours, and then the effect fades. And there's no mortality benefit. Why? Because most ARDS deaths come from multi-organ failure, not from hypoxaemia. Nitric oxide changes where the blood goes. It doesn't touch the lung injury.

The harms are on the card, and each has a reason. Methaemoglobinaemia, because nitric oxide oxidises the iron in haemoglobin to its ferric form. Nitrogen dioxide, which is toxic, formed when nitric oxide meets oxygen. Rebound pulmonary hypertension if you stop it suddenly, because it suppresses the body's own production. And renal dysfunction, an association seen in meta-analyses.

[[So it's rescue only. A short bridge in refractory hypoxaemia or acute right-heart failure, while you do the things that work.]]

For Patient A, it might buy a few hours. It won't buy him survival. And there's a whole list of therapies like that.

steps.bridge: It sits on the list of therapies with no survival benefit. Next: the V/Q fix that does save lives →

lesson.text:
This card is a list, and the panel likes to hear you give it quickly. The therapies shown to be ineffective in ARDS.

Exogenous surfactant, in adults. Beta-two agonists: intravenous salbutamol in BALTI-2, which caused harm, and inhaled, in ALTA. Statins, in SAILS and HARP-2. Ketoconazole, lisofylline, ibuprofen, and intravenous prostaglandin E one. N-acetylcysteine, procysteine, glutamine and the other antioxidants. Neutrophil elastase inhibitors, and activated protein C. Keratinocyte growth factor, which harmed. Aspirin for prevention, in LIPS-A. And inhaled nitric oxide and HFOV, with no survival benefit.

{{**Ineffective in ARDS:** surfactant (adults) · β₂-agonists (BALTI-2 IV, harm; ALTA inhaled) · statins (SAILS, HARP-2) · ketoconazole, lisofylline, ibuprofen, IV PGE₁ · NAC, procysteine, glutamine, antioxidants · elastase inhibitor, activated protein C · KGF (harm) · aspirin prevention (LIPS-A) · iNO, HFOV}}

Don't memorise it as a list of names. Each one made sense on paper. None changed survival.

[[What does reduce mortality? Low tidal volume and prone positioning. No drug has consistently done so.]]

One honest caution. Corticosteroids are the nearest exception. DEXA-ARDS found lower mortality with dexamethasone, and ATS, in twenty twenty-four, makes a conditional recommendation for steroids. But the trials as a whole haven't been consistent. You'll meet them later.

And one of those two works through the same idea as nitric oxide, better matching. So why does prone save lives, when nitric oxide doesn't?

Patient A has already been turned prone. Let's see why that was the right move.

Think of him lying on his back first. His lung is heavy and wet, and most of its mass lies towards the back. On top of the back of the lung sits the weight of that wet lung, the heart, and the abdomen pushing up through the diaphragm. So the back of the lung, the dorsal lung, collapses. And the back is also where most of the blood flows. Collapsed lung, full of blood. A big shunt.

Look at the picture on your screen.

{{pic}}

On the left, supine. The aerated baby lung sits at the front. The collapsed lung is at the back, where most of the blood is.

Now turn him prone. Four things happen.

First, the ventilation. The pressure gradient from front to back, steep when he's supine, becomes more even. The weight comes off the dorsal lung, and it re-opens. And because there's more lung mass at the back, the back gains more alveoli than the front loses.

Second, the perfusion. Here's the subtle part. Blood flow doesn't swing with gravity nearly as much as ventilation does. It stays mostly dorsal. So now the re-opened back lung meets the blood that was always there. [[Prone opens the back lung, where the blood already is. So matching improves and shunt falls.]]

Third, the heart and the secretions. The heart now rests on the sternum, not on the lung. The abdomen moves off the diaphragm. The right ventricle is unloaded, because re-opened lung relieves hypoxic vasoconstriction and lowers the plateau and the CO2. And the dependent airways now point down, so secretions drain.

Fourth, and most important, the injury. The lung fits the shape of the chest better, so the stretch spreads more evenly. Fewer regions are over-stretched. [[More even strain means less ventilator-induced lung injury.]]

And that's the answer to our paradox. [[Prone saves lives through less lung injury, not through better oxygen.]] That's why a patient whose PaO2 doesn't rise when you turn him still benefits. Nitric oxide improves the numbers and leaves the injury. Prone eases the injury, and in most patients the oxygen improves as well.

The trial that proved it, PROSEVA, in twenty thirteen, proned patients for at least sixteen hours a day, and cut twenty-eight-day mortality from about thirty-three to sixteen percent. We'll see who to prone, and when, in the ECMO question.
lesson.cap: A, supine: baby lung in front, collapsed back lung where blood flows. B, prone: back lung re-opened, blood still there.

spine: What it does: inhaled, it reaches only ventilated alveoli and dilates the vessels beside them. Blood moves away from shunt, so V/Q improves.
Bonus: it lowers pulmonary artery pressure without systemic hypotension.
Evidence: oxygenation improves for 24 to 72 hours, but there is no mortality benefit.
Harms: methaemoglobinaemia, nitrogen dioxide, rebound pulmonary hypertension on withdrawal, and renal dysfunction.
Where I use it: rescue only, as a short bridge in refractory hypoxaemia or acute right-heart failure. Prone positioning improves V/Q and does improve survival.

open.text:
Let me start with a paradox.

Patient A's second day. A P to F of about seventy. You start inhaled nitric oxide, and within the hour his PaO2 climbs. The numbers look wonderful. And yet, if you ask the trials, giving it doesn't make him any more likely to leave the ICU alive.

How can a drug improve the very thing that's failing, the oxygen, and not change survival at all?

The answer goes back to the line that runs through this block. Oxygen fixes ventilation-perfusion mismatch, not shunt. Nitric oxide does something clever. It doesn't open any alveoli. It moves the blood, away from the shunt and towards the alveoli that are already working. That's a real improvement in matching. But it does nothing to the injury that's actually killing him.

[[Better oxygen numbers are not the same as a healing lung.]]

That idea, that a therapy can improve the gas and not the outcome, is one of the most important lessons in ARDS. It's the pattern behind a long list of failed therapies. And it's why the one manoeuvre that also improves matching, and does save lives, is so interesting.

What is the professor really checking? First, the mechanism, and why inhaled, not intravenous. Second, the honest evidence. Third, the harms. And fourth, where you'd still use it. The resident who offers nitric oxide for refractory hypoxaemia as if it were a treatment has missed the point.

So here's the plan. How nitric oxide works, and its limits. The long list of therapies that failed. And then prone positioning, the matching fix that does save lives.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Inhaled nitric oxide reaches only ventilated alveoli and dilates the vessels beside them. Blood moves away from shunt, and matching improves.]]

The bonus. It lowers the pulmonary artery pressure without systemic hypotension.

The evidence. Oxygenation improves for twenty-four to seventy-two hours. But there's no mortality benefit.

The harms. Methaemoglobinaemia, nitrogen dioxide, rebound pulmonary hypertension on withdrawal, and renal dysfunction.

Where I use it. Rescue only, as a short bridge in refractory hypoxaemia or acute right-heart failure. [[Prone positioning also improves matching, and it does improve survival.]]

That's your answer. What it does, the bonus, the evidence, the harms, and where you'd use it.

But here's something to carry forward. Patient A has been prone, paralysed, on a high PEEP and a hundred percent oxygen. And for more than six hours, his P to F has stayed below eighty. Every lever on the ventilator is pulled. His lung can't be opened safely any further.

So what's left? Bypass the lung altogether. When do you call the ECMO team? That's next.

questions.text: When will you put this patient on ECMO? (VV-ECMO indications)

steps.bridge: Prone first; ECMO only after optimisation by EOLIA criteria. Next: the full list of indications →

lesson.text:
Before ECMO comes prone positioning. That's the order, and the panel will check it.

Who gets proned? A P to F below one hundred and fifty, on an FiO2 of at least sixty percent and a PEEP of at least five. For how long? At least sixteen hours a day. Those are the PROSEVA criteria. [[Prone if the P to F is below one hundred and fifty, for at least sixteen hours a day.]]

Why does it save lives? You've just learned it. It makes the transpulmonary pressure gradient more uniform, so ventilation is more even, and there's less ventilator-induced lung injury. In the exam, that statement cost you a mark. Say it plainly: prone works by making the stretch more even.

And then ECMO, only after optimisation, by the EOLIA criteria. A P to F below fifty for three hours. Or below eighty for six hours. Or a pH below seven point two five, with a PaCO2 of sixty or more, for six hours.

[[Prone first. ECMO only after optimisation, by the EOLIA criteria.]]

And one more line the exam has asked. VV-ECMO is for refractory hypoxaemia with a preserved heart. If the heart is failing too, that calls for a different circuit, VA.

steps.bridge: Refractory hypoxaemia, refractory hypercapnia, or a severe air leak. Next: how the trials and ELSO select patients →

lesson.text:
The indications fall into three groups, and each matches a way the lung can fail.

The first is oxygenation. A P to F below eighty on an FiO2 of ninety percent or more, despite optimal ventilation and prone. EOLIA put it more precisely, below fifty for three hours, or below eighty for six. That's refractory hypoxaemia.

The second is ventilation. A PaCO2 above eighty, or being unable to keep the plateau at thirty or below while you try to clear the CO2. EOLIA's version is a pH below seven point two five with a PaCO2 of sixty or more for six hours. That's refractory hypercapnia. And notice what it really means. To clear his CO2, you'd have to give breaths that injure his lung. ECMO clears the CO2 instead, so the ventilator can stay gentle.

The third is a severe air leak. A large bronchopleural fistula, where much of each positive-pressure breath escapes through the hole. ECMO lets you turn the pressures right down, and give the leak a chance to close.

[[Three indications. Refractory hypoxaemia, refractory hypercapnia, and a severe air leak.]]

And the relative contraindications, which we'll meet properly in a moment. Ventilation at high pressures for more than seven days. A contraindication to anticoagulation. Irreversible disease. And severe brain injury.

Patient A. A P to F below eighty for more than six hours, after optimisation. He's in the first group.

steps.bridge: EOLIA entry: P/F under 50 for 3 h, under 80 for 6 h, or pH under 7.25. Next: who should not go on →

lesson.text:
Now, how the trials and ELSO pick their patients. Three systems, and the panel expects you to know the first one word-perfect.

{{**EOLIA entry:** P/F <50 for 3 h · or <80 for 6 h (FiO₂ ≥0.8) · or pH <7.25 + PaCO₂ ≥60 for 6 h
**CESAR:** Murray ≥3 or pH <7.20
**ELSO:** P/F <80 on FiO₂ 0.9 + Murray 3–4 → indicated (~80% mortality) · P/F <150 + Murray 2–3 → consider (~50%)
**All exclude:** ventilated ≥7 days at high settings}}

EOLIA's entry criteria. [[A P to F below fifty for three hours, or below eighty for six, or a pH below seven point two five with a PaCO2 of sixty or more for six hours.]] All on an FiO2 of eighty percent or more.

CESAR used the Murray score, three or more, or a pH below seven point two. The Murray score takes four things, the chest film quadrants, the P to F ratio, the PEEP and the compliance, scores each from nought to four, and averages them.

ELSO frames it by expected mortality. A P to F below eighty on an FiO2 of ninety percent, with a Murray score of three to four, carries about an eighty percent mortality. That's where ECMO is indicated. A P to F below one hundred and fifty, with a Murray of two to three, carries about fifty percent. That's where you consider it, and start talking to the centre.

EOLIA also had a long list of exclusions. Age under eighteen, pregnancy, a BMI over forty-five, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, chronic lung disease, a very high SAPS score. But look at the one item every system shares. [[Every system excludes the patient ventilated for a week or more at high settings.]] We'll see why in the next card.

And before any of this, the card is clear. First, optimise. PEEP, a neuromuscular blocker, prone, diuresis, recruitment, and a trial of inhaled nitric oxide. ECMO is what you reach for after all of that has failed.

steps.bridge: Seven days of high settings, bleeding in the brain or no exit are contraindications. Next: scores to judge the odds →

lesson.text:
The contraindications make sense once you see ECMO for what it is. A bridge. It buys time for the lung to heal, or for a transplant. So it's only worth building if there's land on the other side.

And ECMO needs anticoagulation, because blood clots on the circuit. So the contraindications follow from those two facts. No recovery, no exit, or bleeding that heparin would make worse. [[Most contraindications are relative. The firm one is irrecoverable disease with nowhere to go.]]

Take them one at a time.

Ventilation at high settings, an FiO2 above ninety percent and a plateau above thirty, for seven days or more. Why seven days? Because by then, injurious ventilation has often pushed the lung into scarring, fibroproliferation, and a scarred lung recovers less. The bridge gets longer, and the land may not be there.

Major immunosuppression, with neutrophils under four hundred. And non-recoverable disease, major brain damage or terminal cancer. These carry poor survival. The bridge leads nowhere.

A recent or expanding bleed in the brain. Heparin for the circuit can make it grow.

Now the indications column. Severe ARDS despite optimal care. Life-threatening hypoxaemia. A bridge to lung transplant. And here's the one that surprises people. Pulmonary haemorrhage is an indication, not a contraindication. Why, if he's bleeding? Because modern circuits can run for a time with little or no heparin. And ECMO lets the bleeding lung rest.

There's no absolute age limit. The risk simply rises with age.

Patient A. Two days on the ventilator, a reversible pneumonia, no bleeding, no immunosuppression. There is land on the other side.

steps.bridge: RESP predicts VV survival; days ventilated before ECMO count. Next: what the trials showed →

lesson.text:
Scores help you judge the odds, and they help you talk to the family.

For VV-ECMO, the RESP score. It weighs the diagnosis, the days ventilated before ECMO, immunosuppression, brain dysfunction, prior nitric oxide, a bicarbonate infusion, cardiac arrest, the PaCO2, the peak pressure, and age. Class one, a score of six or more, predicts about ninety percent survival. Class five, about twenty.

[[RESP predicts survival on VV-ECMO, and the days ventilated before ECMO is one of its items.]] That's the seven-day rule again, built into the score.

For VA-ECMO in cardiogenic shock, it's the SAVE score. Diagnosis, with myocarditis doing best, age, weight, organ failures, diastolic pressure, pulse pressure, ventilation, and bicarbonate.

And beyond the scores, the patient. Age, reversibility, comorbidity, frailty, how long he's been ill and how fast it's moving, other organ failures, anatomy for the cannulas, whether he can be transferred, and his own wishes.

So far, so logical. But does ECMO actually work? That's where the trials come in.

steps.bridge: CESAR favoured transfer; EOLIA missed significance with crossover. Next: the whole decision in one place →

lesson.text:
Two trials, and each has a flaw you must be able to name.

CESAR, from the United Kingdom, published in two thousand and nine. One hundred and eighty patients. Notice what was randomised. Not ECMO itself, but transfer to an ECMO centre, against conventional care in the referring hospital. Survival without disability at six months was sixty-three against forty-seven percent, a relative risk of nought point six nine. Significant.

But only seventy-five percent of the ECMO arm actually received ECMO. And conventional care wasn't protocolised. [[CESAR showed the benefit of referral to an ECMO centre, not of ECMO itself.]]

EOLIA, in twenty eighteen, was designed to answer the question directly. Two hundred and forty-nine patients with very severe ARDS. Early ECMO, against conventional care with ECMO allowed as rescue. Sixty-day mortality, thirty-five against forty-six percent. An eleven-point difference. And yet a p value of nought point nought nine. Not significant.

Why? Because twenty-eight percent of the controls crossed over to rescue ECMO. And the trial was stopped early. Both of those shrink the difference a trial can show.

[[EOLIA: sixty-day mortality thirty-five against forty-six percent, not significant, with twenty-eight percent crossover.]]

{{| **CESAR** | **EOLIA**
Design | 180; transfer to ECMO centre | 249; early ECMO vs rescue ECMO
Result | 63 vs 47% (RR 0.69, P = 0.03) | 35 vs 46% (P = 0.09)
Flaw | 75% got ECMO; control not protocolised | 28% crossover; stopped early}}

One detail the panel may test. EOLIA has two published p values. Nought point nought nine for the primary outcome, and nought point nought seven for the survival curve. Both not significant.

Then a Bayesian re-analysis, by Goligher, asked a different question. Given these data, how likely is it that ECMO helps? And it found that benefit was likely. That's the honest summary. EOLIA missed its endpoint, but the evidence as a whole leans towards ECMO, in the right patients, at the right centre.

So here's the whole decision, the way you'd give it.

First, optimise. A tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo, a plateau of thirty or less, PEEP, prone, and paralysis if needed.

Then the EOLIA criteria, despite all that. A P to F below fifty for more than three hours, or below eighty for more than six. Or a pH below seven point two five with a PaCO2 of sixty or more for more than six hours, with the rate already raised to thirty-five and the plateau kept at thirty-two or below. That last condition matters. It means you've tried to clear the CO2 with the ventilator, and couldn't do it safely.

Ventilated for less than seven days. A reversible cause. An experienced centre.

And when not. Irreversible disease with no transplant option. Unable to anticoagulate. Severe immunosuppression. A moribund patient. Very severe brain injury.

The guidelines. [[ESICM in twenty twenty-three recommends VV-ECMO strongly, in selected severe ARDS at experienced centres. ATS in twenty twenty-four is conditional.]]

So for Patient A, the call is made early, inside his first week, and the centre is phoned before he's moribund, not after.

spine: First: optimise. Tidal volume 6 mL/kg, plateau 30 or less, PEEP, prone, paralysis if needed.
When (EOLIA criteria): P/F under 50 for over 3 h, or under 80 for over 6 h, or pH under 7.25 with PaCO2 60 or more for over 6 h, with rate 35 and plateau 32 or less.
Who: ventilated for under 7 days, with a reversible cause, at an experienced centre.
When not: irreversible disease with no transplant option, unable to anticoagulate, severe immunosuppression, severe brain injury, moribund.
Evidence: EOLIA (2018, n = 249): 60-day mortality 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09. 28% of controls crossed over; Bayesian re-analysis favours benefit. CESAR also favoured referral.
Guidelines: ESICM 2023 strong for VV-ECMO in selected severe ARDS; ATS 2024 conditional.

open.text:
Patient A has reached the edge.

Prone. Paralysed. A tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo. A high PEEP. An FiO2 of one. And still, for more than six hours, a P to F below eighty. You've done what the evidence asks of you, and his lung still can't do the job.

There's one more option. Take the blood out of his body, pass it through an artificial lung, and put it back. VV-ECMO. It takes over the gas exchange, so you can turn the ventilator right down and let the injured lung rest.

[[ECMO doesn't treat the lung. It buys time for the lung to heal.]]

But it's not a free option. It needs large cannulas, anticoagulation, a specialist team, and often a transfer. And it only makes sense if there's somewhere to go at the end of the bridge.

So the question has two halves. When, and when not. And the trials behind it are among the most argued about in critical care. One of them missed its primary endpoint, and is still the main reason we offer ECMO today.

What is the professor really checking? First, that you optimise before you think of ECMO. Second, the EOLIA criteria, exactly. Third, who should not go on. Fourth, CESAR and EOLIA, with their numbers and their flaws. The resident who says ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia, and stops, has given a fraction of the answer.

So here's the plan. Prone first. The indications. How the trials and ELSO select patients. The contraindications. The scores that judge the odds. The two trials. And the whole decision in one place.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[First, optimise. Six millilitres per kilo, a plateau of thirty or less, PEEP, prone, and paralysis if needed.]]

When? By the EOLIA criteria. A P to F under fifty for over three hours, or under eighty for over six. Or a pH under seven point two five with a PaCO2 of sixty or more for over six hours, with the rate at thirty-five and the plateau at thirty-two or less.

Who? Ventilated for under seven days, with a reversible cause, at an experienced centre.

When not? Irreversible disease with no transplant option. Unable to anticoagulate. Severe immunosuppression. Severe brain injury. Moribund.

The evidence. [[EOLIA, twenty eighteen, two hundred and forty-nine patients. Sixty-day mortality thirty-five against forty-six percent, a p value of nought point nought nine.]] Twenty-eight percent of controls crossed over, and a Bayesian re-analysis favours benefit. CESAR also favoured referral.

The guidelines. ESICM twenty twenty-three, strong, in selected severe ARDS. ATS twenty twenty-four, conditional.

That's your answer. First optimise, then when, who, when not, the evidence, and the guidelines.

But here's something to carry forward. Every turn in this block began with one moment we haven't looked at yet. The six-hour mark on high flow, when Patient A's ROX fell and you decided to intubate. Almost no oxygen reserve, and a blood pressure that may fall the moment you induce. That may be the most dangerous ten minutes of his whole illness.

So how do you put the tube in safely? That's next.

questions.text: How do you safely intubate a critically ill patient?

steps.bridge: Sit him up, pre-oxygenate with NIV, use a video laryngoscope. Next: the same bundle for every hypoxaemic patient, with the evidence →

lesson.text:
This card is about the obese patient. But hear it with Patient A in mind, because the physiology is the same. Two different patients, one problem. A small oxygen tank, emptied fast.

In obesity, the heavy abdomen pushes the diaphragm up. So the functional residual capacity falls, and lying flat makes it worse. Alveoli at the bases close. His oxygen use is higher too. So during apnoea he desaturates within a couple of minutes, not the six to eight of a lean adult.

[[Obesity shrinks the oxygen store and raises the demand on it. ARDS shrinks the store with flooded lung. Either way, he desaturates fast.]]

So every step of the bundle either adds to the store, or keeps it open.

Sit him up. Semi-sitting, the abdomen falls away from the diaphragm, and the functional residual capacity rises.

Pre-oxygenate with CPAP or NIV, not just a face mask. The PEEP keeps the basal alveoli open, so more lung holds oxygen. And add apnoeic oxygenation, oxygen flowing in while he isn't breathing, so the store keeps being topped up.

[[Semi-sitting, CPAP or NIV pre-oxygenation, and apnoeic oxygenation. Each one enlarges the tank or keeps it open.]]

Then rapid sequence induction, and a video laryngoscope. Why video? Because it raises first-pass success. And in this patient, every extra attempt costs a desaturation he can't afford.

The rest of the card is about NIV around surgery in the obese. NIV is preferred over high flow in hypercapnic failure, sleep apnoea, or obesity hypoventilation, because those patients need extra ventilation and a splinted upper airway, which high flow doesn't give. Avoid high tidal volumes, give enough PEEP against the weight of the abdomen, and set a high back-up rate. Before elective surgery, start CPAP about two weeks ahead, so he's used to the mask.

And after surgery, NIV pays off. Respiratory complications fall, with a relative risk of nought point three three. Unplanned ICU admission, nought point four three. After anaesthesia and opioids, the obese patient's bases collapse and his upper airway obstructs. CPAP and NIV splint both. That's why NIV is first-line for post-operative respiratory failure in obesity.

So, back to Patient A. Sit him up. Pre-oxygenate with NIV. Oxygen flowing during apnoea. A video laryngoscope. Is there trial evidence for doing this in every hypoxaemic patient, not just the obese?

There is, and it's recent. Two trials, and you should have both numbers ready.

First, the oxygen. PREOXI, published in twenty twenty-four. About thirteen hundred critically ill adults being intubated. Pre-oxygenation with NIV, against a face mask. The outcome was hypoxaemia, a saturation below eighty-five percent, between induction and two minutes after the tube went in.

[[PREOXI: hypoxaemia in nine point one percent with NIV, against eighteen point five with a face mask. About half the rate.]]

Why does NIV win? The same reason as in the last card. The PEEP holds alveoli open, so more of the lung fills with oxygen. A face mask can raise the oxygen in the open alveoli, but it can't open the shut ones. That's shunt again, the theme of this whole block.

Second, the tube. DEVICE, in twenty twenty-three. About fourteen hundred patients, in emergency departments and ICUs. Video laryngoscope against direct laryngoscopy.

[[DEVICE: first-attempt success eighty-five point one percent with video, against seventy point eight with direct.]]

{{**PREOXI** 2024, n = 1,301: hypoxaemia (SpO₂ <85%) 9.1% NIV vs 18.5% face mask
**DEVICE** 2023, n = 1,417: first-pass success 85.1% video vs 70.8% direct
**Bundle:** semi-sitting · NIV + apnoeic O₂ · VL, bougie, best operator, failed-airway plan · fluid if responsive, pressor ready · cautious ketamine/etomidate · waveform ETCO₂ · protective settings}}

Then the rest of the bundle, by the danger it answers.

For the tube. A video laryngoscope first, a bougie, the most experienced operator, and a failed-airway plan said out loud before you start.

For the circulation. Fluid, if he's fluid-responsive. A vasopressor drawn up, or already running. And a cautious dose of the induction drug, ketamine or etomidate. [[Expect the blood pressure to fall, and have the pressor ready before you induce, not after.]] As an anaesthetist, you know this reflex well. In the ICU patient, the fall can be faster and deeper.

And after the tube. Confirm it with waveform capnography. Then start lung-protective settings from the very first breath. Not after the chest film. Not on the next ward round. The first breath. His lung has already been injured, and the ventilator mustn't add to it.

So for Patient A. Semi-sitting. NIV pre-oxygenation, and oxygen flowing during apnoea. A video laryngoscope in the most experienced hands. A cautious dose of ketamine, with a pressor running. Capnography. And then, the first breath.

spine: Why it is dangerous: little oxygen reserve (shunt, small FRC), and blood pressure falls with induction and positive pressure.
Oxygen: semi-sitting, pre-oxygenate with NIV, plus apnoeic oxygenation. PREOXI (2024): hypoxaemia 9.1% with NIV vs 18.5% with face mask.
Tube: video laryngoscope first, bougie, most experienced operator, failed-airway plan. DEVICE (2023): first-pass success 85.1 vs 70.8%.
Circulation: fluid if responsive, pressor drawn up or running, cautious dose of ketamine or etomidate.
After: confirm with waveform capnography and start lung-protective settings from the first breath.

open.text:
Go back to the six-hour mark. Patient A's ROX has fallen to about three. His rate is thirty-six. His saturation is eighty-nine on eighty percent oxygen. You've decided to intubate.

You've intubated hundreds of patients in theatre. Healthy, pre-oxygenated, with a full tank of oxygen in their lungs. This is not that.

Think about the tank. In a healthy adult, the oxygen store during apnoea is the gas left in the lungs after a normal breath out, the functional residual capacity. That's why a well pre-oxygenated patient can stay apnoeic for several minutes before he desaturates. But Patient A's lungs are flooded and collapsed. His functional residual capacity is small, and much of his blood is shunting past alveoli that hold no gas at all. So when he stops breathing, his oxygen falls within seconds.

And there's a second danger. He's been holding up his blood pressure with a high sympathetic drive. Your induction drug takes that away. Then positive pressure squeezes his venous return. So the pressure falls, at the same moment as the oxygen.

[[Two dangers, both from physiology. Almost no oxygen reserve, and a circulation that falls with induction and positive pressure.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, that you see these two dangers before you pick up the laryngoscope. Second, a bundle that answers each one. Third, the two recent trials behind it. And fourth, what you do in the first minute after the tube is in.

So here's the plan. First the card that teaches the bundle in the obese patient, who shares Patient A's small oxygen tank. Then the bundle for every hypoxaemic patient, with the evidence.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Why is it dangerous? [[Little oxygen reserve, from shunt and a small functional residual capacity. And a blood pressure that falls with induction and positive pressure.]]

Oxygen. Semi-sitting, pre-oxygenate with NIV, and add apnoeic oxygenation. PREOXI, twenty twenty-four: hypoxaemia nine point one percent with NIV, against eighteen point five with a face mask.

The tube. A video laryngoscope first, a bougie, the most experienced operator, and a failed-airway plan. DEVICE, twenty twenty-three: first-pass success eighty-five point one against seventy point eight percent.

The circulation. Fluid if he's responsive, a pressor drawn up or running, and a cautious dose of ketamine or etomidate.

And after. Confirm with waveform capnography, and start lung-protective settings from the first breath.

That's your answer. Why it's dangerous, the oxygen, the tube, the circulation, and what comes after.

And that closes this block. Patient A has taken us from the definition to the PEEP, the oxygen, high flow, nitric oxide, ECMO, and the tube. One idea sat under all of it. [[Oxygen feeds the units that breathe. PEEP wakes the ones that don't.]]

But here's something to carry forward. The tube is in. The capnograph shows its square waves. And the nurse turns to you with the question every ARDS patient eventually asks. What settings? What tidal volume, by which weight? What plateau, what PEEP, what rate, and what pH will you accept?

How will you ventilate this ARDS patient? That's next.

questions.text: How will you ventilate this ARDS patient?

steps.bridge: Tidal volume follows lung size, which follows height and sex. Next: where to start and how to adjust →

lesson.text:
Why height? Because the lungs grow with the skeleton.

A tall man has big lungs. A short man has small ones. And for the same height, a woman's chest and lungs are smaller than a man's. But fat, and oedema fluid, add kilograms without adding a single alveolus. So the size of the lung follows height and sex, not actual weight.

[[Lung size follows height and sex, not actual weight. That's why the breath is sized to predicted body weight.]]

The formulas are simple once you see their shape. For a man, fifty, plus zero point nine one for every centimetre above one hundred and fifty-two point four. For a woman, the same slope, but starting at forty-five point five.

Why that odd number, one fifty-two point four? It's five feet. So a five-foot man starts at fifty kilos, and he gains about nine hundred grams of predicted weight for every centimetre above that. If you think in inches, it's two point three kilos per inch over five feet. And the woman starts four and a half kilos lower, because at the same height her lungs are smaller.

{{**Predicted body weight**
Men: 50 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4)
Women: 45.5 + 0.91 × (height cm − 152.4)
Inches: 50 (or 45.5) + 2.3 × (height in − 60)
**Our patient:** 170 cm man → 50 + 0.91 × 17.6 ≈ **66 kg**}}

Now our man. One seventy minus one fifty-two point four is seventeen point six. Times zero point nine one is about sixteen. Add fifty. His predicted weight is about sixty-six kilos.

See what that does. Six millilitres per kilo of his actual weight would be six hundred millilitres. Of his predicted weight, it's about four hundred. Six hundred millilitres is nine millilitres per kilo of his predicted weight. [[Size the breath to his actual weight, and you've quietly given an obese man a large breath.]]

The same error catches the short patient and the woman. Studies of real practice show they are the ones most often given too large a breath, because a volume picked by eye, without the height, suits an average-sized man.

So the first thing you say to the panel is not a volume. It's this. I measure his height, and I calculate his predicted body weight.

Now, with that weight in hand, where do you start, and how do you get to the target?

steps.bridge: Start 8, reach 6 mL/kg, plateau 30 or less, rate up to 35. Next: the one number that best predicts survival →

lesson.text:
The ARDSNet protocol is a set of steps, and every step has a reason. Let's walk them.

First, the tidal volume. You don't start at six. You start at eight millilitres per kilo of predicted weight, and you come down by one millilitre per kilo at a time, at intervals of two hours or less, until you reach six.

Why not cut straight to six? Because minute ventilation is tidal volume times rate. Cut the breath suddenly, and minute ventilation falls with it. The carbon dioxide climbs fast and the pH drops. So you step the volume down while you raise the rate, and the minute ventilation holds while the body adjusts. It's like lowering a heavy load one step at a time instead of dropping it.

For our man, eight per kilo is about five hundred and thirty. Six per kilo is about four hundred.

Second, the rate. You can go up to thirty-five breaths a minute. Why stop there? Because every extra breath carries the same fixed dead space, and every extra breath shortens the time to breathe out. At high rates, the time to breathe out gets too short, gas is trapped, the auto-PEEP builds, and each added breath gains less. Thirty-five is the protocol's cap on that trade-off.

Third, the plateau. Keep it at thirty or below. If it's higher, the breath is still too big for the open lung, so the tidal volume comes down again, one millilitre per kilo at a time, to a floor of four. Four is the protocol's floor. Below that, dead space takes up so much of each breath that clearing the carbon dioxide becomes very hard.

[[Start at eight, step down to six. Plateau thirty or below. If it's still above thirty, step down towards four.]]

Fourth, the pH. The protocol's goal is seven point three to seven point four five. If the pH falls, you raise the rate first, up to thirty-five. Why the rate first? [[The rate removes carbon dioxide without adding any stretch.]] Only if the pH is below seven point one five at a rate of thirty-five may the tidal volume go back up, and bicarbonate be considered.

And here's the point where your notes and the protocol seem to disagree. Your notes say accept a pH above seven point two. The protocol says seven point three to seven point four five. Both are right. The protocol gives the goal. Accepting a pH of seven point two or more, as the price of a protected lung, is permissive hypercapnia, and it's standard practice. Say it that way and you'll never be caught.

{{**ARDSNet: start and adjust**
Vt start 8 mL/kg PBW → down 1 mL/kg every ≤2 h → **6 mL/kg**
Rate up to **35/min**
Plateau **≤30**; if higher, Vt down in 1 mL/kg steps to **4 mL/kg**
pH goal 7.30–7.45; accept **≥7.20** (permissive hypercapnia)
pH <7.15 at rate 35 → Vt may rise; consider bicarbonate}}

One honest caution. A plateau above thirty is a warning, not always a lung problem. Remember the heavy chest wall from the oesophageal balloon lesson. In an obese man, part of that plateau is spent on the chest wall.

So the plateau is one ceiling. But there's a second number, and it predicted survival better than any other.

steps.bridge: Driving pressure under 15 matters most because it scales to the baby lung. Next: how to set PEEP and oxygen →

lesson.text:
You met driving pressure in its own lesson. Plateau minus PEEP, which equals the tidal volume divided by the compliance. The breath, divided by the open lung. Amato showed it was the ventilator number most strongly linked to survival.

Here's why it belongs here. Six per kilo is sized to our man's height. It doesn't know how much of his lung is still open. [[Driving pressure is the check on your six per kilo. Keep it at fifteen or below.]] If it sits above fifteen with a plateau under thirty, the breath is still too big for his baby lung.

So you've sized the breath. Now, how much PEEP and how much oxygen?

steps.bridge: Aim SpO2 88 to 95% and move along the PEEP-FiO2 table. Next: should PEEP be higher →

lesson.text:
You know these tables from the PEEP lesson. The oxygen target is modest on purpose, a PaO2 of fifty-five to eighty, an SpO2 of eighty-eight to ninety-five percent. Above that, the oxygen dissociation curve is flat, so chasing a higher number buys very little oxygen content at the cost of more FiO2 and more pressure.

And the table climbs PEEP and FiO2 together. Why? Because in ARDS low oxygen is mostly shunt, and shunt answers to PEEP, not to oxygen. [[Every step up in oxygen comes with a step up in PEEP.]] On the lower table, our man's FiO2 of zero point six goes with a PEEP of ten.

But which table, lower or higher?

steps.bridge: Higher PEEP helps only in moderate to severe ARDS. Next: should I recruit the lung →

lesson.text:
You met these three trials in the PEEP lesson. ALVEOLI, LOVS and EXPRESS each compared higher with lower PEEP. None of them showed a difference in mortality on its own. Higher PEEP gave better oxygenation and less need for rescue therapy.

But pooled together, a pattern appeared. [[Moderate to severe ARDS, a P to F ratio of two hundred or less, benefits from higher PEEP. Mild ARDS may be harmed.]]

Our man's ratio is one hundred and twenty. So he gets the higher table. And if higher PEEP helps, should you go further, and force the lung open?

steps.bridge: Stepwise recruitment raised mortality in ART, so avoid it. Next: the next step if P/F stays low →

lesson.text:
You met recruitment in its own lesson. The classic manoeuvre is a CPAP of forty centimetres of water for thirty to forty seconds. It can drop the blood pressure, cause barotrauma, and desaturate him.

And the ART trial tested stepwise recruitment, with PEEP titrated to the best compliance, against low PEEP. Recruitment gave a higher mortality and more barotrauma.

[[So in your plan, there is no routine, prolonged recruitment manoeuvre.]] Both the American and the European guidelines advise strongly against prolonged high-pressure manoeuvres.

So you've set everything, and the P to F ratio is still one hundred and twenty. What next?

steps.bridge: Prone early when P/F is under 150, for 16 hours or more. Next: the full starting plan in one place →

lesson.text:
Next, you turn him over. This is PROSEVA, the trial that made prone positioning standard care.

Know the entry criteria exactly. A P to F ratio below one hundred and fifty, on an FiO2 of zero point six or more, a PEEP of at least five, and six per kilo, after twelve to twenty-four hours of stabilisation. Proned within thirty-six hours of intubation, for sessions of at least sixteen hours. Your notes say twelve to eighteen. Quote the trial's sixteen.

[[PROSEVA cut twenty-eight-day mortality from thirty-two point eight to sixteen percent. It halved it.]]

And why had earlier prone trials failed? They proned late, briefly, and in milder ARDS. [[PROSEVA worked because it proned early, for long sessions, in the sickest.]]

Our man qualifies. Why prone works gets its own lesson.

Now let's put the whole plan together.

This is the card you'll actually speak. Let's build it the way you'd say it at the bedside, step by step, each with its reason.

Step one. Measure the height and calculate the predicted body weight. Because the lung follows height and sex, not the weighing scale.

Step two. Volume control, with a tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo of predicted weight, within a range of four to eight. A plateau of thirty or below. A driving pressure of fifteen or below. Because the open lung is small, and these three numbers keep each breath from over-stretching it.

Step three. PEEP and FiO2 by the ARDSNet table, the higher table in moderate to severe ARDS. Target an SpO2 of eighty-eight to ninety-five percent. Because shunt needs open alveoli, not more oxygen.

Step four. Raise the rate up to thirty-five to hold the minute ventilation, and accept the carbon dioxide while the pH stays at seven point two or above. Because a moderate acidosis does less harm than a stretched lung.

Step five. If the plateau is still above thirty, step the tidal volume down towards four. And before you blame the lung, check two things. Is the chest wall stiff, which a balloon in the oesophagus will show? And is there auto-PEEP, which an expiratory hold will show?

Step six. The guidelines. The American Thoracic Society, in twenty twenty-four, suggests higher PEEP without prolonged recruitment manoeuvres. That's a conditional recommendation. The European society, in twenty twenty-three, made no recommendation on PEEP. And both advise strongly against prolonged high-pressure recruitment.

Step seven. If the P to F ratio stays below one hundred and fifty, prone him. Then the other adjuncts. Then ECMO, by criteria.

{{**Ventilating ARDS: the starting plan**
PBW from height and sex
Vt **6 mL/kg PBW** (4–8) · plateau **≤30** · ΔP **≤15**
PEEP/FiO₂ table (higher if moderate–severe) · SpO₂ **88–95%**
Rate up to 35 · accept CO₂ while pH **≥7.20**
Plateau still >30 → Vt to 4; check Pes and auto-PEEP
P/F <150 → prone · adjuncts · ECMO by criteria}}

[[Say it in one breath. Six per kilo predicted weight, plateau under thirty, driving pressure under fifteen, PEEP by the table, accept the carbon dioxide, and prone if the ratio stays under one fifty.]]

And the evidence under step two is the founding trial of this whole field, ARMA. Six against twelve millilitres per kilo cut mortality from thirty-nine point eight to thirty-one percent. We'll tell its full story with the other big trials.

Now the trap the professor is listening for. Don't say, six millilitres per kilo of his weight. Say, six per kilo of predicted body weight, from his height. [[One word, predicted, separates the resident who has read the protocol from the one who has used it.]]

spine: Start: work out predicted body weight from height and sex. Tidal volume 6 mL/kg PBW (range 4 to 8), plateau 30 or less, driving pressure 15 or less.
Why: the ARDS lung is small, not stiff. Driving pressure scales the breath to the open lung and was most linked to survival (Amato 2015).
PEEP and oxygen: ARDSNet PEEP-FiO2 table, higher table if moderate to severe. SpO2 88 to 95%. No prolonged recruitment manoeuvres.
CO2: rate up to 35, then accept a high CO2 while pH stays 7.20 or more. If plateau is still over 30, step tidal volume down to 4 mL/kg.
Next steps: prone if P/F stays under 150. PROSEVA: 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%. Then ECMO by criteria.
Evidence: ARMA (2000): 6 vs 12 mL/kg cut mortality from 39.8 to 31.0%. Check for a stiff chest wall and auto-PEEP if pressures stay high.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient.

A man of forty, with pneumonia, has just been intubated. He is one hundred and seventy centimetres tall, and he weighs one hundred kilos. His chest film is white on both sides. On an FiO2 of zero point six, his PaO2 is seventy-two. That's a P to F ratio of one hundred and twenty. The nurse is holding the ventilator settings card, and she's waiting for you.

What's the first number you need? Most residents reach for his weight. That's the trap. You need his height.

This is a scenario question, and that changes what the professor is checking. He doesn't want a list of facts about ARDS. He wants to watch you set a ventilator, in order, with a reason for every number. Where do you start the tidal volume, and why from height? What are your pressure limits? How do you set PEEP and oxygen? What do you do when the carbon dioxide climbs? And what is your next move when the oxygen still won't come up?

You already own most of the pieces. Driving pressure, the PEEP tables, recruitment. Today we put them together into one plan you can say in a minute, for this man.

So here's the plan. First, predicted body weight. Then the ARDSNet protocol, how to start and how to adjust. Then a quick return to driving pressure, the PEEP and oxygen tables, the higher PEEP trials, and recruitment. Then the next step when the P to F ratio stays low, prone positioning. And finally, the whole starting plan in one place.

close.text:
So let's bring it together, for our man.

I measure his height and calculate his predicted body weight. I ventilate in volume control at six millilitres per kilo of that weight, within four to eight, with a plateau of thirty or below and a driving pressure of fifteen or below.

Why? Because the ARDS lung is small, not stiff. Driving pressure scales the breath to that open lung, and it was the number most linked to survival.

I set PEEP and FiO2 by the ARDSNet table, the higher table because his ARDS is moderate to severe. I aim for an SpO2 of eighty-eight to ninety-five percent. And I don't use prolonged recruitment manoeuvres.

For carbon dioxide, I raise the rate up to thirty-five, and accept a high carbon dioxide while the pH stays at seven point two or more. If the plateau is still above thirty, I step the volume down towards four.

[[If the P to F ratio stays below one hundred and fifty, I prone him. PROSEVA halved twenty-eight-day mortality. Then ECMO, by criteria.]]

And the evidence: ARMA, six against twelve per kilo, cut mortality from thirty-nine point eight to thirty-one percent. If the pressures stay high, I check for a stiff chest wall and for auto-PEEP.

That's your answer. The start, the reason, PEEP and oxygen, carbon dioxide, the next steps, and the evidence.

But here's something to carry forward. All of this rests on one picture, a small open lung sitting on top of a heavy, collapsed one. Gattinoni didn't imagine that picture. He saw it, on CT.

So what happens when the examiner puts that CT in front of you, and says, describe it? That's next.

questions.text: Spotter: CT chest in ARDS.

steps.bridge: The ARDS lung is small, not stiff: only a small part stays aerated. Next: what that looks like on CT →

lesson.text:
You met the baby lung in the lung injury lesson. Gattinoni, from his CT studies, showed that the ARDS lung is small, not stiff. Only a small, non-dependent part stays aerated, sometimes the size of a child's lung, and that part has near-normal compliance. So compliance measures how much lung is open.

And the card adds one line that matters today. [[The baby lung is a functional region, not an anatomical one. It shifts with position.]]

That's exactly what you are looking at on this CT. So let's read it.

steps.bridge: Aerated front, ground glass middle, collapsed back: gravity on a heavy lung. Next: why the small lung sets our pressure limit →

lesson.text:
Look at the picture on your screen. Panel A is the supine patient, like your CT.

{{pic}}

Describe it from the front to the back, in three zones.

At the front, the non-dependent lung, you see near-normal, aerated lung. Black on CT, as lung should be. That is the baby lung.

In the middle, ground glass. A haze through which you can still see the vessels. This is lung that is part-filled, oedematous, poorly aerated, but not yet airless.

At the back, the dependent lung, dense consolidation. White, airless, collapsed lung.

[[Three zones, front to back. Aerated at the front, ground glass in the middle, dense consolidation at the back.]]

Now the why. And this is the part that earns the marks.

The ARDS lung is full of oedema, so it is heavy. And every layer of that heavy lung presses on the layers below it. In a patient lying on his back, the squeeze builds from the front to the back. The top layer carries nothing, so it stays open. The middle carries some weight, so it's part-filled. The bottom carries the weight of everything above it, plus the heart and the abdomen, and it is squeezed shut.

Think of a wet sponge lying on a table. Dry and open on top. Squashed flat at the bottom, by its own weight. Gattinoni called this the sponge lung.

[[The gradient is gravity, acting on a heavy, wet lung.]]

How do we know it's gravity, and not fixed damage? Because when the patient is turned prone, much of the dense area moves to the new lowest part, within minutes. Squeezed-shut lung can move like that. True consolidation, pneumonia filling the alveoli, stays where it is.

And that's the bridge to proning. Look at panel B. Turned over, the back re-opens, and the collapse moves to the front, which is now lowest. And there is less lung at the front than at the back. So the patient gains more open lung than he loses.

Finally, a good spotter answer doesn't stop at the lungs. Look for the complications and the cause. Barotrauma, a pneumothorax or a pneumomediastinum. Effusions. And the original cause, such as a pneumonia.

So your answer sounds like this. An axial CT of a supine patient, showing a gradient from front to back. Aerated lung at the front, ground glass in the middle, dense dependent consolidation. This is the baby lung sitting on a sponge lung. I'd also look for barotrauma, effusions and the cause.

One honest caution. Small, not stiff, is true mainly in early ARDS. In the later, fibrotic phase, the lung tissue itself does become stiff.

Now, what does that thin band of open lung at the front mean for the pressures you set?
lesson.cap: A, supine: aerated baby lung in front, collapse behind. B, prone: the back re-opens; some collapse moves to the front.

steps.bridge: Driving pressure scales each breath to that small open lung. Next: how turning him moves the collapse →

lesson.text:
That thin black band at the front of the CT is the whole lung your breath can go into. And driving pressure is how you measure the breath against it.

You know the formula. Driving pressure is the plateau minus the PEEP. And it equals the tidal volume divided by the compliance. Now see it against the CT. The compliance is roughly the size of that band, because each open unit behaves almost normally. So a small band means a small compliance, and the same breath gives a bigger driving pressure.

Take two patients, each given four hundred millilitres. One has a compliance of forty. His driving pressure is ten. The other has a compliance of twenty, a thinner band on CT. His driving pressure is twenty. Same breath, same millilitres per kilo. Twice the stretch.

[[Six per kilo can still over-stretch a baby lung. Driving pressure shows the real strain.]]

The target is below fifteen. Why fifteen? In Amato's data, the risk of death climbed steadily as the driving pressure rose, and fifteen became the usual working line. So it's a practical ceiling, not a proven safe line.
