Now the trap. This exact point has been asked in the entrance exam, and most candidates got it wrong. When there is auto-PEEP, which PEEP goes into the formula?

The total PEEP. That's the set PEEP plus the auto-PEEP, read from an end-expiratory hold.

Why? Because the trapped gas is already holding the alveoli open above the set PEEP. The breath starts from that higher level, not from the set one. So if you subtract only the set PEEP, you overstate the driving pressure.

{{**Driving pressure = plateau − TOTAL PEEP** (set + auto-PEEP, from an expiratory hold)
Plateau 28 · set PEEP 10 · auto-PEEP 3
Wrong: 28 − 10 = 18 · **Right: 28 − 13 = 15**}}

Say the plateau is twenty-eight, the set PEEP ten, and the hold shows three of auto-PEEP. Subtract the set PEEP and you get eighteen, and you'd cut a breath that didn't need cutting. Subtract the total PEEP, thirteen, and the true driving pressure is fifteen.

[[With auto-PEEP, use the total PEEP. Set PEEP alone overstates the driving pressure.]]

And why does it matter more than tidal volume, or plateau alone? Because Amato found it the variable most strongly linked to survival, even when the tidal volume and the plateau were within their limits. One honest caution. That's an association, from a re-analysis of trials. It isn't proof that lowering driving pressure causes the benefit.

So the CT shows you the small lung, and driving pressure protects it. But the CT also showed you the collapse moving. What happens when you turn him over?

steps.bridge: Prone reopens the back where the blood flows, so V/Q improves. Next: who gets proned and for how long →

lesson.text:
You met these effects alongside nitric oxide. Turned prone, the pleural pressure gradient becomes more uniform, and the dorsal lung, where more of the lung mass lies, is recruited. Perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so ventilation and perfusion match better and shunt falls. The heart and abdomen no longer press on the lung, the right ventricle is unloaded, and secretions drain.

[[More even stretch means less lung injury, and that, not better oxygen, is where the survival benefit comes from.]]

On your CT, that's the big white zone at the back turning black. So who gets turned, and for how long?

You met this card in the ECMO lesson. Prone him if the P to F ratio is below one hundred and fifty on an FiO2 of zero point six or more and a PEEP of at least five, for sixteen hours or more a day. It saves lives by making the transpulmonary pressure gradient more uniform, so there's less lung injury.

And if that fails, the EOLIA criteria for VV-ECMO, after optimisation. A ratio below fifty for three hours, below eighty for six hours, or a pH below seven point two five with a PaCO2 of sixty or more for six hours.

[[The CT explains the order of that ladder. Turning the patient over comes before the circuit.]]

spine: What I see: a front-to-back gradient. Aerated, near-normal lung at the front; ground glass in the middle; dense consolidation at the back.
What it means: the front aerated part is the baby lung, small, not stiff (Gattinoni). The back collapses under the weight of the oedematous lung above: the sponge lung.
Why it matters: a normal breath over-stretches the baby lung, so keep tidal volume low and driving pressure under 15.
Proning: the back reopens while perfusion stays mostly at the back, so V/Q improves and shunt falls. Prone if P/F is under 150, for 16 hours or more a day.
Also look for: pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum (barotrauma), effusions and the original cause, such as pneumonia.

open.text:
Let me start with two pictures of the same patient.

The first is his chest X-ray. White on both sides, from top to bottom. It looks as though the whole lung is equally sick.

The second is his CT, taken the same morning, lying on his back. And it tells a completely different story. The damage isn't spread evenly at all. It's arranged in layers, from the front of the chest to the back.

That difference is what this spotter is about. The professor hands you the CT and says, describe it. What he's really checking is three things. Can you describe it in an orderly way, front to back, rather than calling the whole thing bilateral consolidation? Can you explain why it looks like that? And can you say what that picture means for the way you ventilate and position the patient?

A resident who says, bilateral consolidation, ARDS, has named the film. A resident who says, there's a gradient from front to back, and here's why, has understood the disease. That's the gap between a pass and a good mark.

So here's the plan. First, a quick return to the baby lung. Then the CT itself, its three layers and the reason for them. Then what the small open lung means for the pressures you set. Then how turning the patient moves the collapse. And finally, who gets proned and for how long.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

What do I see? A gradient from front to back. Aerated, near-normal lung at the front. Ground glass in the middle. Dense consolidation at the back.

What does it mean? The aerated front is the baby lung. Small, not stiff, as Gattinoni showed. The back has collapsed under the weight of the oedematous lung above it. That's the sponge lung.

[[The ARDS lung is small, not stiff, and gravity decides where the small part is.]]

Why does it matter? Because a normal breath over-stretches that small lung. So I keep the tidal volume low and the driving pressure under fifteen, using the total PEEP if there's auto-PEEP.

Proning turns the picture over. The back re-opens while the blood flow stays mostly at the back, so the match improves and shunt falls. I prone if the P to F ratio stays under one hundred and fifty, for sixteen hours or more a day.

And I also look for pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum, effusions, and the original cause, such as a pneumonia.

That's your spotter answer. What I see, what it means, why it matters, proning, and what else to look for.

But here's something to carry forward. We've seen that proning moves the collapse. We've said it saves lives. Yet in some patients the oxygen barely improves when they're turned, and they still benefit. How can that be?

So why does prone positioning really work? That's next.

questions.text: Why does prone positioning work?

steps.bridge: Only a small part of the lung is open, and gravity decides where. Next: what changes when he is turned prone →

lesson.text:
Start where the CT left us. Gattinoni's baby lung. In ARDS only a small, non-dependent part of the lung stays aerated, and it has near-normal compliance. The lung is small, not stiff.

[[The baby lung is not a fixed place. It's wherever gravity lets the lung stay open.]] Gattinoni called the heavy lung a sponge lung, squashing its own lower layers. And because it's functional, not anatomical, it moves when the patient moves. That single fact is why proning can work at all.

steps.bridge: The back reopens where the blood is, and stretch evens out. Next: who to prone and for how long →

lesson.text:
You met these four effects with nitric oxide. One, the pleural pressure gradient becomes more uniform, and the dorsal lung is recruited. Two, perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so the match of air to blood improves and shunt falls. Three, the heart and abdomen come off the lung, the right ventricle is unloaded, and secretions drain. Four, the strain becomes more even, so there's less lung injury.

[[Keep the order. Oxygen comes from the better match. Survival comes from the more even strain.]] We'll build the full chain in the last card of this question.

steps.bridge: P/F under 150 on FiO2 0.6 or more, 16 hours a day. Next: the trial that proved it →

lesson.text:
You met this card in the ECMO lesson. Prone him if the P to F ratio is below one hundred and fifty on an FiO2 of zero point six or more, with a PEEP of five or more, for at least sixteen hours a day. And it saves lives by making the transpulmonary pressure gradient more uniform, so ventilation is more even and lung injury less.

Notice what that card says the benefit is. Not the oxygen. The evenness. And if proning fails, the same card carries the EOLIA criteria for ECMO. That's the next rung.

steps.bridge: PROSEVA halved 28-day mortality with early, long sessions. Next: when to stop and what can go wrong →

lesson.text:
You met PROSEVA when we ventilated our patient with pneumonia. A P to F ratio below one hundred and fifty, early, within thirty-six hours of intubation, for sessions of at least sixteen hours. Twenty-eight-day mortality fell from thirty-two point eight to sixteen percent.

And remember why the earlier prone trials had failed. They proned late, briefly, and in milder ARDS. [[With proning, the dose and the timing are part of the treatment.]]

Now let's build the whole answer.

Look at the picture on your screen. Panel A is the patient on his back. Panel B is the same patient turned prone.

{{pic}}

Let's build the why, step by step.

First, the weight. Lying supine, the wet, heavy lung, the heart and the abdomen all press down on the back of the lung. And the back is where most of the lung tissue is, and where most of the blood flows. So the biggest part of the lung, with the most blood, is squeezed shut. That's a large shunt.

Turn him prone, and the back is now on top. The weight comes off it, and it re-opens.

Second, the blood. Here's the key. Ventilation swings with gravity. Perfusion doesn't swing nearly as much. It stays mostly dorsal, even when he's prone. So the lung you've just re-opened is lung that still has its blood. Air meets blood again.

[[Prone, the back lung re-opens while the blood stays there. So ventilation and perfusion match better, and shunt falls.]]

And the front? It's now lowest, so it collapses a little. But there's less lung at the front than at the back. So he gains more open lung than he loses.

Third, the stretch. In the supine patient, the squeeze from top to bottom is steep. The open part at the front takes almost every breath, and it gets over-stretched. Prone, the lung fits the shape of the chest better, and the heart rests on the sternum instead of on the lung. The squeeze from top to bottom becomes more even. So each breath spreads more evenly, and fewer regions are over-stretched.

[[That more even stretch means less lung injury. And that, more than the oxygen, is why proning saves lives.]]

Now the puzzle from the start makes sense. The patient whose PaO2 barely moved still had his strain spread more evenly. His lung was still protected.

Fourth, the right heart. The re-opened lung relieves hypoxic vasoconstriction. The PaCO2 falls. The alveolar pressure falls, so there's less squeeze on the vessels. All three lower the pulmonary vascular resistance. The right ventricle is unloaded.

Then, when. A P to F ratio below one hundred and fifty, on an FiO2 of zero point six or more and a PEEP of at least five. Early, within thirty-six hours. Sessions of sixteen hours or more. PROSEVA, twenty thirteen, four hundred and sixty-six patients. Twenty-eight-day mortality sixteen percent against thirty-two point eight. The European guideline of twenty twenty-three recommends it strongly.

When do you stop? Only when the gain holds after he's back on his back. A P to F ratio of one fifty or more, on a PEEP of ten or less and an FiO2 of zero point six or less, still true at least four hours after turning supine. Why wait four hours? Because the gain often fades once he's supine again.

{{**Prone: when and when to stop**
Start: P/F <150 on FiO₂ ≥0.6 and PEEP ≥5 · within 36 h · sessions **≥16 h**
Stop: P/F **≥150** on PEEP ≤10 and FiO₂ ≤0.6, **≥4 h after turning supine**
Contraindications: unstable spine · raised ICP · open abdomen or recent sternotomy · massive haemoptysis}}

And who shouldn't be turned? The patients who can't stand the turn, or the face-down pressure. An unstable spine. Raised intracranial pressure. An open abdomen or a recent sternotomy. Massive haemoptysis.

What goes wrong? Pressure sores, especially on the face. The tube displaced. Lines lost. So the turn is a team job, planned, with someone holding the airway.

One honest caution. The more-even-stretch explanation is the best account we have of why survival improves. It fits the trials, but it's an explanation, not something PROSEVA itself measured. Say, the benefit seems to come from less lung injury.
lesson.cap: A, supine: the back is squashed where most blood flows. B, prone: it re-opens with its blood; stretch evens out.

spine: Why it works: the dorsal lung reopens while perfusion stays mainly dorsal, so V/Q matches better and shunt falls.
Also: the pleural pressure gradient becomes more uniform, so stretch spreads evenly: less lung injury. The heart and abdomen no longer press on the lung, and the right ventricle is unloaded.
When: P/F under 150 on FiO2 0.6 or more and PEEP 5 or more, early (within 36 h), sessions of 16 hours or more.
Evidence: PROSEVA (2013, n = 466): 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%. ESICM 2023 recommends it strongly.
Stop: when P/F stays 150 or more on PEEP 10 or less and FiO2 0.6 or less, at least 4 hours after turning supine.
Caution: unstable spine, raised ICP, open abdomen. Watch for facial pressure sores, tube displacement and line loss.

open.text:
Let me start with a puzzle.

Two patients with severe ARDS are turned prone. In the first, the PaO2 jumps within the hour. In the second, it barely moves. The obvious conclusion is that proning helped the first and failed the second.

But that's not what the evidence says. Patients whose oxygen doesn't improve still seem to benefit. So whatever makes proning save lives, it isn't simply the oxygen.

That's the heart of this question. Why does prone positioning work? It sounds like a one-line answer. It isn't. What the professor is really checking is whether you can give the mechanism in order, cause before effect. Can you separate the oxygen effect from the lung-protection effect, and say which one saves lives? Then do you know the entry criteria, the trial, when to stop, and when not to prone at all?

The resident who says, it improves oxygenation, has given the one answer that isn't enough. That's the trap.

You've already met most of the parts. The baby lung, the effects of proning, the PROSEVA numbers. So we'll move through those quickly, as reminders. Then, at the end, we build the whole answer in one piece, with the picture.

So here's the plan. The baby lung and gravity. What changes when he's turned. Who to prone and for how long. The trial that proved it. And then the full answer: why, when, when to stop, and what can go wrong.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Why does it work? [[The dorsal lung re-opens while perfusion stays mainly dorsal. So ventilation and perfusion match better, and shunt falls.]]

And more than that. The pleural pressure gradient becomes more uniform, so the stretch spreads evenly, and there's less lung injury. The heart and abdomen no longer press on the lung, and the right ventricle is unloaded.

When? A P to F ratio under one hundred and fifty, on an FiO2 of zero point six or more and a PEEP of five or more. Early, within thirty-six hours. Sessions of sixteen hours or more.

The evidence. PROSEVA, twenty thirteen, four hundred and sixty-six patients. Twenty-eight-day mortality sixteen against thirty-two point eight percent. The European guideline of twenty twenty-three recommends it strongly.

When do I stop? When the ratio stays at one fifty or more, on a PEEP of ten or less and an FiO2 of zero point six or less, at least four hours after turning supine.

And the caution. Not with an unstable spine, raised intracranial pressure, or an open abdomen. And watch for facial pressure sores, tube displacement and line loss.

That's your answer. Why, the more important why, when, the evidence, when to stop, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Everything we've said about where the gas goes, we've learned from a CT, taken once, in a scanner, far from the bedside. What if you could watch where each breath goes, live, at the bedside, with no radiation at all? And use it to choose the PEEP?

That's electrical impedance tomography. And it's next.

questions.text: What is electrical impedance tomography?

lesson.text:
Start with one physical fact. Electric current passes easily through salty tissue and fluid. It passes poorly through air.

So the resistance of the chest to a small current, its impedance, depends on how much air is in it. [[As a region fills with gas, its impedance rises. As it empties, its impedance falls.]] Fluid does the opposite. It lowers the impedance.

Now the machine. A belt of sixteen to thirty-two electrodes goes round the chest. It passes small, painless currents between the electrodes, one pair after another, and measures the voltages all the way round. Because it reads from so many angles, the machine can rebuild a cross-sectional picture of the chest, a slice. And it does this many times a second. So you see a live image of which part of that slice took the breath.

What makes it useful? Four things. It's radiation-free. It's at the bedside. It's continuous. And it's regional. It shows you front against back, and left against right. The CT showed you layers once. EIT shows you how those layers behave, breath after breath.

Now the main use, titrating PEEP. You do a decremental PEEP trial. You start with the PEEP high, and you step it down.

At high PEEP, the front of the lung, the non-dependent part, is already over-full. It's near the top of its stretch, so each centimetre of water buys very little extra volume. That's over-distension. As you step the PEEP down, the front relaxes and takes the breath more easily. But now the back, the dependent part, starts to collapse, and it stops ventilating. That's collapse.

So as the PEEP falls, over-distension falls, and collapse rises. Plot the two, and look at the picture on your screen.

{{pic}}

[[Choose the PEEP where the two curves cross. That's the best compromise between collapse and over-distension.]]

Costa and colleagues described this method in two thousand and nine. And see how it joins up with everything you know. The table gives one PEEP for everyone. The balloon tells you about the chest wall. EIT tells you where, in this lung, the breath is going.

What else can it show you? A pneumothorax, as a sudden loss of ventilation on one side, because that lung no longer fills. Pendelluft, which you met with patient self-inflicted lung injury. That's gas swinging from one region of the lung to another inside the chest, during a forceful breath, without ever passing the mouth. The effect of proning, as you watch the back take a bigger share of each breath. And even perfusion. A small bolus of concentrated saline, injected centrally, is highly conductive. As it passes through the lung's vessels, the impedance dips wherever blood is flowing. So you can set a map of blood against a map of air.

{{**EIT**
Principle: air ↑ impedance, fluid ↓ · belt of 16–32 electrodes · live cross-section
Strengths: radiation-free · bedside · continuous · regional
PEEP: decremental trial → PEEP where collapse and over-distension cross
Also: pneumothorax · pendelluft · proning · V/Q with a saline bolus
Limits: one slice · no proven outcome benefit · cost}}

Now the limits, and this is where you keep your marks. First, it sees one slice of the chest, at the level of the belt, not the whole lung. Second, it costs. And third, no outcome benefit has been proven. [[It's a tool, not a treatment. It guides the PEEP. It doesn't prove the PEEP is right.]]

So in the viva, sell it for what it is. A bedside window onto regional ventilation, most useful for choosing PEEP in the patient where the table is clearly not enough.
lesson.cap: Stepping PEEP down: over-distension at the front falls, collapse at the back rises. Choose PEEP where they cross.

spine: What it is: a belt of 16 to 32 electrodes passes small currents round the chest. Air raises impedance, so it builds a live image of where each breath goes.
Why useful: bedside, continuous, radiation-free and regional (front vs back, left vs right).
PEEP titration: on a decremental PEEP trial, collapse rises as PEEP falls and over-distension rises as PEEP rises. Choose the PEEP where the two curves cross.
Also shows: pneumothorax (sudden loss on one side), pendelluft, the effect of proning, and ventilation-perfusion with a saline bolus.
Caution: it images one slice only, it costs, and no outcome benefit is proven. It is a tool, not a treatment.

open.text:
Let me start with a problem you've already met.

You've set your patient's PEEP by the table. The table gives a number for an FiO2. But the table has never seen his lung. It doesn't know whether that PEEP is holding his dependent lung open, or over-stretching the baby lung at the front.

The CT would tell you. It showed you the layers, front to back. But you can't wheel a ventilated patient to the scanner every time you change the PEEP.

So imagine a belt, wrapped round his chest, that shows you, breath by breath, which part of his lung is taking the gas. No radiation. At the bedside. Running all day.

That belt exists. It's electrical impedance tomography, EIT.

What is the professor really checking here? First, do you understand the principle, why air changes what the belt sees. Second, what can it show you. Third, how do you use it to set PEEP. And fourth, its limits. This is a newer tool, and the trap is to oversell it. The resident who says it improves survival has walked into it.

So here's the plan, all on one card. The principle. What makes it useful. How it titrates PEEP. What else it shows. And its limits.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

What is it? A belt of sixteen to thirty-two electrodes passes small currents round the chest. Air raises the impedance, so the machine builds a live image of where each breath goes.

Why is it useful? It's at the bedside, continuous, radiation-free, and regional. Front against back, left against right.

[[For PEEP, I do a decremental trial. Collapse rises as the PEEP falls, over-distension rises as it climbs. I choose the PEEP where the two curves cross.]]

It also shows a pneumothorax, as a sudden loss on one side, pendelluft, the effect of proning, and, with a saline bolus, ventilation against perfusion.

And the caution. It images one slice only, it costs, and no outcome benefit is proven. It's a tool, not a treatment.

That's your answer. What it is, why it's useful, PEEP titration, what else it shows, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. So far, everything we've done for the ARDS lung has been on the ventilator, or about the ventilator. Breath size, PEEP, position. Yet some patients stay desperately hypoxic, however well you set the machine.

So what else is there? Fluids, paralysis, steroids, ECMO, nitric oxide. Which of them are proven, and which are not? That's the non-ventilatory management of severe ARDS. And it's next.

questions.text: What is the non-ventilatory management of severe ARDS?

steps.bridge: Prone early and long is the one proven lifesaver. Next: how much fluid should he get →

lesson.text:
You know this one. PROSEVA. A P to F ratio below one hundred and fifty, on an FiO2 of zero point six or more, proned within thirty-six hours, for sessions of at least sixteen hours. Twenty-eight-day mortality fell from thirty-two point eight to sixteen percent.

[[Prone comes first. It's the adjunct with the strongest survival evidence, and both guidelines back it strongly.]] It's cheap, it needs no drug and no machine, only a team. Everything else on this list comes after it.

Next, how much fluid should he get?

steps.bridge: Keeping him dry gave more ventilator-free days, not lower mortality. Next: should I paralyse him →

lesson.text:
Start with the mechanism. In ARDS the capillaries leak. So how much water crosses into the lung depends on the pressure pushing it out. Raise the filling pressures with fluid, and you push more water into the lung. That shrinks the aerated lung, and stiffens it. It's like a leaking hose. The higher you turn the tap, the faster the leak.

So the FACTT trial, in two thousand and six, asked the obvious question. One thousand patients, over seven days. A conservative strategy, aiming for a CVP below four or a wedge pressure below eight. Against a liberal strategy, a CVP of ten to fourteen or a wedge of fourteen to eighteen.

The difference in fluid was huge. Over the week, the conservative arm came out about even, minus one hundred and thirty-six millilitres. The liberal arm was nearly seven litres positive.

And the result? Sixty-day mortality was twenty-five point five against twenty-eight point four percent. Not significant. But ventilator-free days rose, fourteen point six against twelve point one. More ICU-free days. And no increase in shock or in dialysis.

[[Conservative fluids gave more ventilator-free days, not lower mortality.]] That fits the mechanism. Less lung water, more open lung, faster weaning.

And there's a trap on this card. [[FACTT applied only after shock had resolved.]] During shock, too little fluid harms the organs. So the strategy begins once the circulation is stable.

The same trial also compared catheters. A pulmonary artery catheter against a central venous catheter gave the same outcome, twenty-seven point four against twenty-six point three percent, with more catheter complications. So you don't need a PA catheter to guide the fluid plan.

So don't say, conservative fluids reduce mortality. Say, once he's out of shock, I keep him dry, because it gets him off the ventilator sooner.

Now, should you paralyse him?

steps.bridge: ACURASYS helped under deep sedation; ROSE found no benefit. Next: do steroids help →

lesson.text:
This is the story of two trials that seemed to disagree, and why.

The idea behind paralysis is simple. A patient fighting the ventilator, or pulling hard against it, adds his own effort to every breath. That can over-stretch the lung. So stop the effort, and you protect the lung.

ACURASYS, in two thousand and ten, tested it. A cisatracurium infusion for forty-eight hours, in early ARDS with a P to F ratio below one hundred and fifty. It found better adjusted ninety-day survival, less barotrauma, and no excess weakness.

Then ROSE, in two thousand and nineteen, asked the same question again. The same drug, for the same forty-eight hours. And it found no difference in ninety-day mortality. Forty-two point five against forty-two point eight percent.

Why did they differ? Look at the control arms. [[In ACURASYS, the controls were deeply sedated. In ROSE, they were lightly sedated.]] ROSE also used higher PEEP, and there was less proning in ROSE.

So the two trials asked different questions. ACURASYS asked, is paralysis better than deep sedation? ROSE asked, is paralysis better than light sedation? Against light sedation, paralysis added nothing.

[[So paralysis is no longer routine. It's selective: severe dyssynchrony, proning, or a high plateau.]]

And the panel's favourite follow-up: which trial do you believe? Your answer. ROSE reflects how we sedate today, lightly. So I don't paralyse routinely. I use a short course when the patient is fighting the ventilator and I can't protect his lung any other way.

Now, do steroids help?

steps.bridge: Early dexamethasone helps; starting after day 14 harms. Next: when does he need ECMO →

lesson.text:
The steroid story is a story about timing. And to understand it, think about the phases of ARDS.

In the first week, inflammation drives the leak. Steroids damp inflammation, so early on, they meet their target. After about two weeks, the lung has moved into a phase of repair and fibrosis. Inflammation is no longer the main driver. Steroids now have little to work on, but they still cause muscle weakness, and they may impair repair. An extinguisher helps while the fire burns. Sprayed on the wall being rebuilt, it only does damage.

Now the trials fit that shape.

Meduri gave early, low-dose methylprednisolone. ICU mortality was twenty-one against forty-three percent. A small trial, but in the inflammatory phase.

LaSRS went late. One hundred and eighty patients with persistent ARDS, between day seven and day twenty-eight, given methylprednisolone. No difference in sixty-day or one hundred and eighty-day mortality, and more neuromyopathy. And in the patients started fourteen or more days after onset, sixty-day mortality was thirty-five percent with steroids against eight percent without. That's a subgroup, not the trial's main result. But it gave us a rule.

[[Do not start steroids fourteen or more days after the onset of ARDS.]] The rule is about when you start, not how long you give.

Then DEXA-ARDS, in twenty twenty. Two hundred and seventy-seven patients with moderate to severe ARDS, a P to F ratio of two hundred or less, on a PEEP of ten or more and an FiO2 of zero point five or more. Dexamethasone twenty milligrams daily for five days, then ten milligrams daily for five days. Sixty-day mortality fell from thirty-six to twenty-one percent, with more ventilator-free days.

{{**DEXA-ARDS (2020, n = 277)**
P/F ≤200 on PEEP ≥10, FiO₂ ≥0.5
Dexamethasone 20 mg days 1–5 → 10 mg days 6–10
60-day mortality **21% vs 36%**
Timing rule (LaSRS): do not start **≥14 days** after onset}}

[[Early dexamethasone helps. Starting steroids after two weeks harms.]]

And in COVID, RECOVERY showed that dexamethasone six milligrams lowered mortality in patients needing oxygen.

One honest caution. DEXA-ARDS was stopped early because recruitment was slow, at two hundred and seventy-seven of a planned three hundred and fourteen patients. A strong result, but from a trial that ended early.

Now, when does he need ECMO?

steps.bridge: ECMO if hypoxaemia or acidosis persists after optimal care. Next: what the ECMO trials showed →

lesson.text:
You met the ECMO indications in their own lesson. For oxygenation, a P to F ratio below eighty on an FiO2 of zero point nine or more, despite optimal ventilation and prone. EOLIA's version: below fifty for three hours, or below eighty for six. For ventilation, a PaCO2 above eighty, or a plateau you can't keep at thirty or below. EOLIA's version: a pH below seven point two five with a PaCO2 of sixty or more for six hours. Severe air leaks too. And it's relatively contraindicated after more than seven days at high pressures, or with irreversible disease.

[[ECMO comes after optimal ventilation and proning, not instead of them.]]

So what did the ECMO trials show?

steps.bridge: CESAR favoured referral; EOLIA missed significance with crossover. Next: what about inhaled nitric oxide →

lesson.text:
You met these in the ECMO lesson. CESAR, one hundred and eighty patients, tested transfer to an ECMO centre. Survival without disability at six months was sixty-three against forty-seven percent. But only three quarters of that arm actually received ECMO.

EOLIA, two hundred and forty-nine patients, tested early ECMO. Sixty-day mortality was thirty-five against forty-six percent, p of zero point zero nine, not significant. But twenty-eight percent of the controls crossed over to ECMO, and the trial stopped early.

[[CESAR supports referral to a centre. EOLIA missed significance, but leans towards benefit.]]

So what about inhaled nitric oxide?

steps.bridge: It buys oxygenation for a day or two, not survival. Next: where the two guidelines agree and differ →

lesson.text:
You met nitric oxide in its own lesson. Inhaled, it reaches only ventilated alveoli, and dilates the vessels right beside them. So blood is drawn towards the working lung, the match improves, and the pulmonary artery pressure falls without systemic hypotension.

But the oxygenation gain lasts twenty-four to seventy-two hours, and there's no mortality benefit. It brings methaemoglobinaemia, nitrogen dioxide, rebound pulmonary hypertension on withdrawal, and renal dysfunction.

[[Nitric oxide buys oxygen for a day or two, not survival. It's a rescue, not a treatment.]]

Now put it all on one page. Two guidelines matter. The European society's, from twenty twenty-three. And the American Thoracic Society's, from twenty twenty-four. The panel loves to ask where they differ, so let's walk the list and mark each one.

Prone. Both strongly for. The European guideline names a P to F ratio below one fifty and sessions of sixteen hours or more. The American strong recommendation dates from twenty seventeen, and the twenty twenty-four update didn't revisit it.

Fluids. Conservative, once he's out of shock. That's FACTT, more ventilator-free days.

Paralysis. Here they split. The American guideline makes a conditional recommendation for early paralysis in severe ARDS. The European guideline recommends against a routine continuous infusion. Why the split? ROSE, forty-two point five against forty-two point eight percent, no benefit. The two guidelines weighed the same trials differently.

Steroids. The American guideline makes a conditional recommendation for them. And the evidence is DEXA-ARDS, sixty-day mortality twenty-one against thirty-six percent.

VV-ECMO. The European guideline is strong, the American conditional, both by EOLIA criteria.

Extracorporeal carbon dioxide removal, a low-flow circuit used to allow even smaller breaths. The European guideline is strongly against it. The REST trial, in twenty twenty-one, four hundred and twelve patients, found ninety-day mortality of forty-one point five against thirty-nine point five percent. It was stopped for futility, with more adverse events.

And inhaled nitric oxide. Rescue only. It improves oxygenation, not survival.

{{**Severe ARDS: trial and guideline**
Therapy | Key trial | Guideline
Prone | PROSEVA 16.0 vs 32.8% | both strong for
Fluids post-shock | FACTT: VFDs | —
NMB | ROSE 42.5 vs 42.8% | ATS cond. for · ESICM: not routine
Steroids | DEXA-ARDS 21 vs 36% | ATS cond. for
VV-ECMO | EOLIA 35 vs 46% | ESICM strong · ATS cond.
ECCO₂R | REST 41.5 vs 39.5% | ESICM strong against
iNO | O₂, not survival | rescue}}

[[Both guidelines strongly back proning. They split on paralysis, and on how strongly they back ECMO.]]

And throughout, treat the cause. None of this works if the pneumonia isn't treated.

So in the viva, your answer has a shape. Prone, always, when the ratio is under one fifty. Keep him dry once shock is over. Steroids early, in moderate to severe ARDS. Paralysis only when needed, for a short time. ECMO by criteria, at a centre. Nitric oxide as a rescue. And no ECCO2R.

spine: Prone: P/F under 150, within 36 h, 16 hours or more a day. PROSEVA: 28-day mortality 16.0 vs 32.8%. Both guidelines strong for.
Fluids: conservative once out of shock. FACTT: ventilator-free days 14.6 vs 12.1, mortality not different.
Paralysis: ROSE found no benefit (42.5 vs 42.8%). ATS 2024 conditional for early use in severe ARDS; ESICM 2023 against routine infusion.
Steroids: DEXA-ARDS (2020, n = 277), dexamethasone 20 mg then 10 mg: 60-day mortality 21 vs 36%. Do not start 14 or more days after onset.
ECMO: by EOLIA criteria (2018: 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09). ESICM strong, ATS conditional.
Caution: inhaled nitric oxide is rescue only, with no survival benefit. ECCO2R is advised against (REST: 41.5 vs 39.5%, stopped for futility).

open.text:
Let me start with a patient you know.

Our man with pneumonia. Six millilitres per kilo of predicted weight. A plateau of twenty-eight. PEEP from the higher table. And still, his P to F ratio is ninety. You've done everything right on the ventilator, and it isn't enough.

So what else can you do for him? There's a long list. Proning, fluids, paralysis, steroids, ECMO, nitric oxide. Every textbook gives it. And that's the trap. The panel doesn't want the list. Anyone can read it out.

What the professor is really checking is whether you know which of these has proven benefit, which is only a rescue, and which has been tried and shown not to help. And for each, the trial behind it. And, because two major guidelines now exist, where the European and the American guidelines agree and where they don't.

So think of each item as a question that a trial has already asked. Does it save lives? Does it only make the numbers look better? Or does it harm?

Here's the plan. First, prone positioning, briefly, because you know it. Then fluids. Then paralysis. Then steroids. Then ECMO, who needs it, and what its trials showed. Then nitric oxide. And finally, the guideline split, in one place.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Prone first. A P to F ratio under one fifty, within thirty-six hours, sixteen hours or more a day. PROSEVA, sixteen against thirty-two point eight percent. Both guidelines strongly for.]]

Fluids, conservative once he's out of shock. FACTT gave ventilator-free days of fourteen point six against twelve point one, with no difference in mortality.

Paralysis. ROSE found no benefit, forty-two point five against forty-two point eight. The American guideline is conditional for early use in severe ARDS. The European guideline is against a routine infusion.

Steroids. DEXA-ARDS, twenty twenty, two hundred and seventy-seven patients. Dexamethasone twenty milligrams, then ten. Sixty-day mortality twenty-one against thirty-six percent. And never start fourteen or more days after onset.

ECMO by EOLIA criteria. EOLIA, twenty eighteen, thirty-five against forty-six percent, p of zero point zero nine. The European guideline strong, the American conditional.

And the caution. Inhaled nitric oxide is rescue only, with no survival benefit. ECCO2R is advised against. REST, forty-one point five against thirty-nine point five, stopped for futility.

That's your answer. Prone, fluids, paralysis, steroids, ECMO, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. In the last few lessons, you've met more than a dozen trial names. ARMA, PROSEVA, ROSE, ART, FACTT, EOLIA. Each one changed a single rule. Put them together in order, and they tell one story. How intensive care learned, one trial at a time, to stop hurting the ARDS lung.

So when the professor says, tell me the major ARDS trials, can you tell that story? That's next.

questions.text: Tell me the major ARDS trials.

steps.bridge: Small breaths saved lives: the founding trial. Next: what position adds on top →

lesson.text:
The story starts with the ventilator itself.

Animal work had suggested that big breaths injure the lung. So the ARDS Network ran the trial that founded this field. ARMA, published in two thousand.

Eight hundred and sixty-one patients. A tidal volume of six millilitres per kilo of predicted body weight, against the traditional twelve. A plateau limit of thirty in the low-volume arm, against fifty in the traditional arm.

[[Mortality fell from thirty-nine point eight to thirty-one percent. About nine percent absolute. The trial was stopped early, for benefit.]] The low-volume arm also had more ventilator-free and organ-failure-free days.

And here's the detail that makes the whole story. In the first days, oxygenation was worse in the low-volume arm. Yet survival was better.

[[ARMA's real lesson: the breath that makes the blood gas look better can be the breath that kills.]]

Many of the trials that follow are a version of that idea. And say predicted body weight, never actual. Fifteen years later, Amato's re-analysis of nine ventilation trials sharpened the message. What mattered most was the driving pressure, the breath measured against the open lung.

So after breath size, the next question was position.

steps.bridge: Prone halved 28-day deaths in severe ARDS. Next: does paralysing the patient help too →

lesson.text:
You know PROSEVA well by now. Twenty thirteen. A P to F ratio below one hundred and fifty, proned early, within thirty-six hours, for at least sixteen hours a day. Twenty-eight-day mortality fell from thirty-two point eight to sixteen percent.

The story here is persistence. Earlier prone trials had been negative, because they proned late, briefly, and in milder ARDS. PROSEVA asked the same question with the right dose and the right patients. [[A treatment can fail a trial because it was given wrongly, not because it doesn't work.]]

Next, does paralysing the patient help too?

steps.bridge: ROSE overturned ACURASYS once controls were lightly sedated. Next: what forcing the lung open did →

lesson.text:
You met these two in the non-ventilatory lesson. ACURASYS, in two thousand and ten, gave cisatracurium for forty-eight hours in early severe ARDS, and found better adjusted survival. ROSE, in twenty nineteen, repeated it, and found no difference, forty-two point five against forty-two point eight percent.

The story here is the control arm. ACURASYS compared paralysis with deep sedation. ROSE compared it with light sedation. [[ROSE overturned ACURASYS, because the comparison had changed.]]

So paralysis is now selective. Next, what happened when we tried to force the lung open?

steps.bridge: Recruitment plus titrated PEEP raised mortality in ART. Next: what keeping the lung dry achieves →

lesson.text:
You met ART in the recruitment lesson. Published in twenty seventeen, just over a thousand patients. Stepwise recruitment manoeuvres, with PEEP titrated to the best compliance, against a low PEEP strategy. Twenty-eight-day mortality rose, fifty-five point three against forty-nine point three percent, with more barotrauma.

Here's ARMA's lesson again. Forcing the lung open seems logical. Open alveoli, better oxygen. [[But force on the ARDS lung, however well meant, cost lives.]]

Next, the water in the lung.

steps.bridge: Conservative fluid gave ventilator-free days, not survival. Next: where steroids now stand →

lesson.text:
You met FACTT in the non-ventilatory lesson. Two thousand and six, one thousand patients, a conservative fluid strategy against a liberal one, once shock had resolved. Ventilator-free days rose, fourteen point six against twelve point one. Sixty-day mortality was not different.

The story here is honest. [[Some trials improve how fast the patient gets off the ventilator, without changing who survives.]] That still matters. But don't upgrade it to a mortality benefit.

Next, where do steroids stand?

steps.bridge: Early dexamethasone helped; late steroids harm. Next: the rescue trial for the sickest →

lesson.text:
You met the steroid trials in the non-ventilatory lesson. Meduri's early methylprednisolone looked helpful. LaSRS, given late, showed no benefit and more neuromyopathy, and in patients started after two weeks, harm. Then DEXA-ARDS, in twenty twenty. Early dexamethasone in moderate to severe ARDS cut sixty-day mortality from thirty-six to twenty-one percent.

[[The steroid story is about timing. Early may help. Late harms.]]

And finally, the rescue trial for the very sickest.

steps.bridge: EOLIA missed its primary end-point but leans to benefit. Next: all of them on one page →

lesson.text:
You met these in the ECMO lesson. CESAR favoured transfer to an ECMO centre, sixty-three against forty-seven percent surviving without disability. EOLIA, in twenty eighteen, tested early ECMO. Sixty-day mortality was thirty-five against forty-six percent, with a p value of zero point zero nine, so it missed its primary end-point. But twenty-eight percent of the controls crossed over to ECMO.

And a later Bayesian re-analysis of EOLIA favoured benefit from ECMO in very severe ARDS. [[A trial that misses significance is not proof of no effect.]]

Now let's put them all on one page.

Here are eight trials, each with the question it asked and its verdict.

{{**ARDS trials at a glance**
Trial | Tested | Verdict
ARMA | 6 vs 12 mL/kg | mortality ↓
PROSEVA | prone ≥16 h | mortality ↓
ACURASYS | cisatracurium 48 h | benefit
ROSE | cisatracurium 48 h | no difference
FACTT | conservative fluids | more VFDs only
OSCILLATE | HFOV | mortality ↑
ART | recruitment + high PEEP | mortality ↑
EOLIA | early VV-ECMO | not significant}}

There's one on the list you haven't met in these lessons. OSCILLATE, in twenty thirteen, tested high-frequency oscillation. Tiny breaths at a very high rate, on top of a high mean airway pressure, to hold the lung open. It raised mortality.

Now step back and look for the pattern. It's the story we've been telling.

Two trials clearly cut mortality, and both still stand. ARMA and PROSEVA. One makes each breath smaller. The other spreads it more evenly. Both are gentler on the lung.

Two trials raised mortality. ART and OSCILLATE. Both used high pressure to force the lung open.

And the rest are selective or neutral. Paralysis, once the control arm changed. Fluids, which shortened ventilation without changing survival. ECMO, which missed significance but leans to benefit. And steroids sit outside this pattern. DEXA-ARDS cut mortality by damping inflammation, not by changing the breath.

[[On this table, the trials that cut mortality were gentler on the lung. The ones that forced it open did harm.]]

So your sixty-second answer sounds like this. I'd group them by what they tested. Breath size, ARMA. Position, PROSEVA. Paralysis, ACURASYS and then ROSE. Opening the lung, ART and OSCILLATE, both harmful. Fluids, FACTT. Steroids, DEXA-ARDS. Rescue, EOLIA. And then the line the professor wants. [[Small breaths and early proning I always do. The rest I use selectively.]]

spine: Breath size: **ARMA** (2000, 861 patients): 6 vs 12 mL/kg predicted weight cut mortality **31.0 vs 39.8%**. It founded lung-protective ventilation.
Position: **PROSEVA** (2013): prone ≥16 h a day when P/F <150 cut 28-day mortality **16.0 vs 32.8%**.
Paralysis: **ACURASYS** suggested benefit, but **ROSE** (2019), with lightly sedated controls, found none (**42.5 vs 42.8%**). Not routine.
Opening the lung: **ART** (2017): recruitment with titrated PEEP raised 28-day mortality (**55.3 vs 49.3%**). Fluids: **FACTT**: conservative gave more ventilator-free days, same mortality.
Steroids: **DEXA-ARDS** (2020): early dexamethasone cut 60-day mortality **21 vs 36%**. Rescue: **EOLIA** (2018): ECMO 35 vs 46%, p = 0.09; primary end-point missed.
Practice change: small breaths and early proning I always do; the rest I use selectively. EOLIA's Bayesian re-analysis favours ECMO in the sickest.

open.text:
Let me start with a question. Why was it ever normal to give a patient with ARDS a big breath?

ARDS was first described in nineteen sixty-seven, in a small series of adults whose lungs suddenly became stiff, flooded and unable to oxygenate. For most of the next three decades, the instinct at the bedside was understandable. The blood gases were terrible, so you made them look better. Larger breaths. More pressure. More oxygen. Push the numbers towards normal.

And then, one trial after another, intensive care learned the same hard lesson. Making the numbers look better is not the same as saving the patient. Often, it's the opposite.

That's the story of the major ARDS trials. And it's how you should tell it in the viva.

When the professor says, tell me the major ARDS trials, the trap is to recite names and numbers in a list. Name, year, percentage, next. He'll stop listening by the third one. What he's really checking is whether you can group them by the question each trial asked, give the key numbers for the big ones, and say which ones changed your practice and which didn't.

You've already met almost every one of these trials in other lessons. So today we won't re-teach them. We'll string them together into one story, with a short reminder on each.

Here's the plan. Breath size, the founding trial. Then position. Then paralysis. Then forcing the lung open. Then fluid. Then steroids. Then the rescue for the sickest. And finally, all of them on one page.

close.text:
So let's bring it together, as one story.

Breath size founded the field. ARMA, two thousand, eight hundred and sixty-one patients. Six against twelve millilitres per kilo of predicted weight cut mortality from thirty-nine point eight to thirty-one percent, even though oxygenation was worse at first.

Position came next. PROSEVA, twenty thirteen. Prone for sixteen hours or more a day when the P to F ratio is under one fifty cut twenty-eight-day mortality from thirty-two point eight to sixteen percent.

Paralysis. ACURASYS suggested benefit. But ROSE, in twenty nineteen, with lightly sedated controls, found none, forty-two point five against forty-two point eight. Not routine.

Opening the lung by force. ART, twenty seventeen. Recruitment with titrated PEEP raised twenty-eight-day mortality, fifty-five point three against forty-nine point three. And fluids. FACTT, more ventilator-free days, the same mortality.

Steroids. DEXA-ARDS, twenty twenty. Early dexamethasone cut sixty-day mortality from thirty-six to twenty-one percent. And the rescue, EOLIA, twenty eighteen. ECMO, thirty-five against forty-six percent, a p value of zero point zero nine, missing its end-point, but leaning to benefit.

[[What changed my practice: small breaths and early proning, always. The rest, selectively. And EOLIA's Bayesian re-analysis favours ECMO in very severe ARDS.]]

That's your answer. Breath size, position, paralysis, opening the lung and fluids, steroids and rescue, and how it changed practice.

But here's something to carry forward. Every one of these trials began the same way. A breathless patient, and a doctor at the bedside trying to work out what was wrong. Is this ARDS? Or is it pulmonary oedema, a pneumothorax, a pulmonary embolism?

Today, you can often answer that before the X-ray arrives, with a probe in your hand. That's point-of-care ultrasound of the lung, and the BLUE protocol, a structured way to read it in the breathless patient. And it's next.

questions.text: What is POCUS? Describe lung ultrasound.

steps.bridge: Sliding or B-lines mean the pleura touch; the lung point proves pneumothorax. Next: what airless lung looks like →

lesson.text:
Start where every scan starts, at the pleural line. Put the probe between two ribs. The ribs cast two dark shadows, and between them, a little deeper, runs a bright horizontal line. That is the pleura.

Now, normally there are two layers there. The parietal pleura on the chest wall, and the visceral pleura on the lung, with a thin film of fluid between them. With each breath the lung slides down and up against the chest wall. And on the screen you see that line shimmer. That's lung sliding.

Think of two panes of wet glass sliding over each other. Now slip a sheet of air between them. Ultrasound cannot see past the air, so it sees only the front pane. And the front pane, the chest wall, doesn't move.

[[So lung sliding means the lung is touching the chest wall at that spot. Where you see sliding, there is no pneumothorax.]]

Second, B-lines. These are the vertical comet tails. They start at the pleural line, they move with sliding, and they run all the way to the bottom of the screen. Here's the key. B-lines are born at the visceral pleura, so they can only form where the lung is touching the wall. [[B-lines rule out pneumothorax at that spot. Their negative predictive value is one hundred percent.]]

Now the trap. Most residents think A-lines mean normal lung. A-lines are only echoes of the pleural line, repeating down the screen. And air reflects the beam just as well when it sits in the pleural space. [[So A-lines are seen in normal lung, and in pneumothorax. They tell you there's air under the line, not where that air is.]]

Third, the lung point. At the edge of a pneumothorax, the collapsed lung touches the chest wall on inspiration and peels away on expiration. So in one spot, sliding switches on and off. Nothing else does that. [[The lung point is one hundred percent specific for pneumothorax.]] One caution: in a very large pneumothorax the lung never reaches the wall, so there may be no lung point at all.

Fourth, M-mode, which draws one line of the image over time. Moving lung gives a grainy pattern below the pleural line, like sand under a calm sea. That's the seashore sign. No movement gives straight lines all the way down. That's the barcode sign, also called the stratosphere sign.

And finally, the honest caution. Sliding also stops when the lung is not being ventilated, or is stuck to the wall. A tube in the other main bronchus. Pleural adhesions. A blocked bronchus. A paralysed diaphragm. So absent sliding alone is not proof.

Now, what happens when the lung loses not just its contact, but its air?

steps.bridge: Consolidated lung looks like liver; a dynamic air bronchogram means pneumonia. Next: how pleural fluid looks and is measured →

lesson.text:
Normally the air in the lung hides everything beneath the pleura. But when the alveoli fill with pus, fluid or cells, or collapse, the air is gone. And now the beam can travel into the lung, just as it travels into the liver.

[[Consolidated lung has lost its air, so ultrasound can see into it. It looks like liver. That's called hepatisation.]]

Look at the deep edge of that consolidation, where it meets the aerated lung behind it. It isn't smooth. It's ragged and irregular. That's the shred sign. And when the consolidation lies at the front of the chest, the BLUE protocol calls that the C-profile.

Now look inside it. You'll often see bright dots or short lines. That's air still trapped in the small airways, the air bronchograms. And here is the question the panel loves. Is this pneumonia, or is it atelectasis?

Watch the bright dots as the patient breathes. If they move with each breath, air is flowing in and out of the airway. So the airway is open. And if the airway is open, this cannot be resorption atelectasis, which needs a blocked airway. [[A dynamic air bronchogram means an open airway, so it points to pneumonia, with high specificity.]] Lichtenstein described this in Chest in two thousand and nine.

If the dots are still, the air bronchogram is static. That can be either pneumonia or atelectasis. Two more clues help. Atelectasis loses volume. And it often shows a lung pulse: no sliding, but the heartbeat transmitted through the airless lung to the pleural line.

[[A static air bronchogram, with volume loss and a lung pulse, suggests atelectasis.]]

And if the airways inside are filled with fluid instead of air, think of an obstructed bronchus behind the consolidation.

One link to carry forward. In the BLUE protocol, consolidation or effusion at the back and side of the chest is called PLAPS, posterolateral alveolar or pleural syndrome. You'll meet it in a moment.

So that's airless lung. Now what about fluid that sits outside the lung?

steps.bridge: Effusion is a black space, and its depth gives the volume. Next: how BLUE turns these signs into a diagnosis →

lesson.text:
Pure fluid has nothing inside it to reflect sound. So it is black, anechoic. But add protein, fibrin, cells or debris, and each of those gives an echo.

That simple fact gives you the four ultrasound patterns of an effusion. Anechoic. Complex non-septated. Complex septated. And homogeneously echogenic.

Think of clear water in a glass, which is black on the scan, and a bowl of soup with strands in it, which shows up.

[[Anechoic fluid can be a transudate or an exudate. Any complex pattern means an exudate.]] Echogenic fluid throughout suggests pus or blood.

Now, how much fluid is there? In a supine patient, at the lung base, at the end of expiration, measure the widest distance between the lung and the chest wall. That's the interpleural distance. The volume in millilitres is about twenty times that distance in millimetres.

{{**Volume (mL) ≈ 20 × interpleural distance (mm)**
Supine, at the lung base, end-expiration (Balik formula)
Example: 30 mm → about 600 mL}}

So a gap of thirty millimetres means roughly six hundred millilitres. Treat it as an estimate, not an exact number.

And where does ultrasound beat CT? [[Ultrasound is better than CT at seeing septations, and at guiding the needle.]] Septations are thin and they move. Ultrasound watches them moving in real time, and shows you the safest pocket to drain.

What does contrast CT add? It separates fluid from thickened pleura, and a mass from a loculated effusion. And if the pleura enhances, it's inflamed, which suggests an exudate or empyema.

Now you have every sign. The last card puts them together in the breathless patient.

In two thousand and eight, Daniel Lichtenstein published the BLUE protocol in Chest. Bedside lung ultrasound in emergency. The idea is simple. Scan a few standard points on each side of the chest, add a scan of the leg veins, and read the pattern.

At the front of the chest, two things are recorded. Is there sliding? And are the lines A-lines or B-lines?

Now walk the diagnoses, and for each one ask why.

Pulmonary oedema gives the B-profile. Sliding, with B-lines on both sides at the front. Why both sides? Because cardiogenic water fills the septa everywhere.

[[The B-profile, sliding with bilateral anterior B-lines, means pulmonary oedema.]]

Pneumothorax gives the A-prime profile. The prime means sliding is abolished. So no sliding, and A-lines. Then you look for the lung point to confirm it. A-prime with a lung point has a sensitivity of eighty-eight percent and a specificity of one hundred percent. A-prime without a lung point needs another test.

Now here's the clever part. Look at the A-profile: sliding with A-lines at the front. The front lung is dry. So the cause of the breathlessness is not in the lung tissue there. It's somewhere else. In the vessels, in the airways, or at the back.

[[A dry anterior lung is not a normal answer. It tells you to look in the veins, the airways, or the back of the chest.]]

So with the A-profile, scan the legs. A venous thrombosis makes pulmonary embolism the answer, because in PE the lung itself stays dry. If the veins are free, look at the back for PLAPS. Consolidation or effusion there means pneumonia. And if the veins are free and there's no PLAPS, the problem is in the airways: COPD or asthma.

Pneumonia can show other profiles too, because it is a local, patchy process. The B-prime profile, B-lines without sliding, from inflammatory adhesion. The A-B profile, B-lines on one side only. Or the C-profile, consolidation at the front.

{{**BLUE profile → diagnosis**
B (sliding + bilateral B-lines) | pulmonary oedema
A′ (no sliding, A-lines) + lung point | pneumothorax
A + venous thrombosis | PE
A, veins free, no PLAPS | COPD or asthma
A + PLAPS; B′; A/B; C | pneumonia}}

And the overall accuracy in that study was about ninety percent.

One honest caution. BLUE was built for the breathless patient arriving in the emergency setting. In a ventilated ICU patient, many states overlap, so use it as a framework for your reasoning, not as a verdict.

spine: What it is: POCUS is bedside ultrasound done by the treating doctor to answer a focused question. Lung ultrasound reads the pleura and its artefacts: A-lines and B-lines.
Pleura: lung sliding or B-lines rule out pneumothorax at that spot. The lung point is 100% specific for it. On M-mode, absent sliding gives the barcode sign.
Consolidation: lung looks like liver, with a shred sign. A dynamic air bronchogram means pneumonia; a static one with a lung pulse suggests atelectasis.
Effusion: anechoic, complex non-septated, complex septated or echogenic. Volume (mL) is about 20 × interpleural distance (mm). Septations show better than on CT.
Evidence: BLUE protocol (Lichtenstein, Chest 2008): profile B = pulmonary oedema; A' plus lung point = pneumothorax; A plus venous clot = PE; A plus PLAPS = pneumonia.

open.text:
Let me start with a paradox.

Ultrasound cannot see through air. Sound hits the boundary between tissue and air and bounces straight back. And the lung is a bag of air. So for a long time, the lung was thought to be the one organ ultrasound could never examine.

And yet today, at the bedside of a breathless patient, a probe on the chest can tell you in a few minutes whether he has pulmonary oedema, a pneumothorax, a pneumonia, or an effusion. Often before the X-ray has even been taken.

How? Because we stopped trying to see the lung, and started reading what the air does to the beam. The artefacts themselves are the signal.

First, the word itself. POCUS means point-of-care ultrasound. [[Point-of-care ultrasound is ultrasound done at the bedside, by the doctor treating the patient, to answer one focused question that changes what he does next.]] Not a full radiology study. A yes or no, here and now, and you can repeat it whenever the patient changes.

Now hold one frame in your head for the whole of this lesson. Lung ultrasound sees only a few states of the lung. Dry, aerated lung acts like a mirror and gives horizontal echoes, the A-lines. Wet lung, with water in the septa, gives vertical comet tails, the B-lines. Airless lung looks like solid tissue, like liver. And fluid outside the lung is simply black.

[[Dry lung is a mirror, wet lung is comet tails, airless lung looks like liver, and fluid is black.]]

What is the professor really checking? Can you define POCUS cleanly. Do you know what the normal pleura looks like and what each sign means. Can you describe consolidation and effusion. And can you put it all together in the breathless patient, with the BLUE protocol.

So here is the plan. First the pleura, and pneumothorax. Then airless lung. Then fluid. And finally, the protocol that turns all of these signs into a diagnosis.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[POCUS is focused ultrasound at the bedside, by the treating doctor, to answer one question that changes management.]] Lung ultrasound reads the pleura and the artefacts that air creates.

The pleura first. Sliding or B-lines mean the lung touches the wall, so no pneumothorax there. The lung point proves pneumothorax. On M-mode, absent sliding gives the barcode sign.

Airless lung looks like liver, with a shred sign. A dynamic air bronchogram means pneumonia. A static one, with a lung pulse and volume loss, suggests atelectasis.

Fluid is black when pure, complex when it's an exudate. Twenty times the interpleural distance gives the volume. And ultrasound sees septations better than CT.

[[Then BLUE puts it together. The B-profile is oedema. A-prime with a lung point is pneumothorax. A dry front with a leg clot is PE. A dry front with PLAPS is pneumonia.]]

That's your answer. What it is, the signs, what they mean, and the protocol.

But here's something to carry forward. Of all these signs, the panel's favourite spotter is the one where a missed diagnosis kills quickly. A ventilated patient, a sudden fall in saturation, and a probe in your hand. How exactly do you prove, or exclude, a pneumothorax? That's next.

questions.text: How do you diagnose pneumothorax on ultrasound?

steps.bridge: Sliding or B-lines exclude it; the lung point confirms it. Next: where pneumothorax sits in the BLUE scan of the breathless patient →

lesson.text: You met this card in the last lesson. Sliding and B-lines both need the visceral pleura against the chest wall, so either one rules out pneumothorax at that spot, with a negative predictive value of one hundred percent. A-lines appear in both normal lung and pneumothorax, so they never decide it. The lung point is one hundred percent specific, and on M-mode, absent sliding turns the seashore into a barcode. Today, use it as your sequence: rule out with sliding, rule in with the lung point, and remember the list of things that stop sliding without any pneumothorax.

You met this too. In BLUE, the A-prime profile means no sliding with A-lines at the front, and adding a lung point gives pneumothorax, with a sensitivity of eighty-eight percent and a specificity of one hundred percent. Why does that matter here? Because A-prime without a lung point is not yet a diagnosis. In a large pneumothorax the lung may never reach the wall. If the patient is stable, confirm with another test. If he's crashing with tension physiology, you treat the patient.

spine: What I look for: lung sliding at the pleural line. Sliding present = no pneumothorax at that spot.
Rule out: B-lines also exclude pneumothorax there (negative predictive value 100%).
Rule in: the lung point, where sliding meets no sliding, is 100% specific. On M-mode, absent sliding gives the barcode (stratosphere) sign, not the seashore sign.
Evidence: in the BLUE protocol (Lichtenstein, Chest 2008), profile A' (no sliding, A-lines) plus a lung point = pneumothorax.
Caution: absent sliding is not always pneumothorax. Think of mainstem intubation of the other side, pleural adhesions, endobronchial obstruction, diaphragm paralysis.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient.

Patient A is on the ventilator after a subclavian line. Suddenly his saturation falls, and the peak and the plateau rise together. Remember what that pattern means. Less lung for the same breath. And a tension pneumothorax is on your list.

The portable X-ray is coming. But he's supine. And in a supine patient, free air rises to the front of the chest, the highest point, and spreads out in a thin sheet over the lung. On a supine film that sheet is easy to miss. The ultrasound probe, placed on the front of the chest, sits right on top of it.

What is the professor really checking with this spotter? Not a list of signs. He wants your logic. Which signs rule it out. Which one rules it in. And which finding fools people.

So build it in that order.

[[Rule out first. If you see sliding, or B-lines, or a lung pulse, the lung is touching the wall at that spot, and there's no pneumothorax there.]] A lung pulse is the heartbeat transmitted through the lung to the pleural line. It too needs the lung to touch the wall.

If all three are absent, you have A-lines with no sliding. Now you hunt. Move the probe out, towards the side of the chest, looking for the place where sliding appears and disappears with the breath.

[[Rule in with the lung point, where sliding meets no sliding.]]

And keep one caution ready, because it's the classic trap. Patient B was intubated in a hurry, and the tube has slipped into the right main bronchus. The left lung isn't being ventilated, so on the left there's no sliding. But there's no air in the pleura. The lung is still touching the wall. And so you'll often still see the lung pulse. Pull the tube back, and the sliding returns.

So the two cards today are ones you've met. We'll revisit them quickly, with this question in mind.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[I look for sliding at the pleural line. Sliding, B-lines or a lung pulse rule out pneumothorax at that spot.]]

A-lines alone decide nothing. They are seen in normal lung and in pneumothorax.

[[The lung point, where sliding meets no sliding, is one hundred percent specific.]] On M-mode, absent sliding gives the barcode sign, not the seashore.

In BLUE, A-prime with a lung point means pneumothorax.

And the caution. Absent sliding is not always pneumothorax. Think of a tube in the other main bronchus, adhesions, a blocked bronchus, or a paralysed diaphragm.

That's your answer to the spotter. What you look for, what rules it out, what rules it in, the evidence, and the trap.

But here's something to carry forward. Today, every sign was a yes or a no. Air in the pleura, or not. But in ARDS, in weaning, in fluid decisions, you don't want yes or no. You want how much. How much of this lung has lost its air? Can you put a number on it? That's the lung ultrasound score, and it's next.

questions.text: Spotter: lung ultrasound score image.

steps.bridge: The score runs 0–36: higher means more water and less air. Next: which cut-offs predict the weaning outcome →

lesson.text:
First, the map. Each side of the chest is divided into three zones, anterior, lateral and posterior, and each zone into upper and lower. Six regions a side. Twelve in all.

In each region, you give a score from zero to three. And the four grades are simply the ladder of air loss you already know.

Look at the picture on your screen.

{{pic}}

Zero is normal aeration. A-lines, with two B-lines at most. One is three or more B-lines, well separated. A few wet septa. Two is coalescent B-lines. They've merged into a white field, because much more of the lung is wet. And three is consolidation. The air is gone, and the lung looks like tissue.

[[Zero is A-lines, one is separate B-lines, two is coalescent B-lines, and three is consolidation.]]

Add the twelve regions together and you get a total from zero to thirty-six.

[[The higher the score, the more water and the less air.]]

Think of a frosted window. Clear at first. Then a few streaks. Then the streaks merge and it fogs over. And finally it's solid white.

Let's work one example. Four regions score one, four score two, two score three, and two score zero.

{{4 × 1 + 4 × 2 + 2 × 3 + 2 × 0 = 4 + 8 + 6 = **18**}}

Four, plus eight, plus six. A total of eighteen. Hold that number. We'll see in a moment what it predicts.

Now the uses. It grades ARDS severity and lets you follow it day by day. It tells you about fluid tolerance: if B-lines are rising as you give fluid, the lung is getting wetter. And it helps with PEEP. Bouhemad and colleagues, in two thousand and eleven, used a re-aeration score built on this same ladder. If the score falls as you raise PEEP, lung is re-aerating. That's recruitment you can see.

And now the blind spot, which the panel will test. Over-distended lung is still full of air. So on ultrasound it looks normal. A-lines.

[[Ultrasound cannot see over-distension. A falling score shows re-aeration, but it can't warn you of over-stretch, so check the driving pressure as well.]]

So you can see the lung opening. Can you also predict whether it will stay open when the ventilator is taken away?
lesson.cap: Each of 12 regions scores 0–3: A-lines, separate B-lines, coalescent B-lines, consolidation.

lesson.text:
Think of what a breathing trial really is. Taking the patient off positive pressure hands three loads back to him at once.

The diaphragm has to do the work. The lung has to stay open without PEEP. And the heart has to cope with a chest pressure that swings more negative with each breath.

[[A spontaneous breathing trial is a stress test of the pump, the lung and the heart, all at once.]] And ultrasound can look at each of them.

First the pump. The diaphragm. Two numbers. Excursion is how far the dome moves. An excursion below ten millimetres means diaphragm dysfunction, and it predicts failure. Thickening fraction is how much the muscle thickens as it contracts. Thirty to thirty-six percent or more predicts success. We'll take the diaphragm apart properly in a later lesson.

Second, the lung. Here's where your score comes in. Soummer and colleagues, in two thousand and twelve, looked at it in patients being extubated.

[[A lung score below thirteen predicts extubation success. Above seventeen predicts failure. Between thirteen and seventeen is uncertain.]]

So your worked example, eighteen, predicts failure. Why? Because a poorly aerated lung, once PEEP is gone, loses even more air.

Third, the heart. When the patient breathes on his own, the chest pressure falls more. That raises the venous return, and it raises the afterload on the left ventricle, and the stress of the trial adds an adrenergic surge. A weak or stiff ventricle can't cope, and the pressure backs up into the lung. That's weaning-induced pulmonary oedema.

So an ejection fraction below forty percent predicts failure. So do raised filling pressures: an E over A ratio above two when the ejection fraction is low, or an E over e prime above twelve.

And the last one is clever. Raise the legs. If the cardiac output doesn't rise, the heart is on the flat part of its Starling curve. Then the extra venous return of the trial raises the filling pressure, not the output, and floods the lung.

{{Measure | Value | Predicts
Diaphragm excursion | <10 mm | dysfunction, failure
Thickening fraction | ≥30–36% | success
Lung ultrasound score | <13 | success
Lung ultrasound score | >17 | failure (13–17 uncertain)
LV ejection fraction | <40% | failure
Filling pressure | E/A >2 (low EF) or E/e′ >12 | failure
Leg raising | no rise in output | failure}}

[[The pump, the lung and the heart. Each one can fail the trial, and each one has its own ultrasound sign.]]

One honest caution. These are predictors from single studies, each in its own population. Use them together, with the clinical picture, not as a single cut-off that decides for you.

spine: What it is: the lung ultrasound score. 12 regions (anterior, lateral, posterior; upper and lower; each side), each scored 0–3, total 0–36.
Grades: 0 = A-lines (≤2 B-lines); 1 = ≥3 separated B-lines; 2 = coalescent B-lines; 3 = consolidation. Higher score = more water, less air.
Weaning: score <13 predicts extubation success; >17 predicts failure; 13–17 is uncertain. A score of 18 predicts failure.
Other uses: ARDS severity and follow-up, fluid tolerance (rising B-lines), and PEEP: a falling score shows re-aeration.
Caution: ultrasound cannot see over-distension, so check driving pressure too. Evidence: Bouhemad (AJRCCM 2011) for re-aeration; Soummer (Crit Care Med 2012) for weaning.

open.text:
Let me start with the picture the examiner hands you.

A chest drawn with twelve boxes on it. In each box a small ultrasound image, and next to each a number, zero, one, two or three. And a total at the bottom. Spotter. What is this?

It's the lung ultrasound score. And the question behind it is a good one. We've seen that ultrasound can tell dry lung from wet lung and from airless lung. But in the ICU you rarely need to know only whether. You need to know how much, and whether it's getting better.

Think back to the baby lung. In ARDS, the trouble is how much of the lung has lost its air. CT shows that beautifully, but you can't take the patient to CT every day. The score gives you a rough version of that same picture, at the bedside, as often as you like.

What is the professor really checking? Do you know how the score is built, the twelve regions and the four grades. Do you know what it is used for. And do you know its blind spot.

So the plan. First the score itself and what it measures. Then what it predicts when you take the patient off the ventilator, beside the other ultrasound predictors of weaning.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[The lung ultrasound score divides the chest into twelve regions and scores each from zero to three. The total runs from zero to thirty-six.]]

Zero is A-lines. One is separate B-lines. Two is coalescent B-lines. Three is consolidation. The higher the score, the more water and the less air.

For weaning, below thirteen predicts success, above seventeen predicts failure, and in between is uncertain. A score of eighteen predicts failure.

It follows ARDS, warns you when fluid is making the lung wetter, and shows re-aeration with PEEP.

[[And the caution: ultrasound cannot see over-distension, so check the driving pressure too.]]

That's your answer to the spotter. What it is, the grades, the cut-offs, the uses, and the blind spot.

But here's something to carry forward. Today, grade three was simply consolidation. Now imagine the examiner's next picture. A black space at the base, and floating inside it, a piece of solid lung. Two things at once, fluid and airless lung. Which came first, and what does it mean? That's next.

questions.text: Spotter - lung ultrasound showing pleural effusion with consolidation.

steps.bridge: Flapping lung in fluid is compression; liver-like lung with moving air is pneumonia. Next: how to grade and size the effusion →

lesson.text:
Start with proving it's fluid. Fluid is black, but so are other things. Two signs settle it.

The first is the quad sign. Between two ribs, the black space is framed like a box. The pleural line on the chest-wall side, the lung line on the deep side, which is the surface of the lung, and the two rib shadows at the edges. A collection sitting between the chest wall and the lung.

The second is on M-mode. With each breath, the lung swings towards the chest wall and away again, through the fluid. Over time, that line draws a wave. That's the sinusoid sign.

[[The quad sign shows fluid in the pleural space, and the sinusoid sign shows lung swinging through it with each breath.]]

Now look at the fluid itself. Uniform black can be a transudate or an exudate. But septations, debris, or swirling echoes suggest an exudate, or an empyema.

Now the second question. Why is the lung airless?

Picture Patient A. A large effusion, and the lung at the base floating in it, flapping with each breath like a flag in water. No air bronchograms inside it. That lung has simply been squeezed. Compressive, or passive, atelectasis. The airway is open, there's no infection, and once you drain the fluid, it re-aerates.

[[Lung flapping in a large effusion, with no air bronchograms, is compressive atelectasis. It re-expands once you drain.]]

Now Patient B. The lung beneath the fluid looks like liver. And inside it, bright dots of air move in and out with each breath. You know that sign. A dynamic air bronchogram. The airway is open and air is moving through a consolidated lung. That's pneumonia.

[[Consolidation with dynamic air bronchograms is pneumonia. So the effusion beside it is parapneumonic, and you sample it.]]

Why sample? Because a parapneumonic effusion can turn into an infected, walled-off collection, and only the fluid will tell you. And you do it under ultrasound guidance, at the deepest pocket, away from the lung and the diaphragm.

Last, measure it. The interpleural distance at the base gives you the volume. That's the next card.

steps.bridge: Ultrasound sizes it and sees septations better than CT. Next: how much fluid the chest X-ray misses →

lesson.text: You met this card with lung ultrasound. Four patterns: anechoic, complex non-septated, complex septated, and homogeneously echogenic. Anechoic can be either, but any complex pattern means an exudate. The volume in millilitres is about twenty times the interpleural distance in millimetres, supine, at the base, at end-expiration. Here it matters because the pattern and the size are your first clues to whether this effusion is infected, and ultrasound sees septations better than CT.

Why does all this matter? Because the examination and the chest film miss a lot of fluid.

Start with your hands. Below about three hundred millilitres, the clinical examination can be normal. That number belongs to the examination, not to the film.

Now the erect film. About seventy-five millilitres blunts the posterior sulcus, which you see on the lateral view. About one hundred and seventy-five to two hundred blunts the lateral costophrenic angle on the PA film. And about five hundred hides the diaphragm. The most sensitive film is the lateral decubitus, lying on the side of the effusion, which shows a few tens of millilitres. And ultrasound sees just a few millilitres.

[[Below three hundred millilitres the examination can be normal. The PA film needs about two hundred to blunt the angle, and five hundred to hide the diaphragm.]]

And in your ICU patient, lying flat, the fluid spreads out behind the lung. So the signs change. A blunted costophrenic angle comes first. Then a veil-like haze over the lung, a lost outline of the diaphragm, lower-lobe vessels that are harder to see, and a diaphragm that seems raised.

spine: What I see: an anechoic space above the diaphragm (quad sign; sinusoid sign on M-mode), with consolidated, tissue-like lung beneath it.
