What it means: lung flapping in fluid with no air bronchograms = compressive atelectasis. Dynamic air bronchograms = pneumonia, so a parapneumonic effusion.
Pattern: anechoic, complex non-septated, complex septated or homogeneously echogenic. Septations, debris or swirl suggest an exudate or empyema.
Size: volume (mL) ≈ 20 × interpleural distance (mm) at the base, end-expiration. Examination can be normal below 300 mL; erect PA blunting needs about 200.
What I do: sample a parapneumonic effusion under ultrasound guidance. Evidence: Lichtenstein (Chest 2009) for the dynamic air bronchogram.

open.text:
Here's the image.

The probe is on the side of the chest, low down, aimed at the base. Below, you can see the liver and the bright curve of the diaphragm. Above the diaphragm there's a black space. And inside that black space, moving with each breath, a piece of grey, solid-looking tissue.

That's lung. Airless lung, sitting in an effusion.

Now this spotter has two questions inside it, and residents usually answer only one. The first is easy. Is there fluid? Yes. The second is the one that matters. Why is the lung airless? Has the fluid simply squeezed it, or is the lung itself infected?

Because the answer decides what you do. If the fluid is just compressing the lung, draining it lets the lung re-expand. If the lung is a pneumonia, the fluid next to it is a parapneumonic effusion, and it may be infected. And then you must sample it.

[[Two questions in every effusion spotter. What is the fluid, and why is the lung airless?]]

So the plan. First, how you prove it's fluid, and how you read the lung inside it. Then how you grade and size the effusion. And finally, how much fluid the chest X-ray can miss.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

What I see: a black space above the diaphragm, with the quad sign, and the sinusoid sign on M-mode. And solid, tissue-like lung beneath it.

[[Lung flapping in fluid with no air bronchograms is compressive atelectasis. Dynamic air bronchograms mean pneumonia, so a parapneumonic effusion.]]

The pattern: anechoic, complex non-septated, complex septated, or echogenic. Septations, debris or swirl suggest an exudate or an empyema.

The size: twenty times the interpleural distance at the base. And the examination may be normal below three hundred millilitres, while the PA film needs about two hundred to blunt the angle.

[[What I do: sample a parapneumonic effusion, under ultrasound guidance.]]

That's your spotter answer. What you see, what it means, the pattern, the size, and what you do.

But here's something to carry forward. You've found the fluid, and you've sampled it. Now the real decision. Does it need a tube? And what if it isn't pus, but blood? When, exactly, do you drain, and how do you drain without harming the lung? That's next.

questions.text: Pleural effusion / haemothorax in the ICU — when do you drain?

steps.bridge: Fluid mainly expands the chest wall and flattens the diaphragm, so drainage eases breathing. Next: how ultrasound sizes and grades it →

lesson.text:
Start with the chest at rest. The chest wall wants to spring outwards. The lung wants to recoil inwards. At the end of a normal breath, the chest wall is being held in by the lung's pull.

Now let fluid into the pleural space. Where does it make its room? You'd expect it to squeeze the lung. But the chest wall has been waiting to spring out. So the fluid mostly pushes the chest wall and the diaphragm outwards.

[[Most of the fluid is accommodated by the chest wall expanding, not by the lung shrinking.]] At functional residual capacity, lung volume falls by only about one third of the fluid volume. At total lung capacity, by about one fifth.

That's why oxygenation often changes so little.

So what's the problem? The diaphragm. The fluid pushes it down. First it flattens. Then, with a large effusion, it can even invert. And a muscle works best from a good starting length. A flat or inverted diaphragm starts with short fibres, at a poor point on its length-tension curve. It contracts, but it can't generate much pressure.

Think of a bow that has been flattened. It can no longer be drawn.

[[A flattened diaphragm is a weak diaphragm. That's why breathlessness improves after drainage, even when gas exchange barely changes.]] That's Patient A.

Now the circulation. Raised pleural pressure collapses lung, and collapse raises the pulmonary vascular resistance. That loads the right ventricle, and it can fail. And a large effusion can limit filling of the heart, like tamponade. It reverses when you drain.

And at the extreme, a massive one-sided effusion that pushes the mediastinum across is a tension hydrothorax. It's the fluid version of a tension pneumothorax. Most are malignant.

So now you know why you might drain. Next, how ultrasound shapes the plan.

steps.bridge: Septations on ultrasound change the plan. Next: which parapneumonic findings mandate a tube →

lesson.text: You met this card in the ultrasound lessons. Anechoic fluid can be transudate or exudate; any complex pattern means an exudate. Twenty times the interpleural distance gives the volume. Here it matters for one reason. Ultrasound sees septations better than CT, and septations tell you the fluid is walled into pockets. That changes the plan, and it's where the next card begins.

steps.bridge: Pus, pH <7.20 or septations mean drain now. Next: when blood in the pleura needs a tube →

lesson.text:
A parapneumonic effusion comes in three types. Uncomplicated: free-flowing and sterile, and antibiotics alone will do. Complicated: bacteria have invaded the space, and fibrin begins to form septations. And empyema: frank pus.

Now why do the fluid tests work? As bacteria and neutrophils invade the pleural space, they burn glucose and they make lactate and carbon dioxide. So the glucose falls, and the pH falls. And as cells die, LDH rises.

Think of a sealed jar of milk going sour. The sugar is used up, and the acid rises.

A low pH, a low glucose and a high LDH tell you the pleural space has become a closed, infected collection, like an abscess. And antibiotics alone don't clear an abscess.

So the findings that mandate a chest tube are these.

{{**Drain a parapneumonic effusion if:**
Pus · positive Gram stain · pH <7.20 · glucose <60 mg/dL · LDH >1000 · complex septated pattern on ultrasound}}

[[Pus, a positive Gram stain, a pH below seven point two, a glucose below sixty milligrams per decilitre, an LDH above a thousand, or septations on ultrasound. Any one of these means drain.]]

Now the tube size. And here your card needs an update. The old teaching was a small tube for free fluid and a large one for septations. That has changed. Septations trap fluid in pockets, and intrapleural tPA with DNase breaks them down. The MIST two trial, by Rahman in the New England Journal in two thousand and eleven, showed that the two drugs together improve drainage and cut referral to surgery. Neither drug worked alone. And data from the earlier MIST one trial showed that small-bore drains, of twelve to fourteen French, do as well as large ones.

[[So use a small-bore drain for most, septated effusions included, with intrapleural tPA and DNase. Keep a large-bore tube for thick pus that blocks small ones.]]

If it doesn't settle, re-image, give the intrapleural drugs, and then think of medical thoracoscopy or surgery.

And when does the tube come out? When the sepsis has resolved, and the drainage is below two hundred millilitres a day.

Now, what if the fluid you draw is red?

steps.bridge: Haematocrit >50% of blood confirms haemothorax; drain with a large tube. Next: how to drain without re-expansion oedema →

lesson.text:
Here's the trap. A pleural tap comes back blood-stained, and someone calls it a haemothorax. But even one or two millilitres of blood will colour a whole effusion red. The colour proves nothing.

So you measure it. [[A haemothorax is a pleural fluid haematocrit above half of the blood haematocrit.]] Above half, the space is filling with blood, not serous fluid.

Think of a drop of blood in a glass of water. It turns the whole glass red. The haematocrit tells you whether it's a drop, or half the glass.

A massive haemothorax is more than one and a half litres. And note one detail. Your notes say over twenty-four hours, but in trauma teaching it means on immediate drainage. That much blood means major bleeding, and the patient may need a thoracotomy.

Now the drain. Blood clots, so the tube must be wide. Twenty-eight to thirty French. And it goes in the mid-axillary line, in the safe triangle. That's bounded by pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, and the fifth intercostal space. Why there? It avoids the internal mammary vessels, the breast and the muscle. It stays above the diaphragm, the liver and the spleen. And it drains the whole space.

[[Large bore, twenty-eight to thirty French, in the mid-axillary line.]]

And when do you not insert one? When you suspect aortic dissection or transection. In an aortic injury, the clot and the pressure in the pleura may be all that's holding the bleeding back. Drain it, and you release that tamponade. The patient can exsanguinate. That patient goes to surgery.

Two last practical points. In penetrating trauma, give antibiotic prophylaxis for the drain. And a drain that's in the wrong place can be pulled back, but never pushed further in.

So you've chosen the tube. How fast can you let the fluid out?

When a lung that has been collapsed for days is opened suddenly, two things happen at once.

First, pleural pressure drops sharply. So the pressure across the capillary wall jumps, and fluid is pulled out of the vessels. That's the hydrostatic part. Second, that lung has been hypoxic and short of surfactant. When it's reperfused, its capillaries leak. That's the ischaemia-reperfusion part. Both put water into the alveoli of the lung you've just re-expanded.

[[Re-expansion oedema is a sudden fall in pleural pressure, plus a leaky, reperfused lung.]]

Think of a sponge squeezed for days, released all at once. It soaks up water.

So who's at risk? A lung collapsed for more than three days. A large volume. And rapid drainage. Longer collapse means more ischaemia and more surfactant loss. Faster drainage means a steeper fall in pressure.

[[Drain no faster than five hundred millilitres an hour, and no more than one and a half litres at a time.]] Your notes say over twenty-four hours, but most guidelines mean one drainage session. Stop early if the patient develops chest pain or cough.

And if it happens? Oxygen, and CPAP of five to ten centimetres of water, or NIV if needed. CPAP doesn't remove the water. It keeps the flooded alveoli open, so gas exchange recovers while the leak settles.

And when does any chest drain come out? When the lung is fully expanded, so the space is closed, and the output is low enough for the pleura to reabsorb the rest. Thresholds vary, from about one hundred to two hundred millilitres a day. For a parapneumonic effusion, the sepsis must have resolved too, and two hundred is the usual figure.

spine: Why drain: raised pleural pressure flattens the diaphragm and can cause RV failure or a tamponade-like picture. Dyspnoea improves after drainage even if gas exchange changes little.
Parapneumonic: drain if pus, positive Gram stain, pH <7.20, glucose <60 mg/dL, LDH >1000 or septations. Small-bore for most, septated included, with tPA/DNase.
Haemothorax: pleural haematocrit >50% of blood; massive if >1.5 L. Use a 28–30 Fr drain in the mid-axillary line. Do not insert one if aortic dissection or transection is suspected.
How fast: no faster than 500 mL/h, maximum 1.5 L, to avoid re-expansion oedema (higher risk if collapsed >3 days). Treat it with CPAP 5–10 cmH2O and oxygen.
Removal: lung expanded and output <100–200 mL/day; for parapneumonic effusion, sepsis resolved and <200 mL/day.

open.text:
Let me start with a puzzle.

Patient A has been on the ventilator for a week. He has a large right effusion. His oxygenation is acceptable. But every breathing trial ends the same way, with fast, shallow breathing and distress. You drain a litre and a half. His saturation barely changes. And yet the next morning, he breathes comfortably, and comes off.

Why did draining fluid help a patient whose gas exchange hardly moved?

The answer lies in where the fluid makes its room, and what it does to the diaphragm. And it tells you something important for the viva. [[The reason to drain is not always the oxygen. Often it's the mechanics.]]

Effusions are common in the ICU. More than half of patients have one. And they can delay weaning.

What is the professor really checking? First, do you understand what an effusion does to the chest and the circulation. Second, can you name the findings in a parapneumonic effusion that mean drain now. Third, do you know how to recognise and drain a haemothorax, and when not to. And fourth, do you know how to drain safely, and when to take the tube out.

So here is the plan. First the physiology. Then the ultrasound picture. Then infection, then blood. And finally, how fast, and how to stop.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Why drain? Most of the fluid is taken up by the chest wall, so gas exchange may change little. [[But the diaphragm is flattened and weak, so dyspnoea improves after drainage.]] And raised pleural pressure can cause right ventricular failure, or a tamponade-like picture.

Parapneumonic effusion: drain for pus, a positive Gram stain, a pH below seven point two, a glucose below sixty, an LDH above a thousand, or septations. Small-bore for most, with tPA and DNase. Large-bore only for thick pus.

Haemothorax: a fluid haematocrit above half of the blood's. Massive if more than one and a half litres. A twenty-eight to thirty French drain in the mid-axillary line. And no drain if you suspect an aortic injury.

[[Drain no faster than five hundred millilitres an hour, and no more than one and a half litres at a time, to avoid re-expansion oedema.]] Treat it with CPAP and oxygen.

Remove the drain when the lung is expanded and the output is low, and for infection, once the sepsis has gone.

That's your answer. Why you drain, when, how, how fast, and when to stop.

But here's something to carry forward. Today the hidden culprit was the diaphragm, pushed flat and too weak to do its job. In most ventilated patients, nobody ever looks at it. Yet you can watch it move and thicken with the same probe in your hand. How do you measure the diaphragm, and what does it tell you about weaning? That's next.

questions.text: What is diaphragm ultrasound and how does it help weaning?

steps.bridge: Excursion <10 mm or thickening fraction under about 30% means a weak diaphragm. Next: how it ranks beside the other ultrasound predictors →

lesson.text:
There are two measurements. Excursion, how far the dome moves. And thickening, how much the muscle thickens as it contracts.

First, excursion. Take the low-frequency curved probe. Place it just below the right costal margin, between the midclavicular and anterior axillary lines. Use the liver as your window, and aim the beam up and back, at the back of the dome. Then switch to M-mode.

Now look at the trace on your screen.

{{pic}}

With each breath in, the dome moves down towards the probe, and the M-mode line rises. With each breath out, it falls back. The height of that inspiratory wave is the excursion.

[[An excursion below ten millimetres on quiet breathing means diaphragm dysfunction, and it predicts weaning failure.]] Kim and colleagues set that cut-off, in two thousand and eleven.

Second, thickening. Now take the high-frequency linear probe, and move to the side of the chest, the mid-axillary line, at about the eighth to tenth intercostal space. That's the zone of apposition, where the diaphragm lies flat against the inside of the lower ribs. There you can see the muscle itself, a dark layer between two bright lines, the pleura above and the peritoneum below. Measure its thickness at the end of a breath out, and at the end of a breath in.

{{**Thickening fraction (TF)** = (end-inspiratory − end-expiratory thickness) ÷ end-expiratory thickness × 100
TF ≥30–36% → success · below about 30% → weak diaphragm}}

The thickening fraction is the gain in thickness, divided by the thickness at rest. DiNino and colleagues, in two thousand and fourteen, showed that a fraction of thirty to thirty-six percent or more predicts success. [[Below about thirty percent, the diaphragm is weak.]]

Why two measurements? Because they measure different things. A muscle that contracts gets shorter and fatter. So thickening is the muscle working. Excursion is the dome moving, and a dome can be moved by other forces.

And that's the trap. Put the patient on pressure support, and the ventilator pushes the breath in. The dome moves down because the machine is pushing it, not because the muscle is pulling.

[[Ventilator support can move a diaphragm that isn't working. So measure on the breathing trial, or on very low support.]]

So now you can measure the pump. How does it rank beside the other predictors?
lesson.cap: M-mode under the right costal margin: the height of the inspiratory wave is the excursion; under 10 mm is weak.

steps.bridge: Diaphragm, lung score and LV function each predict outcome; excursion <10 mm means a weak diaphragm. Next: what to scan at each weaning step →

lesson.text: You met this card with the lung score. A breathing trial tests the pump, the lung and the heart, and ultrasound has a sign for each. A lung score above seventeen predicts failure, and so does an ejection fraction below forty percent, or raised filling pressures. Today, the diaphragm row is the one to own: an excursion below ten millimetres means dysfunction, and a thickening fraction of thirty to thirty-six percent or more predicts success. Remember the fix on this card. The older table had two other excursion cut-offs. Use ten millimetres.

So when do you actually pick up the probe? At three moments. And each one asks a different question.

[[Before the trial, who is at risk? During the trial, is he coping? After a failed trial, why did he fail?]]

Before the trial, you're looking for the high-risk patient. A left ventricle with an ejection fraction below forty percent. Moderate to severe diastolic dysfunction. A heart that's preload-independent, on the flat part of its Starling curve. Poor lung aeration. Or a large effusion.

Why does each of these fail the same test? Because the trial raises venous return and left ventricular afterload. A weak or stiff ventricle, or a flat Starling curve, turns that extra return into a high filling pressure, and the lung floods. And poorly aerated lung, or lung under a large effusion, loses even more air once PEEP is gone. Remember the patient with the large effusion. Drain first, then try.

During the trial, you're looking for reassurance. No new B-lines and no new consolidation, so the lung isn't losing air. And a diaphragm that moves and thickens well. Then the pump and the lung are holding.

And after a failed trial, you're a detective. [[New B-lines with a raised E over e prime point to cardiogenic oedema. More consolidation points to derecruitment.]] And each has its own fix. Diuretics or vasodilators for the heart. PEEP and physiotherapy for the lung. And if both are fine and the diaphragm is weak, you've found Patient A's problem. The pump.

Think of it like handing a heavy load back to someone who's been resting. Ultrasound watches to see what buckles.

spine: What it is: bedside ultrasound of the diaphragm. Excursion is how far the dome moves; thickening fraction is how much the muscle thickens as it contracts.
Excursion: curved probe below the right costal margin, liver as the window, M-mode. Excursion <10 mm on quiet breathing = dysfunction and predicts weaning failure.
Thickening: linear probe at the zone of apposition, mid-axillary line. TF = (end-inspiratory − end-expiratory) ÷ end-expiratory × 100. TF ≥30–36% predicts success.
What I do: measure during the breathing trial or on very low support. Scan before the trial for risk, during it to predict, and after a failure to find the cause.
Evidence: Kim (Crit Care Med 2011) set the <10 mm cut-off; DiNino (Thorax 2014) the thickening fraction. Caution: ventilator support moves a diaphragm that is not working.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient who keeps failing.

Patient A has been ventilated for ten days with pneumonia. The pneumonia has settled. His oxygenation is good. His heart is fine on echo. And yet every breathing trial ends in fast, shallow breathing. Something is failing, and it isn't the lung or the heart.

Think back to the breathing trial as a stress test of three things. The pump, the lung and the heart. We've looked at the lung with the score, and the heart with echo. Today, we look at the pump.

The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration. And on the ventilator, it can waste quickly. When the machine does all the work, the muscle has nothing to do, and it weakens. That's often called ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction. Add sepsis, steroids, paralysis and poor nutrition, and many long-term patients reach the trial with a weak pump.

For years, the only ways to test the diaphragm were invasive, or needed special equipment. But the diaphragm sits right under the liver on the right side, and the liver is a perfect window for ultrasound. So you can watch the dome move, and watch the muscle thicken, at the bedside.

What is the professor really checking? Do you know the two measurements and how to do each one. Do you know the cut-offs. And do you know the one trap that makes the numbers lie.

So the plan. First the technique and the numbers. Then where the diaphragm sits among the other ultrasound predictors. And finally, what you scan at each step of weaning.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Diaphragm ultrasound measures two things. Excursion, how far the dome moves. And thickening fraction, how hard the muscle contracts.]]

Excursion: a curved probe under the right costal margin, the liver as the window, M-mode. Below ten millimetres on quiet breathing means dysfunction, and predicts weaning failure.

Thickening: a linear probe at the zone of apposition, in the mid-axillary line. The gain in thickness, divided by the thickness at rest. Thirty to thirty-six percent or more predicts success.

Scan before the trial to find risk, during it to predict, and after a failure to find the cause.

The evidence: Kim, in two thousand and eleven, for the ten millimetre cut-off. DiNino, in two thousand and fourteen, for the thickening fraction.

[[And the caution: ventilator support moves a diaphragm that isn't working, so measure on the trial or on very low support.]]

That's your answer. What it is, how you do it, the numbers, how you use it, the evidence, and the trap.

But here's something to carry forward. Today the diaphragm was too weak. But sometimes the diaphragm is working, and working hard. It's just working at the wrong moment. Pulling when the ventilator isn't giving, or still pulling when the ventilator has stopped. The patient and the machine are out of step. That's patient-ventilator asynchrony, and how to classify it is next.

questions.text: Classify patient–ventilator asynchrony.

steps.bridge: Asynchrony sorts by phase: trigger, flow and cycling; trigger is 80%. Next: how we put a number on it →

lesson.text:
Every assisted breath has three moments where the patient and the machine have to agree. Think of a baton passed in a relay: handed over at the start, carried, and handed back.

First, the start. The patient's brain decides to breathe in, and the ventilator must notice and begin. That's the trigger.

Second, the middle. While the breath goes in, the machine has to give the flow the patient wants. That's the flow phase.

Third, the end. The brain decides to stop breathing in, and the machine must stop pushing at the same moment. That's cycling, the switch from inspiration to expiration.

[[So asynchrony sorts by phase: trigger, flow and cycling. Each type is a mismatch at one of those three hand-overs.]]

Now fill in each group.

Trigger asynchrony has four members. Ineffective effort: the patient pulls, and no breath comes. Double trigger: one long effort gets two breaths. Auto-trigger: a breath comes with no effort at all. And reverse trigger, where the machine's breath sets off the patient's effort. We'll take double and reverse triggering apart in the next question.

Flow asynchrony has two. Flow starvation, where the machine gives less flow than the patient demands, and the patient sucks against the circuit. And insufficient pressurisation.

Cycling asynchrony has two, and here's how to name them without getting muddled. Ask whose breath ends first. If the machine stops while the patient is still breathing in, that's premature cycling. The patient's inspiratory time is longer than the ventilator's. If the machine keeps pushing after the patient has started to breathe out, that's delayed cycling. The ventilator's time is longer.

[[Premature cycling: the machine stops first. Delayed cycling: the patient stops first.]]

And notice a connection. Push premature cycling far enough, and the patient's continuing effort triggers a second breath. That's double triggering. So the groups aren't walls. A fault at one hand-over can spill into the next.

Which group is commonest? Trigger, about eighty percent. And the commonest single type is ineffective effort.

Why does ineffective effort win? Go back to auto-PEEP. Say five centimetres of water are trapped in the alveoli. Before the sensor sees anything, the patient must lower his alveolar pressure by those five, plus the trigger threshold. A weak or tired patient never gets there. And here's the twist the panel likes. Too much support makes it worse. Big breaths leave less time to empty, so more gas is trapped. And they blunt the drive, so the efforts get weaker.

[[Ineffective effort often means too much help, not too little.]]

That's the opposite of the bedside instinct, where you see a struggling patient and turn the support up.

So how do you put a number on all this?

steps.bridge: An index >10% is significant and affects about a quarter of patients. Next: does it change outcome →

lesson.text:
With the asynchrony index.

It's the number of asynchronous events, divided by the total number of breaths, times a hundred. But here's the detail most residents miss. The total isn't just the breaths the machine gave. [[The denominator is ventilator breaths plus wasted efforts.]] Every effort the patient made counts, including the ones the machine ignored.

{{**Asynchrony index** = asynchronous events ÷ (ventilator breaths + wasted efforts) × 100
Example: 12 wasted efforts, 100 ventilator breaths → 12 ÷ 112 = **10.7%**}}

Take twelve wasted efforts against a hundred machine breaths. Twelve, divided by a hundred and twelve. Just over ten percent.

And that's the threshold. [[An asynchrony index above ten percent is significant.]]

How common is that? Thille found it in about a quarter of ventilated patients, twenty-four percent. Across studies the range runs from about twelve to forty-three percent, and it's highest on non-invasive ventilation.

So a quarter of your patients are out of step with the machine on more than one breath in ten. Does that matter?

Three studies, and each one goes a step further.

First, Thille, in two thousand six. Patients with an index above ten percent stayed on the ventilator twenty-five days, against seven. Tracheostomy, thirty-three percent against four. But mortality was not significantly different.

Then de Wit, in two thousand nine, looking only at ineffective efforts. An ineffective-effort index above ten percent meant longer ventilation, six days against two, and longer ICU and hospital stays. Again, mortality was not significant.

Then Blanch, in two thousand fifteen. Fifty patients, monitored continuously, eight point seven million breaths. Not a sample of a few minutes, but the whole course. And through that lens, a high index went with an ICU mortality of sixty-seven percent against fourteen. Hospital mortality, sixty-seven against twenty-three.

[[Asynchrony is linked to longer ventilation and more tracheostomies, and with continuous monitoring, to higher mortality.]]

One honest caution. These are associations. The sicker patient may simply fight the machine more. No trial has yet shown that fixing asynchrony saves lives. But the link is consistent, and most of the fixes cost nothing.

And one detail worth keeping. Asynchrony is commoner in assist-control than in pressure support, mainly through double triggering.

spine: What it is: a mismatch between the patient's effort and the ventilator breath, classified by the phase where it happens.
Trigger: ineffective effort, double trigger, auto-trigger, reverse trigger. This group is 80%; ineffective effort is the commonest single type.
Flow: flow starvation and insufficient pressurisation. Cycling: premature (patient's inspiration longer than the ventilator's) or delayed (ventilator's longer).
Measure: asynchrony index = asynchronous events ÷ (ventilator breaths + wasted efforts) × 100. Above 10% is significant; Thille found it in 24%.
Evidence: Thille 2006: index >10% meant ventilation 25 vs 7 days and tracheostomy 33% vs 4%. Blanch 2015: ICU mortality 67% vs 14%.

open.text:
Let me start with a patient who looks settled.

He's on pressure support, recovering from pneumonia. The numbers on the screen look fine. A rate of eighteen, a good tidal volume, a saturation of ninety-six. The nurse says he's comfortable. But stand at the bedside and watch his neck and his belly for a minute. Every so often his muscles pull, and nothing happens. The machine doesn't notice. And now and then two breaths come one on top of the other, with no breath out between them.

That's patient-ventilator asynchrony. The patient and the machine are breathing to two different clocks. [[Asynchrony is a mismatch between what the patient's brain asks for and what the ventilator delivers.]]

In the waveform lesson, you learned to spot three of these on the screen. Today we step back and put them all in order.

What is the professor really checking with this question? First, that you have a framework, not a list. There are many named asynchronies, and the resident who reels them off at random sounds lost. The one who sorts them by the phase of the breath sounds like he has seen them. Second, can you put a number on it. And third, does it matter? The trap is to call asynchrony a nuisance that a little more sedation will fix. It isn't a nuisance. It is linked to longer ventilation, and in one study, to a far higher mortality.

So here's the plan. First, the classification, by the three hand-overs of every breath. Then the index that measures it. And finally, the evidence that it changes outcome.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Asynchrony is a mismatch between the patient's effort and the ventilator's breath, and you classify it by the phase where it happens.]]

Trigger: ineffective effort, double trigger, auto-trigger and reverse trigger. This group is about eighty percent, and ineffective effort is the commonest single type.

Flow: flow starvation and insufficient pressurisation.

Cycling: premature, when the machine stops first, and delayed, when the patient stops first.

You measure it with the asynchrony index: the events, divided by the ventilator breaths plus the wasted efforts. Above ten percent is significant, and Thille found that in about a quarter of patients.

And it matters. Thille linked it to twenty-five days of ventilation against seven, and tracheostomy in thirty-three percent against four. Blanch linked it to an ICU mortality of sixty-seven percent against fourteen.

That's your answer. What it is, the three phases, the index, and the evidence.

But two members of the trigger group look almost the same on the screen. Two breaths stacked together. In one, the patient started it. In the other, the machine did. How do you tell them apart, and why does it change what you do? That's next.

questions.text: What is double triggering? How is it different from reverse triggering?

steps.bridge: Double triggering is the patient outlasting the machine's inspiratory time. Next: reverse triggering, where the machine starts the effort →

lesson.text:
Double triggering is two inspirations in a row, not separated by an expiration.

Here's how it happens. In volume control, the machine's breath ends on a fixed time or volume. But the patient's brain has its own inspiratory time, its own neural clock. If the brain's inspiration is longer than the machine's, the machine stops while the patient is still pulling. He keeps pulling against a machine that has gone quiet. The airway pressure falls past the trigger. And the machine, doing exactly what it's told, gives him a second breath.

[[In double triggering, the ventilator's inspiratory time is shorter than the patient's, so the continuing effort triggers a second breath.]]

You'll recognise that as premature cycling, taken to its end.

Who gets it? Think of who has a long, strong neural inspiration. A patient with high demand. A low P to F ratio. A short set inspiratory time. And volume control, where the inspiratory time is fixed whatever the patient wants. Here's the uncomfortable connection. Six millilitres per kilo can leave an air-hungry ARDS patient wanting more than you give. So the patient you're working hardest to protect is the one most likely to double trigger.

Now why it matters. The second breath doesn't start from empty. It starts at the end of the first, with the first breath still in the lung. So the volumes add. A set breath of three hundred and fifty millilitres can become six hundred and fifty in the lung.

[[Breath stacking can almost double the delivered volume, which defeats lung-protective ventilation.]]

You set six per kilo, and the lung can receive nearly twice that. To count it, there's a stacking index: a hundred times the stacked breaths, divided by the stacked plus the normal breaths.

How do you fix it? Lengthen the machine's breath to match the effort. Increase the inspiratory time, or the tidal volume. Or switch to pressure support, where the breath ends on the patient's own falling flow, so it lasts as long as he does. Sedation, which lowers the drive, comes last.

Why last? Because in one study, changing the ventilator settings cut breath stacking by about ninety percent. More sedation cut it by about half, and that was not significantly better than doing nothing.

[[Fix double triggering with the ventilator first, and sedation last.]]

Now the twin that looks the same on the screen, and has the opposite cause.

steps.bridge: Reverse triggering is machine-led, in deep sedation, and also stacks breaths. Next: the one fix for each asynchrony →

lesson.text:
Reverse triggering turns the usual order upside down. [[The ventilator breath triggers the patient's effort, not the other way round.]]

Picture a deeply sedated patient on a controlled mode. No drive of his own, you'd think. The machine inflates his lung, and late in that breath, his diaphragm contracts. The passive inflation itself is thought to set off a reflex contraction. His respiratory centre locks onto the rhythm of the machine.

And because the machine sets the beat, the effort repeats in a fixed pattern. That's entrainment. One effort for every machine breath, or one for every two, or one for every three. Like a listener clapping along to a song, once a bar, or once every two bars.

Who gets it? Deeply sedated patients on controlled modes. Deep sedation removes the patient's own rhythm, and a controlled mode gives a steady beat to lock onto. It was named only in two thousand thirteen, by Akoumianaki and colleagues, and it's easy to miss, because the patient looks completely passive.

How is it detected? On the standard curves it can pass for a passive breath, or for double triggering. The proof is an oesophageal pressure trace, or the diaphragm's electrical activity, showing a negative swing that begins late in each machine breath.

[[Reverse triggering is confirmed on oesophageal pressure or diaphragm EMG: the effort begins after the machine breath has started.]]

Why does it matter? Two reasons. First, if the effort outlasts the machine breath, it triggers another. Breath stacking again, with a larger tidal volume. Second, if the effort falls during your inspiratory hold, it pulls the plateau down. You remember the lesson on the hold. A sloping or wavy plateau you can't trust. Here, the plateau understates the real stress on the lung.

[[Reverse triggering stacks breaths, and makes the plateau pressure unreliable.]]

So now you have the distinction. Double triggering: the patient starts it, and the machine is too short. Reverse triggering: the machine starts it, and the patient follows. Both stack breaths.

Now let's turn the whole classification into action.

Here's the idea that makes this card easy. [[Each asynchrony is one setting out of step with the patient, so each has one knob.]] Name what's out of step, and you've named the fix.

Auto-triggering. Breaths with no effort at all. The trigger is too sensitive, and the machine fires on noise: a leak, water in the circuit, or the beat of the heart. So make the trigger less sensitive, and fix the leak.

Ineffective triggering. Effort with no breath. The effort is being spent cancelling auto-PEEP before the trigger sees it. Look at the picture you met with COPD, the next breath starting while gas is still flowing out.

{{pic}}

So reduce the auto-PEEP. Lower the support or the tidal volume, so smaller breaths leave more time to empty. And in a flow-limited airway, as in COPD, add external PEEP, up to about eighty percent of the auto-PEEP. That narrows the gap the patient has to cross, without adding much trapped gas.

Double triggering. Two breaths for one long effort. The breath is too short, so make it longer. In volume control, raise the inspiratory time. In pressure support, raise the support, or lower the cycle-off percentage. That ends the breath later, at a smaller share of the peak flow, so it lasts as long as the effort.

Delayed cycling. The patient is breathing out against a machine that's still pushing. The breath is too long. So raise the cycle-off percentage, to forty or fifty percent in COPD. There, slowly emptying airways make the inspiratory flow decay slowly, so the default cycle-off comes too late.

Flow starvation. The scooped pressure curve. The flow is too low. Raise it, or switch mode.

{{Asynchrony | Looks like | Knob
Auto-trigger | breath, no effort | trigger less sensitive; fix leak
Ineffective | effort, no breath | ↓ auto-PEEP; add PEEP
Double | two breaths, one effort | ↑ Ti; ↓ cycle-off %; ↑ PS
Delayed cycling | exhales against vent | ↑ cycle-off %
Flow starvation | scooped pressure | ↑ flow; switch mode}}

[[Too sensitive, too much trapped gas, too short, too long, too little flow. Each fault has its own knob.]]

Notice how few of these say more sedation. The ventilator is almost always the first answer.
lesson.cap: A, normal lung: flow reaches zero. B, COPD: the next breath starts while gas still flows out, so auto-PEEP.

spine: Double triggering: two inspirations with no expiration between. The ventilator's inspiratory time is shorter than the patient's, so the continuing effort triggers a second breath.
Reverse triggering: the ventilator breath triggers the patient's effort. Seen in deeply sedated patients on controlled modes, often entrained 1:1, 1:2 or 1:3.
The difference: in double triggering the patient starts it; in reverse triggering the machine does. Reverse triggering is confirmed on oesophageal pressure or diaphragm EMG.
Why it matters: both stack breaths, so delivered volume can almost double (350 becomes 650 mL). Reverse triggering also makes plateau pressure unreliable.
What I do: for double triggering, increase inspiratory time or tidal volume, lower the cycle-off %, switch to pressure support, or sedate.

open.text:
Let me start with two traces that look the same.

Patient A has ARDS, on volume control at six millilitres per kilo. He's awake enough to be hungry for air. On his flow curve you see two breaths stacked together, the second starting before the first has been breathed out.

Patient B is also on volume control, deeply sedated, with no breathing of his own that you'd expect. And yet on his flow curve, you see the same thing. Stacked breaths.

Same picture. Opposite stories. In Patient A, the patient's brain is leading, and the machine's breath is too short. In Patient B, the machine is leading, and the patient's diaphragm is following.

[[Double triggering is patient-led. Reverse triggering is machine-led.]]

What is the professor checking? That you can define each one cleanly. That you know who gets each. That you know why both are dangerous: both can nearly double the breath, and that undoes everything you're doing to protect the lung. And that you know the fix. The trap is to reach for more sedation. For double triggering, sedation is the weakest fix. And reverse triggering turns up in exactly the patient who is already deeply sedated.

So here's the plan. Double triggering first. Then reverse triggering. Then the one knob for each asynchrony.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Double triggering is two inspirations with no expiration between them. [[The ventilator's inspiratory time is shorter than the patient's, so the continuing effort triggers a second breath.]] It's patient-led, in a hungry patient on volume control.

Reverse triggering is the machine breath triggering the patient's effort. It's machine-led, in a deeply sedated patient on a controlled mode, often entrained one to one, one to two, or one to three. You confirm it on oesophageal pressure or diaphragm EMG.

[[The difference: in double triggering the patient starts it; in reverse triggering the machine does.]]

Why both matter: both stack breaths, so the delivered volume can almost double, three hundred and fifty becoming six hundred and fifty. And reverse triggering makes the plateau unreliable.

What you do for double triggering: lengthen the breath. A longer inspiratory time or a bigger tidal volume, a lower cycle-off, or pressure support. Sedation comes last.

That's your answer. The two definitions, the difference, why they matter, and the fix.

But notice something about every fix today. You were adjusting a setting so that a fixed machine could match a changing patient. What if the machine could listen to the patient directly, and change itself, breath by breath? That's the idea behind the newer modes. NAVA, PAV and closed-loop ventilation. And it's where we go next.

questions.text: What are the newer ventilator modes — NAVA, PAV, closed-loop?

steps.bridge: Closed-loop modes differ in what sets the pressure and whether they wean. Next: PAV, which follows the patient's flow →

lesson.text:
Four closed-loop modes, and three questions for each. What sets the pressure? Can it ventilate a passive patient? And does it wean by itself?

{{Mode | Pressure set by | Passive? | Auto-wean?
PAV | inspiratory flow | No | No
NAVA | diaphragm EMG (EAdi) | No | No
SmartCare | rate kept in a comfort zone | No | **Yes**
ASV | minimum work of breathing | **Yes** | **Yes**}}

In PAV, the pressure is set by the patient's inspiratory flow. In NAVA, by the diaphragm's electrical activity. In SmartCare, by keeping the breathing rate inside a comfort zone. And in ASV, by the minimum work of breathing.

Now the two columns that catch residents. Passive patients first. PAV, NAVA and SmartCare all follow the patient's own breathing. No breathing, nothing to follow. [[ASV is the only one of the four that works in a passive patient.]] It keeps a guaranteed rate of its own.

And automatic weaning? Only SmartCare and ASV. PAV and NAVA follow the patient closely, but they don't decide by themselves to hand him more of the work.

[[PAV and NAVA follow the patient. SmartCare and ASV also wean him.]]

Now take them one at a time, starting with PAV.

steps.bridge: PAV gives a fixed share of the work but needs a triggering patient. Next: NAVA, which reads the diaphragm directly →

lesson.text:
Go back to the equation of motion from the very first lesson. The pressure a breath needs is flow times resistance, plus volume times elastance. Pushing through the airways, plus stretching the lung.

Normally, the patient's muscles provide part of that pressure and the ventilator the rest. PAV asks a simple question. What if the machine measured the patient's flow and volume at every instant, and supplied a fixed share of the pressure they need?

[[PAV delivers pressure in proportion to the patient's instantaneous effort, so the ventilator does a constant fraction of the work of each breath.]]

Think of power steering. However hard you turn the wheel, it adds a fixed share. Turn gently, a little help. Turn hard, a lot.

So what do you set? Only the PEEP, the FiO2, and the percentage of support. No tidal volume, no inspiratory pressure. Those come from the patient.

But there's a catch. To turn flow and volume into pressure, the machine must know the resistance and the compliance. Get those wrong, and the share is wrong. So it measures them almost continuously. The newer version, PAV plus, does it with brief pauses at the end of inspiration.

What does it buy you? Comfort, synchrony, and better coupling between what the brain asks for and what the lung receives. The tidal volume varies from breath to breath, as natural breathing does. And patients need less sedation.

Now the limitations. Each one follows from the principle. The patient must trigger. No effort means no flow, and no flow means no help, so PAV can't ventilate a passive patient. Effort spent cancelling auto-PEEP makes no flow, so it gets no help either. And then the leak. To the machine, a leak looks like inspiratory flow. So it keeps pushing, and pushing. That's runaway, over-assistance.

[[No effort, no help. And a leak looks like effort, so it causes runaway.]]

So PAV reads the result of the patient's effort, the flow. What if you could read the command itself?

steps.bridge: NAVA runs on diaphragm electrical activity, so leaks and auto-PEEP do not matter. Next: what both gain over pressure support →

lesson.text:
Follow a single breath from the brain down. The brain decides to breathe. The signal runs down the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm fires, electrically. Then the muscle contracts, the pressure in the chest falls, and only then does gas move.

Look at that chain on your screen.

{{pic}}

Pressure support waits near the bottom, for a fall in pressure or a change in flow. PAV reads the flow, the result. NAVA reaches higher up the chain. [[NAVA reads the electrical activity of the diaphragm, the brain's command, before any pressure or flow appears.]]

That signal is called the EAdi. It's picked up by an array of electrodes on a nasogastric tube, sitting at the level of the crural diaphragm. And it does three jobs. It triggers the breath, it sizes it, and it cycles it off.

What do you set? The NAVA level, in centimetres of water per microvolt. Each microvolt of diaphragm activity buys that much pressure. So the pressure delivered is the NAVA level times the EAdi. A strong drive gets strong support. A weak drive, less.

{{**NAVA:** pressure = NAVA level (cmH₂O/µV) × EAdi (µV)}}

Now see why it solves the problems of the last question. With auto-PEEP, a pneumatic trigger waits until the trapped pressure is cancelled, so a weak effort is missed. But the EAdi rises at the start of the effort, whatever is trapped in the lung. And a leak changes the flow, not the electrical signal. [[Leaks and auto-PEEP can't fool NAVA, because it never waits for pressure or flow.]] That's why its synchrony is so good. And the EAdi itself becomes a monitor of the drive.

The limitations follow from the chain too. It needs every link above the diaphragm intact: a drive, a phrenic nerve, a working diaphragm. Deep sedation flattens the EAdi. A phrenic injury or a paralysed diaphragm silences it. It needs a special catheter, so it's relatively invasive. There's a learning curve. And there are few outcome data.

So what do PAV and NAVA actually achieve, compared with pressure support?
lesson.cap: A breath runs from brain to flow. NAVA reads the diaphragm's command; PAV reads the resulting flow.

steps.bridge: Both improve synchrony and prevent over-assistance; NAVA has more double triggers. Next: ASV, which also works in passive patients →

lesson.text:
Go back to pressure support. The set pressure arrives whatever the drive. At a high level, every breath gets the same big push, and it overshoots.

In PAV and NAVA, the pressure follows the effort. And that closes a feedback loop. As the lung fills, the drive tends to fall. A falling drive means less pressure. So the large, over-stretching breath becomes less likely.

[[Because support follows effort, PAV and NAVA prevent over-distension at high levels of assist.]]

Like walking with a partner who matches your pace, rather than one who pulls you at a fixed speed.

Three more gains follow. Fewer ineffective efforts, because over-assistance causes many of them. The patient's own breath-to-breath variability comes back, the natural irregularity that pressure support flattens out. And better coupling between the brain's command and the breath the lung receives.

Then the drawback of NAVA, a favourite in the viva. More double triggering. Why? NAVA ends the breath when the EAdi falls to about seventy percent of its peak. So a dip in the signal within one effort can end the breath, and the rest of the effort starts another. And it needs that special catheter.

[[NAVA's drawback: more double triggering, and a special catheter.]]

And the honest caution. No proven benefit on clinical outcome yet. Better physiology and better synchrony, but no outcome trial to show for it.

Both PAV and NAVA need a breathing patient. Now the mode that doesn't.

steps.bridge: ASV picks rate and volume for minimum work with Otis' formula. Next: how INTELLiVENT closes the whole loop →

lesson.text:
Adaptive support ventilation starts from an old piece of physiology.

For any given minute ventilation, you can breathe fast and shallow, or slow and deep. Fast and shallow wastes work, because much of each small breath only fills the dead space. Slow and deep wastes work too, because each big breath has to stretch the lung further. Somewhere in between is one rate that costs the least. Otis showed this, and it's called Otis' formula. Think of a cyclist's best cadence, neither spinning nor grinding.

[[ASV uses Otis' formula to pick the rate that gives the minimum work of breathing for the target minute ventilation.]]

What does the clinician set? Three main controls. The percentage of minute volume, the PEEP and the FiO2. You also enter a pressure limit, usually thirty, and the patient's height and sex, which give the ideal body weight.

The percentage of minute volume is the target as a share of normal. In adults, a hundred percent is about a hundred millilitres per kilo of ideal weight per minute. So a man with an ideal weight of seventy kilos gets about seven litres a minute at a hundred percent. You start at about a hundred to a hundred and ten, and raise it when CO2 production is high.

{{**ASV:** set %MinVol, PEEP, FiO₂ (+ pressure limit, height, sex)
100% MinVol ≈ 100 mL/kg ideal weight/min → IBW 70 kg ≈ 7 L/min
Start at 100–110%}}

Which measurement drives it? The expiratory time constant, resistance times compliance, measured breath by breath. Look again at the picture you met with COPD.

{{pic}}

A long time constant, as in COPD, needs a long time to breathe out. So ASV picks a slower rate and bigger breaths. A short one, as in ARDS, empties fast, so it gets a faster rate and smaller breaths. [[The time constant sets the rate: long in COPD, so slow and deep; short in ARDS, so fast and shallow.]]

And here's what sets ASV apart from PAV and NAVA. It keeps a guaranteed rate, so it becomes whatever the patient needs. No effort at all, and it gives pressure-controlled breaths. Some effort, but a rate below target, and it gives pressure SIMV. A rate above target, and it gives only pressure support.

[[ASV fills in whatever the patient leaves. That's why it works in a passive patient, and why it weans.]]

As the patient takes over, the mandatory breaths fade away, and he's left on pressure support alone.
lesson.cap: A, short time constant: the lung empties fast. B, long time constant, as in COPD: emptying is slow and incomplete.

lesson.text:
ASV still leaves you three knobs: the minute volume, the PEEP and the FiO2. INTELLiVENT-ASV takes those too. [[INTELLiVENT is fully closed loop: the minute volume, PEEP and FiO2 are all adjusted automatically.]]

It does that with two controllers, each with its own sensor.

The ventilation controller watches the end-tidal CO2, or the rate, and sets the minute volume from it.

The oxygenation controller watches the SpO2, and sets the PEEP and the FiO2 from it, following the ARDSNet table or an open-lung approach.

[[End-tidal CO2 drives the ventilation. SpO2 drives the PEEP and FiO2.]]

Where does the clinician come in? He tells the machine the patient's condition: ARDS, brain injury, or chronic hypercapnia. That sets the target ranges the controllers aim for.

And it weans. Its Quick Wean function runs in three stages: screening, observation, and then an automatic spontaneous breathing trial.

SmartCare, from the first card, weans automatically too, by keeping the breathing rate in a comfort zone, but only in a patient who is breathing.

One honest caution to finish. All of these modes give better synchrony, more comfort, and often less sedation. But the outcome data are few. Say that, and the panel knows you've read beyond the brochure.

spine: What they are: modes where the ventilator adjusts support from a patient signal, instead of fixed settings.
PAV: pressure in proportion to instantaneous flow and volume; set PEEP, FiO2 and % support. Needs a triggering patient; leaks can cause runaway over-assistance.
NAVA: diaphragm electrical activity from a nasogastric electrode triggers, sizes and cycles the breath; pressure = NAVA level × EAdi. Needs intact drive, phrenic nerves and a working diaphragm.
ASV: set %MinVol, PEEP and FiO2; Otis' formula picks the rate for minimum work, driven by the expiratory time constant. Works in passive patients and weans.
INTELLiVENT-ASV: fully closed loop. End-tidal CO2 sets ventilation, SpO2 sets PEEP and FiO2, and it runs an automatic breathing trial. SmartCare also weans automatically.
Caution: better synchrony, comfort and less sedation, but few outcome data.

open.text:
Let me start with pressure support.

Your patient takes a small, shallow breath. Pressure support gives him ten centimetres of water. A moment later he sighs, a big, deep pull. Pressure support gives him ten. He gasps in distress. Ten.

[[Pressure support gives the same help whatever the effort.]] It's a good mode, and you use it every day. But it can't hear how hard the patient is trying. Too little help for the big effort, too much for the small one. And too much help, as you learned in the last two questions, means ineffective efforts and over-stretch.

The newer modes all try to fix that. Each one listens to a different signal from the patient, and adjusts the support from it, instead of from a fixed setting. Proportional assist ventilation, PAV, listens to the flow. NAVA listens to the electrical activity of the diaphragm. Adaptive support ventilation, ASV, reads the lung's mechanics and works out the cheapest way to breathe. And INTELLiVENT closes the loop completely, with the end-tidal CO2 and the saturation.

What is the professor checking? Not that you've used them. Most residents haven't. He's checking that you understand the principle of each: what signal it reads, what you set, and in whom it can't work. And he wants the honest caution at the end. Better synchrony and comfort, yes. Proven outcome benefit, not yet. The trap is to sell these modes as the answer to weaning.

So here's the plan. First, all of them at a glance. Then PAV. Then NAVA. Then what those two achieve. Then ASV. And finally, INTELLiVENT.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[The newer modes adjust the support from a signal from the patient, instead of from fixed settings.]]

PAV gives pressure in proportion to the patient's instantaneous flow and volume. You set the PEEP, the FiO2 and the percentage of support. It needs a triggering patient, and a leak can cause runaway over-assistance.

NAVA reads the diaphragm's electrical activity from a nasogastric electrode, and uses it to trigger, size and cycle the breath. The pressure is the NAVA level times the EAdi. It needs an intact drive, phrenic nerve and diaphragm.

Both improve synchrony and prevent over-assistance, though NAVA brings more double triggering.

ASV: you set the minute volume percentage, the PEEP and the FiO2. Otis' formula picks the rate for minimum work, driven by the expiratory time constant. It works in passive patients, and it weans.

INTELLiVENT closes the whole loop. End-tidal CO2 sets the ventilation, SpO2 sets the PEEP and FiO2, and it runs its own breathing trial. SmartCare weans automatically too.

And the caution: better synchrony, comfort and less sedation, but few outcome data.

That's your answer. What they are, each mode's signal and limits, and the caution.

But notice a thread that ran through today. Deep sedation flattens NAVA's signal. It's where reverse triggering appears. And a heavily sedated patient can't take the work back from ASV. So how should we sedate a ventilated patient at all? How deep, with what, and how do we measure it? That's next.

questions.text: Sedation and sedation scores — how do you sedate a ventilated patient?

steps.bridge: Pain is everywhere in the ICU and drives delirium; self-report comes first. Next: how to score pain when the patient cannot speak →

lesson.text:
Start with pain, because it's everywhere.

ICU patients have pain at rest, and more during the things we do to them. Arterial line insertion. Wound drain removal. Turning. Suctioning. And the most painful of all, chest tube removal. We do these every day without thinking of them as painful procedures.

[[Pain in the ICU comes at rest and with routine care: turning, suctioning, and most of all, chest tube removal.]]

And untreated pain does harm. The heart rate may go up or down, and so may the blood pressure. The saturation falls. The patient fights the ventilator. And pain drives delirium.

So much of what looks like agitation is really pain. Treat the pain, and the sedative dose can fall.

How do you assess it? [[Self-report is the best assessment, whenever the patient can give it.]] A numerical rating scale, nought to ten, spoken or shown on a card. Even an intubated patient can often point or nod.

And if he can't report? Then you use a behavioural tool: the BPS or the CPOT.

One trap here. Vital signs alone are not valid measures of pain. A fast heart rate may be pain, or fever, or bleeding. Use the vital signs only as a cue to go and assess.

steps.bridge: BPS >5 or CPOT >2 means pain. Next: how PADIS treats it before any sedative →

lesson.text:
Two behavioural scales. You need their domains and their cut-offs.

The Behavioural Pain Scale has three domains: facial expression, upper limb movement, and compliance with the ventilator. Each scores one to four, so the total runs from three to twelve. [[A BPS above five means pain.]] And notice the trap. The lowest BPS is three, not zero. Three is no pain.

The Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool has four domains: face, body movement, muscle tension, and either compliance with the ventilator or, after extubation, vocalisation. Each scores nought to two, so the total runs from nought to eight. [[A CPOT above two means pain.]]

{{ | BPS | CPOT
Domains | face, upper limbs, ventilator | face, body, muscle tension, ventilator or voice
Score | 1–4 each (3–12) | 0–2 each (0–8)
Pain if | > 5 | > 2}}

So the CPOT carries straight on after extubation, with vocalisation in place of the ventilator. The BPS has a separate non-intubated version.

steps.bridge: Opioids first, spared by paracetamol, ketamine or gabapentinoids. Next: how to score the depth of sedation →

lesson.text:
Now the treatment, and the principle that runs through all of PADIS. [[Analgesia first. Treat the pain before you reach for the sedative.]]

Opioids are the mainstay. But they have a price: respiratory depression, ileus, tolerance, withdrawal, and immunosuppression. So you spare them.

The opioid-sparing drugs are worth listing cleanly. Paracetamol. Nefopam, a reuptake inhibitor that spares the kidney and the gut. Low-dose ketamine, after surgery. And for neuropathic pain, gabapentin, pregabalin or carbamazepine. In trauma and surgery, regional anaesthesia, which you know well from theatre.

What not to use routinely? Intravenous lidocaine. And NSAIDs, because of the kidney and the gut.

Non-drug measures help too: massage, music, relaxation, cold therapy. And there's no role for hypnosis, or for volatile agents as analgesics.

And one practical rule. [[Pre-empt procedural pain. Give the analgesic before the chest tube comes out, not after.]]

With the pain treated, you can now ask how deep the patient should be.

steps.bridge: RASS runs from +4 to −5 by eye contact and response. Next: what depth PADIS asks us to aim for →

lesson.text:
The depth score you'll be asked for is RASS, the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. Ten points, from plus four down to minus five, with zero in the middle: alert and calm.

Don't learn it as ten lines. Learn the logic.

Above zero is agitation, and it climbs by danger. Plus one is restless: anxious, but not aggressive. Plus two, agitated: moving without purpose, fighting the ventilator. Plus three, very agitated: pulling at tubes, aggressive. Plus four, combative: violent, a danger to staff.

Below zero is sedation, and it falls by what it takes to get a response. [[Minus one and minus two both make eye contact to voice. Over ten seconds is minus one. Under ten seconds is minus two.]] Minus three, he moves to your voice but makes no eye contact. Minus four, no response to voice, but he moves to a physical stimulus. Minus five, no response to voice or touch.

{{**RASS**
+4 combative · +3 very agitated · +2 agitated · +1 restless
0 alert and calm
−1 drowsy: eye contact to voice > 10 s
−2 light: eye contact to voice < 10 s
−3 moderate: moves to voice, no eye contact
−4 deep: moves only to physical stimulus
−5 unarousable}}

So the two hinges below zero are eye contact, and the stimulus. Voice with eye contact is light. Voice without eye contact is moderate. Only touch is deep.

And RASS is also the first step of the delirium assessment. You can test for delirium only at minus three or above. At minus four or minus five the patient is comatose. Record that, and come back later.

steps.bridge: Aim light, RASS −2 to +1, with propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. Next: which drug has which pitfall →

lesson.text:
So what depth should you aim for? [[PADIS asks for light sedation: a RASS of minus two to plus one.]] On the Riker scale, that's three to four. He opens his eyes to your voice and holds your gaze, at least briefly, and he may be a little restless. That's the target. Not a still patient.

Why light? Deep sedation keeps patients on the ventilator longer, adds delirium, and in cohort studies is linked to higher mortality. And remember what we said about pain. Much agitation is pain. So the order is analgesia first, what's called analgosedation, and then the least sedation needed.

How do you keep it light? Two ways. Daily interruption, where the sedative is stopped each day and the patient is allowed to wake. Or nurse-protocolised targets, where the nurse titrates to the RASS goal through the day. Both work.

Which drug? [[Propofol or dexmedetomidine, over benzodiazepines.]] Especially after cardiac surgery. Benzodiazepines accumulate and worsen delirium. Propofol and dexmedetomidine wear off quickly, so a light target is easier to hold.

When can't you use RASS? In a paralysed patient. He can't open his eyes or move, so RASS reads minus five whatever his awareness. There, use an objective brain monitor such as BIS, which you know from theatre. It's the only objective guide to depth then, though an imperfect guard against awareness.

Physical restraints are not recommended. They provoke agitation and delirium, they cause injury, and restrained patients still self-extubate. Use them only if absolutely necessary.

And a newer note for the panel. The two thousand twenty-five update suggests dexmedetomidine over propofol when light sedation or less delirium is the priority. It's a conditional suggestion, not a rule.

So now, the drugs themselves.

steps.bridge: Midazolam accumulates, propofol risks PRIS, dexmedetomidine slows the heart. Next: how sedation links to weaning →

lesson.text:
Here's the trick that makes this table easy. [[Almost every problem with these drugs follows from how each one is cleared.]] Learn the clearance, and the pitfall writes itself.

Midazolam has an active metabolite cleared by the kidney. So it accumulates, especially in renal failure, and it causes delirium. Lorazepam has no active metabolite, but the intravenous form is dissolved in propylene glycol, and at high doses that gives a lactic acidosis with a raised osmolar gap. Diazepam has a long half-life and active metabolites, so its effect is prolonged.

Propofol is fast on and fast off. That's its strength. Its problems are hypotension, and PRIS, the propofol infusion syndrome: a failure of the mitochondria to use fat, at doses over four to five milligrams per kilo per hour for days. It shows as acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and heart failure. And propofol comes as a ten percent lipid emulsion, one point one kilocalories per millilitre. So count it as feeding, and watch the triglycerides and the pancreas.

Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-two agonist, cleared by the liver. It cuts sympathetic outflow, so it causes bradycardia and hypotension. A fast loading dose can first cause a transient hypertension, through alpha-two receptors on the vessels. And its great gift. [[Dexmedetomidine causes no respiratory depression.]]

Now the opioids. Remifentanil is broken down by non-specific esterases in blood and tissue, so it never accumulates, whatever the liver and kidney are doing. Its problems are rigidity and hyperalgesia. Fentanyl is fat-soluble. Over a long infusion it fills the body fat, and leaks back out after you stop. Think of fat as a sponge that soaks up the drug and wrings it out later. Morphine releases histamine, so it drops the pressure, and its active metabolite is cleared by the kidney, so it accumulates in AKI. Hydromorphone is five to ten times as potent as morphine.

{{Drug | Clearance | Pitfall
Midazolam | active metabolite, renal | accumulates; delirium
Lorazepam | glucuronidation | propylene glycol
Propofol | fast on/off; 1.1 kcal/mL | ↓ BP; PRIS > 4–5 mg/kg/h
Dexmedetomidine | α2; hepatic | bradycardia; no resp. depression
Remifentanil | tissue esterases | rigidity, hyperalgesia
Morphine | M6G, renal | histamine; AKI}}

You know most of these from theatre. The ICU difference is time. A drug that's harmless for three hours can be a problem over three days.

steps.bridge: Pairing awakening with a breathing trial improved 1-year survival. Next: the bundle that ties pain, sedation and delirium together →

lesson.text:
Now the link to weaning. Three findings on this card.

First, delirium. If the patient is delirious on the day of his first breathing trial, extubation fails more often, forty percent against twenty-five. Re-intubation, thirty-five against seventeen. More tracheostomies, fewer simple weans. ICU mortality was not changed. But the delirious brain makes a poor weaner.

Second, the sedation strategy. Daily sedation interruption or targeted light sedation, and both are safe. [[Pairing the awakening trial with a breathing trial improved one-year survival.]] We'll meet that trial properly in the next question.

Third, nutrition. Obesity doesn't worsen the outcome. A body mass index below twenty does make weaning difficult, with a low drive and little muscle.

And the last card ties all of this into one bundle.

The ABCDEF bundle. A: assess, prevent and manage pain. B: both trials, the spontaneous awakening trial and the spontaneous breathing trial, done together. C: choice of analgesia and sedation. D: delirium, assess, prevent and manage. E: early mobility and exercise. F: family engagement.

[[ABCDEF: pain, both trials, choice of drugs, delirium, early mobility, and family.]]

Notice that it follows the order of today's lesson. Pain first. Then light sedation, paired with breathing. Then the right drug. Then the brain.

Around the bundle sits delirium prevention without drugs. Limit noise, confusing stimuli and constant light. Protect sleep and the day-night rhythm. Reorient the patient, stimulate him, bring the family in, perhaps some music. Mobilise early. And give him back his glasses and hearing aids. PADIS two thousand eighteen suggests this multicomponent approach, as a conditional recommendation, on low-quality evidence.

And avoid the drugs that cause delirium: benzodiazepines, anticholinergics such as atropine and antihistamines, and high-dose steroids. And avoid stopping opioids, benzodiazepines or propofol suddenly.

spine: Principle: analgesia first, then the least sedation needed. Assess pain by self-report (0–10 scale), or by BPS (pain if >5) or CPOT (pain if >2).
Pain: opioids are the mainstay. Spare them with paracetamol, nefopam, low-dose ketamine or gabapentinoids. Avoid routine NSAIDs and IV lidocaine.
Target: light sedation, RASS −2 to +1 (Riker SAS 3–4), by daily interruption or a nurse-led protocol. Use BIS only when scales cannot be used, as in paralysis.
Drugs: propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. Midazolam accumulates and causes delirium; propofol risks PRIS above 4–5 mg/kg/h; dexmedetomidine causes bradycardia.
Evidence: awakening paired with a breathing trial (ABC trial) improved 1-year survival. Delirium on the day of the first trial means more extubation failure (40% vs 25%).
Bundle: ABCDEF: pain, both awakening and breathing trials, choice of drugs, delirium, early mobility, family. Avoid physical restraints.

open.text:
Let me start with two ways of looking after the same patient.

Patient A is intubated for pneumonia. He's on a midazolam infusion. Eyes closed, no movement, perfectly still. The nurses say he's comfortable. Nobody has asked him.

Patient B has the same pneumonia. He's on fentanyl, with a little propofol. He opens his eyes when you say his name. He nods when you ask about pain. He sits in the chair for an hour, and his daughter visits.

For years, Patient A was the picture of good ICU care. A still patient was a safe patient. We now know he's the one more likely to stay on the ventilator longer, to become delirious, and, in cohort studies, to die.

[[The goal of ICU sedation is a patient who is comfortable, calm and rousable, not a patient who is still.]]

What is the professor really checking? First, the order. Pain before sedation. Most residents start with the sedative, and that's the trap. Second, the scores, for pain and for depth, with their cut-offs. Third, the target, and the drugs that make it easier to hold. And fourth, how all of it ties into weaning and delirium, in one bundle.

So here's the plan. Pain first: why it matters, how to score it, and how to treat it. Then the depth score, RASS. Then the PADIS target and the drug choice. Then the pitfalls of each drug. And finally, how sedation links to weaning, and the bundle that holds it all together.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Analgesia first, then the least sedation needed.]] Assess pain by self-report, on a nought-to-ten scale. If he can't report, use the BPS, where pain is above five, or the CPOT, where pain is above two.

Treat pain with opioids, and spare them with paracetamol, nefopam, low-dose ketamine or gabapentinoids. Avoid routine NSAIDs and intravenous lidocaine.

Target light sedation, a RASS of minus two to plus one, by daily interruption or a nurse-led protocol. Use BIS only when the scales can't be used, as in paralysis.

Choose propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. Midazolam accumulates and causes delirium. Propofol risks PRIS above four to five milligrams per kilo per hour. Dexmedetomidine causes bradycardia.

The evidence: awakening paired with a breathing trial improved one-year survival. And delirium on the day of the first trial means more extubation failure, forty percent against twenty-five.

Tie it together with the ABCDEF bundle, and avoid physical restraints.

That's your answer. The principle, pain, the target, the drugs, the evidence and the bundle.

But the panel's next move is usually a challenge. Light sedation is a guideline. Where's the proof? Which trials moved us from Patient A to Patient B? That's next: the PADIS approach, and the evidence behind it.

questions.text: What is the PADIS guideline approach to sedation?

steps.bridge: PADIS means analgesia first and light sedation without benzodiazepines. Next: the trials behind going light →

lesson.text: You met this card in the last question. PADIS asks for analgesia first, then light sedation, a RASS of minus two to plus one, held by daily interruption or nurse-protocolised targets, with propofol or dexmedetomidine preferred over benzodiazepines. [[Analgesia first, then light sedation without benzodiazepines.]] Today the question is why. What evidence put that rule into the guideline?

steps.bridge: Daily interruption and paired awakening and breathing trials shortened ventilation and saved lives. Next: what this means at the first weaning trial →

lesson.text:
The evidence came in steps, and each step answered a doubt the last one left.

It starts with the harm. In cohort studies, deep sedation early, in the first forty-eight hours, was linked to later extubation and higher mortality. But that's an association. Sicker patients may simply be sedated more deeply. So we needed trials.

The first was Kress, in two thousand. Stop the sedative infusion every day, and let the patient wake. [[Daily sedation interruption shortened ventilation and ICU stay.]]

Then the ABC trial, Girard, in two thousand eight. The idea was simple. If you wake him, test on the same morning whether he can breathe. So the awakening trial was paired with a breathing trial. [[Paired awakening and breathing trials gave more ventilator-free days and lower one-year mortality.]] That's the trial behind the B in the bundle.

Then a natural question. If daily interruption works, and a nurse protocol that keeps sedation light also works, should you do both? SLEAP, in two thousand twelve, tested exactly that. Every patient had a nurse-led protocol, and half also had daily interruption. Adding the interruption gave no faster extubation, only more sedative and more nursing work. [[You need light sedation, by either route. You don't need both.]]

{{**The light-sedation evidence**
Cohorts: early deep sedation → later extubation, ↑ mortality
Kress 2000: daily interruption → shorter ventilation and ICU stay
ABC, Girard 2008: SAT + SBT → more ventilator-free days, ↓ 1-year mortality
SLEAP 2012: protocol + daily interruption = protocol alone; no need for both}}

So PADIS two thousand eighteen put it together. Light over deep sedation, a RASS of minus two to plus one. Analgesia first. Propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines.

Now the caution that sets you apart. Deep sedation still has a place. Severe ARDS early, especially when the patient is paralysed. Raised intracranial pressure. Status epilepticus. In them, deep sedation is the treatment, not the error.

[[Light is the default. Deep is a prescription, for a reason you can name.]]

And that paired trial, awakening with breathing, matters most on one particular day.

steps.bridge: Delirium at the first trial raises extubation failure; paired trials help. Next: how the ABCDEF bundle puts it into practice →

lesson.text: You met this card in the last question. Delirium on the day of the first breathing trial raised extubation failure, forty percent against twenty-five, and re-intubation, thirty-five against seventeen. Daily interruption or targeted light sedation is safe either way. [[Pairing awakening with a breathing trial improved one-year survival.]] That's the ABC trial you just heard, seen from the weaning side. Light sedation isn't only about comfort. It's what gives the first weaning trial its best chance.

And the bundle, from the last question. ABCDEF: assess and manage pain, both awakening and breathing trials, choice of analgesia and sedation, delirium, early mobility, and family. Around it, the non-drug measures: protect sleep, reorient, glasses and hearing aids, mobilise, bring the family in. Notice that the B is the ABC trial itself. [[The bundle is the evidence, turned into a daily routine.]]

spine: What it is: PADIS 2018 covers pain, agitation and sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep. The core rule: analgesia first, then light sedation.
Target: RASS −2 to +1, by daily interruption or nurse-protocolised targets. Propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. No physical restraints unless essential.
Evidence: Kress 2000: daily interruption shortened ventilation and ICU stay. ABC trial (Girard 2008): paired awakening and breathing trials lowered 1-year mortality.
SLEAP 2012: adding daily interruption to a nurse protocol gave no faster extubation, only more sedative and nursing work. One approach is enough.
Bundle: ABCDEF, plus non-drug delirium prevention: protect sleep, reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, early mobility, family.
Caution: deep sedation still has a place: severe early ARDS, paralysis, raised ICP, status epilepticus.

open.text:
Let me start with the question the panel loves to ask after sedation. Who says light is better?

Not so long ago, a ventilated patient was often kept deeply asleep until the day he was ready to come off. It seemed kind. It seemed safe. Then a series of trials asked a simple question. What if we let him wake up?

This question is about the PADIS guideline, from two thousand eighteen. PADIS stands for pain, agitation and sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep. It's the frame that holds the whole of ICU comfort care together.

What is the professor checking? That you know the core rule: analgesia first, then light sedation. That you know the target and the drug preference. And above all, that you can name the trials. Kress, the ABC trial, SLEAP. Then the caution that sharp candidates add: deep sedation is not always wrong.

You met the principles in the last question. So today we go over them quickly, and spend our time on the evidence.

So here's the plan. The PADIS rule, briefly. Then the trials. Then what this means at the first weaning trial. And finally, the bundle.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

PADIS, from two thousand eighteen, covers pain, agitation and sedation, delirium, immobility and sleep. [[The core rule: analgesia first, then light sedation.]]
