The target is a RASS of minus two to plus one, held by daily interruption or nurse-protocolised targets. Propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines. No physical restraints unless essential.

The evidence. Kress, two thousand: daily interruption shortened ventilation and ICU stay. The ABC trial, Girard, two thousand eight: paired awakening and breathing trials lowered one-year mortality. SLEAP, two thousand twelve: adding daily interruption to a nurse protocol gave nothing more, so there's no need for both.

The bundle is ABCDEF, with non-drug delirium prevention: protect sleep, reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, early mobility, and family.

And the caution: deep sedation still has a place, in severe early ARDS, paralysis, raised intracranial pressure and status epilepticus.

That's your answer. What it is, the target, the evidence, the bundle and the caution.

But PADIS left you with two preferred drugs, propofol and dexmedetomidine, and didn't choose between them. The panel will ask you to. Which one, and what do the head-to-head trials actually show? That's next.

questions.text: Dexmedetomidine versus propofol - what is the evidence?

steps.bridge: Propofol is fast on and off but drops pressure; dexmedetomidine spares breathing but slows the heart. Next: what PADIS prefers →

lesson.text: You met these drugs in the sedation lesson. Propofol is fast on and fast off, but it drops the blood pressure, and at high doses for days it risks PRIS. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-two agonist. It cuts sympathetic outflow, so it slows the heart and can lower the pressure, but it causes no respiratory depression. [[Propofol's price is hypotension. Dexmedetomidine's price is bradycardia.]] Keep those two prices in mind, because they're what the trials found.

steps.bridge: PADIS puts both ahead of benzodiazepines for light sedation. Next: what the head-to-head trials actually show →

lesson.text: And where PADIS puts them. For light sedation, a RASS of minus two to plus one, propofol or dexmedetomidine are both preferred over benzodiazepines. They sit on the same step. The two thousand twenty-five update leans gently towards dexmedetomidine when light sedation or less delirium is the priority, but only as a conditional suggestion. [[The guideline puts both drugs ahead of benzodiazepines, and leaves the choice between them open.]] The trials try to settle it.

Four trials, in the order they came.

First, MIDEX and PRODEX, in two thousand twelve. Dexmedetomidine against midazolam, and against propofol. Dexmedetomidine kept light sedation as well as either. It shortened ventilation compared with midazolam, and patients could communicate better. A promising start.

Then the big one. SPICE III, in two thousand nineteen, about four thousand patients. Early dexmedetomidine as the main sedative, against usual care. Ninety-day mortality was the same, twenty-nine point one percent in each arm. And there was more bradycardia and hypotension with dexmedetomidine. [[SPICE III: early dexmedetomidine gave the same ninety-day mortality, with more bradycardia and hypotension.]] One subgroup to know: possible harm at sixty-five or younger, and possible benefit in older patients. A subgroup, so a hypothesis, not a rule.

Then MENDS2, in two thousand twenty-one, in sepsis. Dexmedetomidine against propofol, head to head. No difference in days alive without delirium or coma, in ventilator-free days, in ninety-day death, or in later cognition. So the delirium promise didn't appear in sepsis either.

And the newest, A2B, in JAMA, two thousand twenty-five, one thousand four hundred and four patients. Dexmedetomidine or clonidine, against propofol. Did the alpha-two agonists get patients off the ventilator faster? No. There was more agitation, and more severe bradycardia. One hundred and eighty-day mortality was the same.

{{Trial | Comparison | Result
MIDEX/PRODEX 2012 | dex vs midazolam, propofol | equal light sedation; shorter MV vs midazolam
SPICE III 2019, n≈4,000 | early dex vs usual care | 90-day mortality 29.1% both; ↑ bradycardia, ↓ BP
MENDS2 2021, sepsis | dex vs propofol | no difference
A2B 2025, n=1,404 | dex or clonidine vs propofol | no faster extubation; ↑ agitation, bradycardia}}

[[No trial has shown dexmedetomidine beating propofol on outcome. A2B found no faster extubation, and more agitation and bradycardia.]]

So what do you do? Propofol stays the usual default, and A2B backs that, even though the two thousand twenty-five update leans the other way. Dexmedetomidine has its niches. Light sedation. Agitated delirium that is stopping extubation. And the patient who isn't intubated, because it spares the breathing. Avoid it when deep sedation is needed, or with bradycardia or heart block.

[[Propofol is the default. Dexmedetomidine is a tool for specific jobs.]]

spine: Pharmacology: propofol is fast on and off but causes hypotension and PRIS. Dexmedetomidine is an α2 agonist (0.2–1.4 µg/kg/h, EU): no respiratory depression, but bradycardia.
Guideline: PADIS prefers propofol or dexmedetomidine over benzodiazepines, for light sedation (RASS −2 to +1).
Evidence: SPICE III (2019, about 4,000): early dexmedetomidine, same 90-day mortality (29.1% each), more bradycardia and hypotension. MENDS2 (2021, sepsis): no difference.
More evidence: A2B (JAMA 2025, n = 1,404): dexmedetomidine or clonidine vs propofol: no faster extubation, more agitation and severe bradycardia, same 180-day mortality.
What I do: propofol as the usual default (PADIS 2025 leans to dexmedetomidine for light sedation). Dexmedetomidine for agitated delirium blocking extubation; avoid with bradycardia.

open.text:
Let me start with a choice you make every week.

A man of sixty, ventilated for pneumonia, on day three. He's getting better. You want him light, rousable, ready to wean. Propofol, or dexmedetomidine?

Dexmedetomidine has a seductive story. It sedates without touching the breathing. The patient stays rousable, and can still be assessed. It doesn't act through GABA, so it should cause less delirium. On paper, it's the perfect drug for light sedation.

So the question is a fair one. Did the trials bear out the story?

What the professor is checking is whether you know the pharmacology of both, where PADIS puts them, and then the trials, with their honest results. The trap is to answer from the story, not from the evidence. The big trials were mostly neutral, and the newest one leaned the other way.

So here's the plan. The two drugs, briefly. Where PADIS puts them. And then the trials, one by one.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Propofol is fast on and off, but causes hypotension and PRIS. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-two agonist, with no respiratory depression, but it causes bradycardia.

PADIS prefers either over benzodiazepines, for light sedation, a RASS of minus two to plus one.

The evidence. SPICE III, two thousand nineteen, about four thousand patients: early dexmedetomidine gave the same ninety-day mortality, twenty-nine point one percent in each arm, with more bradycardia and hypotension. MENDS2, two thousand twenty-one, in sepsis: no difference. And A2B, two thousand twenty-five, one thousand four hundred and four patients: no faster extubation, more agitation and severe bradycardia, and the same one hundred and eighty-day mortality.

[[Propofol as the default. Dexmedetomidine for light sedation, for agitated delirium blocking extubation, and for the non-intubated patient. Avoid it with bradycardia or heart block.]]

That's your answer. The pharmacology, the guideline, the trials, and what you do.

But one phrase keeps coming back. Agitated delirium. It's the one place where dexmedetomidine has a clear job. So what exactly is delirium? How do you diagnose it at the bedside, in a patient who can't speak, and what actually treats it? That's next.

questions.text: How do you diagnose and manage delirium in the ICU?

steps.bridge: Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention from brain inflammation and transmitter imbalance. Next: the arousal scale we check first →

lesson.text:
Start with the definition, from DSM five.

[[Delirium is a disturbance of attention and awareness, developing over hours to days, and fluctuating.]] Often there's an extra disturbance in cognition as well. It isn't explained by a neurocognitive disorder the patient already had. And it has a cause: an illness, a drug, intoxication or withdrawal.

Notice the key words. Attention. Hours to days. Fluctuating. Every bedside tool you'll meet is built on them.

Where does it sit in the ICU? It's the commonest form of acute encephalopathy in the critically ill.

Why does it happen? Think of the brain as one more organ caught in the storm of critical illness. Three things go wrong.

First, inflammation reaches the brain. The microglia and astrocytes are activated, and they release interleukin-one, TNF and nitric oxide.

Second, the barrier and the vessels are injured. The blood-brain barrier and the endothelium are damaged, and the brain can no longer match its blood flow to its activity. That's impaired neurovascular coupling.

Third, the transmitters fall out of balance. Above all, too little acetylcholine. And our own drugs push the same way. GABA-acting sedatives and anticholinergics both tip the balance further.

[[Delirium is neuroinflammation, barrier injury and transmitter imbalance, with too little acetylcholine at its heart.]]

And what sets it off? The same systemic triggers that injure every other organ. Inflammation. Hypoxaemia. Low perfusion. Metabolic upset, of sodium or glucose.

You've seen the brain's fragility after surgery: the elderly patient who is muddled for days after a hip fracture repair. ICU delirium is the same organ, under a longer and harder strain.

So before you can test what he's thinking, you need to know how awake he is.

steps.bridge: RASS sets the arousal level before we test the content of thought. Next: the four CAM-ICU features →

lesson.text: You met RASS in the sedation lesson. Plus four, combative, down to minus five, unarousable, with eye contact to voice as the hinge at minus one and minus two. Here it's the first step of the delirium assessment. [[You can test for delirium only at a RASS of minus three or above.]] At minus four or minus five, record coma, and reassess later. Arousal first. Then the content of consciousness.

steps.bridge: CAM-ICU positive = 1 + 2 + (3 or 4). Next: the shift-long alternative, ICDSC →

lesson.text:
CAM-ICU has four features, and one rule that joins them.

Feature one: an acute change from baseline, or a fluctuating mental status, over the past twenty-four hours.

Feature two: inattention. You read out ten letters, S A V E A H A A R T, and ask him to squeeze your hand on every letter A. More than two errors is inattention.

Feature three: an altered level of consciousness. That's simply any RASS other than zero. Why any? Because delirium can be hypoactive, drowsy, as well as hyperactive, agitated. Both count.

Feature four: disorganised thinking. Four yes-or-no questions. Will a stone float on water? Are there fish in the sea? Does one pound weigh more than two? Can you use a hammer to pound a nail? Then a simple command. More than one error is disorganised thinking.

And the rule. [[Delirium is feature one, plus feature two, plus either feature three or feature four.]]

{{**CAM-ICU** = 1 + 2 + (3 or 4)
1 acute change or fluctuation
2 inattention: > 2 errors on SAVEAHAART
3 altered consciousness: RASS ≠ 0
4 disorganised thinking: > 1 error}}

Why this structure? Delirium is a disorder of attention. So the tool won't call it without its two core features, the acute change and the inattention. Then it needs one more sign that the brain isn't working clearly. Think of a lock that needs two fixed keys, and then either one of two others.

[[Features one and two are both mandatory.]] And here's the practical shortcut. If the RASS is anything other than zero, feature three is already positive, and with the first two, he's delirious. If the RASS is zero, you go on to feature four.

CAM-ICU is a snapshot, a few minutes at the bedside. For a whole shift, there's another tool.

steps.bridge: ICDSC ≥4 is delirium; 1–3 is subsyndromal. Next: the full approach, from cause to drugs →

lesson.text:
The Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist, the ICDSC. Eight items, one point each. Altered consciousness. Inattention. Disorientation. Hallucinations or delusions. Psychomotor agitation or retardation. Inappropriate speech or mood. Sleep-wake disturbance. And symptom fluctuation.

[[An ICDSC of four or more is delirium. One to three is subsyndromal delirium.]]

The difference from CAM-ICU is time. The ICDSC is scored over a shift, eight to twenty-four hours, from routine observation. So it can catch the fluctuation that a single snapshot misses. It isn't scored if the patient responds only to noxious stimuli, because that's coma.

And one trap. A higher score doesn't mean more severe delirium. It's a screen, not a severity scale.

steps.bridge: Find the cause and treat without drugs; haloperidol does not shorten delirium. Next: the non-drug bundle in detail →

lesson.text:
Now the whole approach, in order.

Screen every shift, with a tool: CAM-ICU, or the ICDSC, four or more of eight. Remember the three types. Hypoactive, the commonest and the most missed. Hyperactive. And mixed. Without a tool, the quiet patient slips through.

Then look for the cause, as you would for any organ failure. Hypoxia. Sepsis. Metabolic upset. Withdrawal. Drugs, especially benzodiazepines and anticholinergics. And the simple things that are easy to forget: urinary retention, pain, and lost sleep. [[Delirium is a sign. Find its cause before you treat the behaviour.]]

Then prevent and treat without drugs. Reorientation. Glasses and hearing aids. Sleep. Early mobilisation. Family. And light sedation.

And then the drugs, where the evidence surprises people. Haloperidol does not shorten delirium. MIND-USA, in two thousand eighteen: haloperidol or ziprasidone against placebo, no difference. AID-ICU, in two thousand twenty-two, a thousand patients: haloperidol against placebo, no difference in days alive and out of hospital at ninety days.

[[Antipsychotics don't shorten ICU delirium. MIND-USA and AID-ICU were both neutral.]]

{{**Delirium: the drug trials**
MIND-USA 2018: haloperidol or ziprasidone = placebo
AID-ICU 2022, n = 1,000: haloperidol = placebo (days alive out of hospital at 90 days)
REDUCE 2018: prophylactic haloperidol, neutral
DahLIA 2016: dexmedetomidine for agitation stopping extubation}}

So PADIS says no routine antipsychotics, and no statins. No prophylactic haloperidol either: the REDUCE trial, in two thousand eighteen, was neutral. The one drug with a job is dexmedetomidine, for agitated delirium that is stopping extubation. That's the DahLIA trial, in two thousand sixteen.

And a short course of an antipsychotic still has a place, for distress, or danger to the patient himself. Treat the danger, not the label.

steps.bridge: Non-drug measures and ABCDEF are the treatment. Next: which drugs have been tried and failed →

lesson.text: You met this bundle in the sedation lesson. Limit noise and light, protect sleep and the day-night rhythm, reorient, bring the family in, mobilise early, and give back the glasses and hearing aids. It sits inside ABCDEF, where D is delirium. [[In delirium, the non-drug measures are not the soft option. They are the treatment.]] And avoid the drugs that cause it: benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, high-dose steroids, and the sudden withdrawal of sedatives.

steps.bridge: Antipsychotics failed, benzodiazepines worsen it, dexmedetomidine has a niche. Next: the exact PADIS rulings →

lesson.text:
Why have the drugs done so badly? Go back to the mechanism. Delirium is linked to too little acetylcholine, too much dopamine, and too much GABA-type inhibition.

Antipsychotics first. Haloperidol, the typical one. Olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine and aripiprazole, the atypicals. They block dopamine, so they calm the agitation. But they don't repair the failure of attention, which is the core of delirium. That fits the trials: calmer patients, but no shorter delirium.

Then the GABA drugs. [[Benzodiazepines worsen delirium, because they press harder on a brake that's already pressed.]] The exception is alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. There, the loss of that GABA effect is itself the cause, so giving it back is the treatment. And propofol? It's GABA-acting too, but it wears off within minutes, so it's preferred over benzodiazepines, which accumulate.

Then the one drug with a niche. Dexmedetomidine sedates through alpha-two receptors in the brainstem, not through GABA. So the patient stays rousable, and can still be assessed. [[Dexmedetomidine gives sedation without GABA, and preserves arousal.]]

And the others, each built on a sound idea. Cholinesterase inhibitors, donepezil and galantamine, follow the acetylcholine idea. But an ICU trial of rivastigmine was stopped for higher mortality. Melatonin and ramelteon target sleep. Statins, such as rosuvastatin, target inflammation. None has proven benefit, though the two thousand twenty-five update now suggests melatonin, conditionally, as a low-risk aid to sleep.

So the theory gave us many candidates, and the trials took almost all of them away.

So what does PADIS actually rule? Four questions, and the answer is mostly don't.

To prevent delirium in all ICU adults: don't use haloperidol, atypical antipsychotics, dexmedetomidine, statins or ketamine.

To treat subsyndromal delirium: don't use haloperidol or atypicals.

To treat delirium routinely: don't use haloperidol, atypicals or statins.

And one yes. [[In a ventilated patient whose agitation is stopping weaning or extubation, use dexmedetomidine.]]

{{Question | PADIS 2018
Prevent, all ICU adults | ✗ haloperidol, atypicals, dexmedetomidine, statins, ketamine
Subsyndromal | ✗ haloperidol, atypicals
Treat routinely | ✗ haloperidol, atypicals, statins
Agitation stopping extubation | ✓ dexmedetomidine}}

Notice that dexmedetomidine appears twice: no for prevention, yes for this one job. That's the kind of detail the panel tests.

All of these are conditional, on low-quality evidence. The two thousand twenty-five update makes no recommendation for or against antipsychotics over usual care. And a short course of haloperidol may still be used for distressing symptoms, such as hallucinations, or danger.

spine: What it is: an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness. The commonest acute encephalopathy in the ICU; hypoactive is the commonest and most missed type.
Diagnose: screen every shift. CAM-ICU: acute change or fluctuation + inattention + either altered consciousness or disorganised thinking. Or ICDSC ≥4 of 8.
Find the cause: hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic upset, withdrawal, drugs (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics), urinary retention, pain, sleep loss.
What I do: non-drug first: reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, sleep, early mobility, family, light sedation. Avoid benzodiazepines unless it is withdrawal.
Evidence: AID-ICU (2022, n = 1,000): haloperidol = placebo for days alive out of hospital at 90 days. MIND-USA (2018): haloperidol or ziprasidone = placebo.
Drugs: no routine antipsychotics. Dexmedetomidine for agitated delirium that stops extubation (DahLIA 2016). A short antipsychotic course only for distress or danger.

open.text:
Let me start with the patient nobody worries about.

Patient A, day five after a laparotomy, is pulling at his lines and shouting at the nurses. Everyone knows he's delirious.

Patient B, in the next bed, is quiet. He lies still, stares at the ceiling, and asks for nothing. The nurses say he's a good patient. He is also delirious. And his kind is the commoner of the two.

[[Hypoactive delirium is the commonest type, and the one most often missed.]]

Delirium is the brain failing, as the kidney fails in AKI. It's the commonest form of acute encephalopathy in the critically ill. And it doesn't announce itself. You have to look for it, with a tool, every shift.

What is the professor checking? That you can define it, with attention at the centre. That you know the two screening tools and their rules exactly. That you go looking for a cause. And that you know the uncomfortable truth about drugs: the antipsychotics we reach for don't shorten it. The trap is to say that haloperidol is the treatment.

So here's the plan. What delirium is, and why it happens. Then the arousal check, RASS. Then CAM-ICU, and then the ICDSC. Then the whole approach. Then the non-drug measures. Then the drugs that were tried. And finally, what PADIS rules about them.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness.]] It's the commonest acute encephalopathy in the ICU, and hypoactive delirium is the commonest and most missed type.

Diagnose it by screening every shift. CAM-ICU: an acute change or fluctuation, plus inattention, plus either altered consciousness or disorganised thinking. Or the ICDSC, four or more of eight.

Find the cause: hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic upset, withdrawal, drugs such as benzodiazepines and anticholinergics, urinary retention, pain, and sleep loss.

What you do: non-drug measures first. Reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, sleep, early mobility, family, and light sedation. Avoid benzodiazepines unless it's withdrawal.

The evidence. AID-ICU, two thousand twenty-two, a thousand patients: haloperidol was no better than placebo for days alive out of hospital at ninety days. MIND-USA, two thousand eighteen: haloperidol or ziprasidone, no better than placebo.

And the drugs: no routine antipsychotics. Dexmedetomidine for agitated delirium that stops extubation, from DahLIA. A short antipsychotic course only for distress or danger.

That's your answer. What it is, how you diagnose it, the cause, what you do, the evidence and the drugs.

But one sedative is left, and you know it well. The one you give every day in theatre, through the breathing circuit. Can the volatile agents sedate an ICU patient? That's next.

questions.text: What is the role of inhaled volatile sedation in the ICU?

lesson.text:
The agents are isoflurane or sevoflurane, given through the ventilator circuit.

The device is the key. The AnaConDa, the anaesthetic-conserving device, sits between the Y-piece and the patient. A syringe pump feeds liquid agent into it. Inside, a reflector catches most of the agent the patient breathes out, and returns it on the next breath. Think of a sponge in the airway, soaking up exhaled agent and giving it back. That's what makes ICU use affordable. Another device, the MIRUS, does the same job. And you need gas monitoring, just as in theatre.

Why use it? [[Volatiles leave through the lungs, not the liver or kidney, so they wash out within minutes and don't build up.]] Fast on, fast off, little accumulation. They're bronchodilators, relaxing airway smooth muscle directly, which matters in refractory bronchospasm. Patients need less opioid. And in Europe, isoflurane is licensed for ICU sedation.

Now the limits, and the first follows from where the device sits. Between the Y-piece and the patient, it adds dead space. On large breaths, that hardly matters. But in ARDS, at six millilitres per kilo, a bigger share of each small breath is wasted, and the CO2 rises.

[[The reflector adds dead space, so with small ARDS breaths, CO2 rises.]]

Then the practical limits. Scavenging the exhaled gas. Cost. Malignant hyperthermia, which you know well. And a renal one. Sevoflurane releases fluoride as it's metabolised. Over days, that can blunt the kidney's response to ADH, giving a dilute polyuria and a high sodium. That's nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, with prolonged use.

And now the trial. SESAR, in JAMA, two thousand twenty-five. Six hundred and eighty-seven patients with ARDS, needing deep sedation. Sevoflurane against propofol. The result went against sevoflurane. Fewer ventilator-free days, and a higher seven-day mortality, nineteen point four percent against thirteen point five. More hypercapnic acidosis, and more AKI.

{{**SESAR** (JAMA 2025, n = 687, ARDS, deep sedation)
Sevoflurane vs propofol
Ventilator-free days: fewer with sevoflurane
7-day mortality: **19.4% vs 13.5%**
More hypercapnic acidosis and AKI}}

Notice how that hypercapnia fits the dead-space problem you just heard. The physiology predicted the harm.

[[In SESAR, sevoflurane did worse than propofol in ARDS. So it is not for routine use in ARDS.]]

So where is its place now? Refractory status asthmaticus, where the bronchodilation is the whole point. And sedation that is failing with intravenous drugs. A rescue, not a routine.

spine: What it is: isoflurane or sevoflurane given through the ventilator circuit by a reflector such as AnaConDa or MIRUS, fed by a syringe pump, with gas monitoring.
Why: fast on and off, little accumulation, bronchodilation and less opioid use. Isoflurane is licensed for ICU sedation in Europe.
Limits: added dead space raises CO2 with small tidal volumes; scavenging and cost; malignant hyperthermia; prolonged sevoflurane can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Evidence: SESAR (JAMA 2025, n = 687, ARDS): sevoflurane vs propofol gave fewer ventilator-free days and higher 7-day mortality (19.4% vs 13.5%).
What I do: not for routine use in ARDS. Keep it for refractory status asthmaticus, or when IV sedation is failing.

open.text:
Let me start in your own operating theatre.

Every day, you keep patients asleep with sevoflurane or isoflurane. Turn the dial up, and they're deep in minutes. Turn it off, and they wake in minutes. Almost no accumulation, and little dependence on the liver or the kidney. The lungs take the agent in, and the lungs give it back.

So why don't we sedate ICU patients this way? For years, the answer was practical. An ICU ventilator has no vaporiser, and it doesn't rebreathe, so most of the agent would be blown away with every breath. Then came a device that solved that problem. And with it, a real question: is volatile sedation better than propofol?

What the professor is checking is whether you know the device and how it works, why volatiles are attractive, their limits, and one trial. The trap is enthusiasm. The anaesthetist in you will want to say yes. The newest trial says be careful.

So here's the plan, in one card. The agents and the device. The advantages. The limits. And then the trial that changed the answer.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

[[Inhaled volatile sedation is isoflurane or sevoflurane, given through the ventilator circuit by a reflector such as the AnaConDa or MIRUS, fed by a syringe pump, with gas monitoring.]]

Why: fast on and off, little accumulation, bronchodilation, and less opioid. Isoflurane is licensed for ICU sedation in Europe.

The limits: the added dead space raises the CO2 with small tidal volumes. Scavenging and cost. Malignant hyperthermia. And prolonged sevoflurane can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

The evidence: SESAR, two thousand twenty-five, six hundred and eighty-seven patients with ARDS. Sevoflurane against propofol gave fewer ventilator-free days, and a higher seven-day mortality, nineteen point four against thirteen point five percent.

What you do: not for routine use in ARDS. Keep it for refractory status asthmaticus, or when intravenous sedation is failing.

That's your answer. What it is, why, the limits, the evidence, and its place.

And that closes the sedation block. Everything in it pointed at one moment. Light sedation, paired awakening and breathing trials, delirium on the day of the first trial. All of it is about the day you ask: can this patient come off the ventilator? So how do you predict it with an index? And when weaning doesn't go to plan, how do you classify it: simple, difficult or prolonged? That's next.

questions.text: Weaning indices and classification of weaning.

steps.bridge: Readiness is a checklist: oxygenation, circulation, mechanics, mentation. Next: the best-known single index, RSBI →

lesson.text:
Start with readiness. Before any index or trial, ask a simpler question. Has the reason he was intubated got better? If the pneumonia is still raging, no number will help him.

Then the checklist, in four parts. Oxygenation, circulation, mechanics, and the patient himself.

Oxygenation first. An SaO2 above ninety percent on an FiO2 of zero point four or less, which is a P to F ratio of at least one hundred and fifty, with a PEEP of eight or less. Why those limits? Think about where he's going. After extubation he'll have a face mask or nasal prongs. No PEEP at all, and only a modest FiO2. [[So the oxygenation criteria ask one thing: can he oxygenate on roughly what he'll get once the tube is out?]]

Circulation. A heart rate of one hundred and forty or less, a systolic pressure between ninety and one hundred and sixty, and no or only minimal vasopressors. Breathing on his own is work, and work needs cardiac output. A circulation that needs propping up has no reserve for it. And coming off positive pressure loads the heart as well. We'll come back to that in the weaning failure lesson.

Mechanics. These ask whether the pump can carry the load. A respiratory rate of thirty-five or less. A maximal inspiratory pressure more negative than minus twenty to minus twenty-five centimetres of water, which measures strength. A tidal volume above five millilitres per kilo, and a vital capacity above ten. An RSBI under one hundred and five. And no significant respiratory acidosis.

And the patient. Awake enough, with adequate mentation. An adequate cough. No excess secretions. A stable metabolic state.

{{**Readiness to wean**
Oxygenation: SaO₂ >90% on FiO₂ ≤0.4 (P/F ≥150), PEEP ≤8
Circulation: HR ≤140, SBP 90–160, no or minimal vasopressors
Mechanics: RR ≤35, MIP ≤ −20 to −25 cmH₂O, VT >5 mL/kg, VC >10 mL/kg, RSBI <105
Clinical: cause resolved, good cough, few secretions, mentation, stable metabolic state}}

Notice that last group. [[The airway is a separate question from breathing. A patient can breathe well on his own and still fail after extubation, because he can't cough or clear his secretions.]] The panel likes that distinction.

One honest caution. These criteria are a screen, not a verdict. They tell you he's ready to be tested, not that he'll pass. That's why we screen every day, and then test with a trial.

But first, the most famous of the mechanical numbers.

steps.bridge: RSBI <105 is sensitive but not specific, so it screens rather than decides. Next: the other indices and their cut-offs →

lesson.text:
In nineteen ninety-one, Yang and Tobin published a simple observation in the New England Journal. Patients who were going to fail weaning had a recognisable way of breathing. Fast, and shallow.

Why would a failing patient breathe like that? Think of the respiratory muscles as a pump under strain. Each breath costs effort, and a big breath costs more. So a pump that can't cope keeps the minute ventilation up the cheapest way it can. Smaller breaths, and more of them.

Now the index. [[The rapid shallow breathing index is the respiratory rate divided by the tidal volume in litres.]] Dividing rate by volume magnifies the pattern. A rising rate pushes the number up, and a falling volume pushes it up too.

Hear the difference. Thirty-five breaths a minute of three hundred millilitres gives about one hundred and seventeen. Twenty breaths of five hundred gives forty.

{{**RSBI = RR ÷ VT (litres)**, breaths/min/L
35 ÷ 0.3 ≈ 117 · 20 ÷ 0.5 = 40
Cut-off **<105** predicts success · sensitivity 97% · specificity 64% · NPV 95%
Yang & Tobin, NEJM 1991}}

The cut-off is one hundred and five. Below it predicts success.

Now the part that matters most. Its sensitivity is ninety-seven percent, but its specificity is only sixty-four. What does that mean at the bedside? Nearly everyone who's going to succeed has a low value. But many patients with a low value still fail, from causes the index can't see. The heart. The airway. Secretions. [[So a high RSBI is a strong warning. A low one doesn't promise success. It screens, and the breathing trial decides.]]

How you measure it matters just as much. Unassisted, with a hand-held spirometer, over one minute. Why unassisted? Because pressure support or CPAP makes each breath bigger and slows the rate. The number falls, and he looks readier than he is. There's a subtler trap too. If you read the rate off the ventilator, efforts that fail to trigger aren't counted. The rate looks lower, and the index reads falsely low. So count every breath.

What else moves it? Fever and sepsis raise the rate, and a narrow tube adds load, so the index rises. And in COPD it's simply less accurate.

One honest caution. Quoting an RSBI measured on pressure support is a classic way to lose marks. The examiner will ask how you measured it. Have the answer ready: unassisted, over one minute, every breath counted.

And the RSBI isn't the only index. There are others, each built on a different idea.

steps.bridge: Drive, strength and load can each be indexed, but none is perfect. Next: how patients are grouped by their weaning course →

lesson.text:
You met these with P-SILI. P zero point one is the pressure drop in the first tenth of a second against a closed valve. It reads the brain's drive, not the lung's mechanics. Below four to five predicts success. CROP joins compliance, rate, oxygenation and inspiratory pressure, and above thirteen predicts success. The integrative weaning index, twenty-five or more.

Here's why they matter for this question. [[Each index looks at one part of the balance between load and capacity. None sees the whole, so none decides alone.]]

That's why, after the indices, we look at how the patient actually does over time. That's the classification.

steps.bridge: This is the ICC 2007 (Boles) system: simple, difficult, prolonged. Next: how WIND fills its gaps →

lesson.text:
The classification you'll be asked for came from an international consensus conference on weaning, published by Boles and colleagues in two thousand seven.

First, the name trap. You'll often see it called Brochard's classification. Say Boles, the consensus conference of two thousand seven.

The idea is to count, starting from the first spontaneous breathing trial. How many trials, and how many days, did it take to get him off?

Simple weaning. He passes the first trial and is extubated. The consensus estimated about sixty-nine percent of patients here. Later cohorts found nearer fifty-five to sixty.

Difficult weaning. He fails the first trial, and needs up to three trials, or up to seven days from the first one. About thirty to forty percent.

Prolonged weaning. He fails three or more trials, or needs more than seven days after the first. Up to about fifteen percent.

{{Group | Definition, from the first SBT | Share
**Simple** | extubated after the first SBT | ICC 69%; later cohorts 55–60%
**Difficult** | up to 3 SBTs or ≤7 days | 30–40%
**Prolonged** | ≥3 failed SBTs (needs >3) or >7 days | up to 15%
Boles et al., Eur Respir J 2007 (ICC), not Brochard}}

Why count this way? [[Each further failure points to a deeper problem.]] The simple weaner mostly needed only the trial. The difficult weaner has a reversible cause to find, often the heart, fluid, or muscle weakness. The prolonged weaner often has chronic heart, lung or muscle failure. We'll walk through those causes in the weaning failure lesson.

And outcome follows. ICU mortality is highest in the prolonged group. Here's a point a sharp panel may press. In a later cohort, Peñuelas and colleagues in two thousand eleven, difficult weaners did about as well as simple ones. [[It's prolonged weaning that clearly carries the higher mortality.]]

Now the blind spot. The clock starts at the first breathing trial. So a patient who never had one isn't classified at all. The patient who got a tracheostomy before any trial. The one who died before he was ever tested. They fall outside. And that's the gap the next system was built to close.

steps.bridge: WIND counts from the first attempt and includes everyone, so it predicts mortality. Next: what helps right around extubation →

lesson.text:
WIND came from Béduneau and colleagues, in two thousand seventeen. And the change is one idea.

[[WIND starts the clock at the first separation attempt, whether that's a breathing trial or an extubation. So it counts every ventilated patient.]]

Separation has a strict meaning. Extubation without death or reintubation for seven days. Or, with a tracheostomy, seven days or more off the ventilator.

Then the groups are by time. Short weaning, separated within one day of the first attempt. Difficult, between one and seven days. Prolonged, more than seven days. And a new group, group zero, the patients who never had a separation attempt at all. The very patients the old system left out.

Look at the picture if you'd like. Two clocks. The old one starts at the first trial and leaves the untried patients outside. WIND starts at the first attempt of any kind, and gives the untried patients a box of their own.

{{pic}}

Why does that matter? Because the point of a classification is to tell you something about outcome. [[In WIND, mortality rises with each group, from short, to difficult, to prolonged.]] So it covers everyone, and it predicts.

In the viva, give both, in order. The consensus groups first, with the right name. Then say: WIND, Béduneau two thousand seventeen, counts from the first separation attempt, includes everyone, and mortality rises by group. That's the complete answer.

One honest caution. The two systems use the same words, difficult and prolonged, with different clocks. So when you quote a figure, say which system it comes from.

So now you know what kind of weaner he is. What helps him at the moment the tube comes out?
lesson.cap: ICC 2007 starts at the first SBT and leaves untried patients out; WIND starts at any first attempt and includes them.

lesson.text:
Three things around extubation can't be tested by the breathing trial. The upper airway. The support you give straight afterwards. And, surprisingly, what the patient himself thinks.

First, the airway. A tube has been sitting in the larynx for days, and the larynx can swell around it. With the tube in, you'd never know. So you test for room. Deflate the cuff, and see whether gas leaks around the tube. That's the cuff leak test.

Picture a ring on a swollen finger. If air can slip past it, there's room. If it can't, the ring is tight. [[A small leak means the larynx is swollen tight around the tube, and after extubation that airway may narrow and cause stridor.]]

So in a patient at risk of laryngeal oedema, you give corticosteroids before extubation. But steroids shrink oedema slowly, over hours. So they work best started twelve to twenty-four hours before, and at least four hours before.

And one caution about the test itself. A good leak doesn't rule out stridor. And a small leak can come from secretions, or simply from a large tube. So it flags risk. It doesn't decide.

Second, NIV. It's used in two different ways around extubation, and the panel wants you to keep them apart. Facilitative NIV is for the COPD patient who has failed his breathing trial. Instead of keeping him intubated, you extubate him early, straight onto NIV. The mask takes over the work, so he spends fewer days with a tube, and has less chance of ventilator pneumonia. Prophylactic NIV is different. The patient has passed his trial, but he's at high risk. You put him on NIV straight after extubation, to stop failure before it starts.

[[Facilitative NIV shortens intubation in COPD. Prophylactic NIV prevents failure in the high-risk patient. Neither is a rescue for failure that has already set in.]]

The evidence for NIV as a weaning strategy is strongest in COPD. A Cochrane meta-analysis of sixteen trials, nine hundred and ninety-four patients, two-thirds of them with COPD, found lower mortality, less weaning failure, less ventilator pneumonia, shorter stays and fewer reintubations. Notice the two-thirds. That's where the benefit is clearest.

Third, and this one surprises people. Ask the patient. Those who felt confident they'd manage succeeded about ninety percent of the time. Those who didn't, about forty-five percent. It costs nothing to ask.

That completes the picture, from readiness to the moment the tube comes out.

spine: Readiness: cause resolved, SaO2 >90% on FiO2 ≤0.4 with PEEP ≤8, stable circulation, awake with a cough. Then screen with an index.
Indices: RSBI = rate ÷ tidal volume (L); <105 predicts success (sensitivity 97%, specificity 64%). Others: P0.1 below 4–5, CROP >13, integrative weaning index ≥25.
Classification: ICC 2007 (Boles): simple = extubated after the first trial; difficult = up to 3 trials or 7 days; prolonged = more than 3 trials or more than 7 days.
WIND (Béduneau 2017): counts from the first separation attempt. Short within 1 day, difficult 1–7 days, prolonged >7 days, group 0 never tried. Mortality rises by group.
Caution: RSBI is falsely low on CPAP or pressure support, so measure it unassisted over 1 minute.

open.text:
Let me start with a question that sounds simple.

Your patient has been on the ventilator for five days. The pneumonia that put him there is clearing. Every morning on the round, someone asks the same thing. Can he come off today?

It's one of the most important questions in intensive care, and it's expensive to get wrong in either direction. Keep him on too long, and every extra day brings more sedation, more risk of ventilator pneumonia, a weaker diaphragm. Take him off too early, and he may fail and need the tube back.

So weaning isn't one decision. It's a sequence. First, is he ready to try? Then a quick bedside number that screens him. Then the real test, the breathing trial. And afterwards, how the whole course went, which tells you what kind of weaner he is.

This question asks for two of those pieces, the indices and the classification. What the professor is really checking is whether you know what each index can and can't tell you. The resident who says the RSBI is under one hundred and five, so he'll succeed, has walked into the trap. And in the classification, he wants the right name, the right year, and the newer system that fixed its blind spot.

So here's the plan. First, the readiness checklist. Then the rapid shallow breathing index, and why it's a screen and not a verdict. Then a quick return to the other indices. Then the classic classification, simple, difficult and prolonged. Then WIND, which counts every patient. And finally, the checks right around extubation.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Before any index, he must be ready. The cause improving. An SaO2 above ninety percent on an FiO2 of zero point four or less, with a PEEP of eight or less. A stable circulation. Awake, with a cough.

Then a screen. [[The RSBI is the rate divided by the tidal volume in litres. Below one hundred and five predicts success. Measure it unassisted, over one minute.]] It's sensitive, not specific, so it screens and the trial decides. P zero point one, CROP and the integrative index each see one part of the balance.

Then classify by the course. The consensus conference, Boles, two thousand seven. Simple, extubated after the first trial. Difficult, up to three trials or seven days. Prolonged, beyond that. [[And WIND, Béduneau two thousand seventeen, counts from the first separation attempt, includes everyone, and mortality rises by group.]]

And the caution. An RSBI measured on CPAP or pressure support is falsely low.

That's your answer. Readiness, the indices with their cut-offs and their limits, the two classifications, and the caution.

But here's something to carry forward. Everything today pointed at one moment, the breathing trial. The index says try. The classification counts trials. So how exactly do you run one? A T-piece, or pressure support? Thirty minutes, or two hours? A large trial has now answered that, and the answer surprised many people. That's next.

questions.text: How do you do an SBT? Which method is better?

steps.bridge: Screen daily: oxygenation, circulation, mechanics, mentation. Next: the bedside index before the trial →

lesson.text:
You met the readiness checklist in the last lesson. The cause improving. An SaO2 above ninety percent on an FiO2 of zero point four or less, with a PEEP of eight or less. A stable circulation without high-dose vasopressors. Awake, with a cough, and few secretions.

Here's why it matters for this question. [[The screen is done every day, and its job is to find the first day he can be tested.]] Every day you miss is a day on the ventilator he may not have needed.

So he passes the screen. One quick number next.

steps.bridge: RSBI <105 says try; the trial itself decides. Next: how to run the trial →

lesson.text:
You met the rapid shallow breathing index too. The rate divided by the tidal volume in litres, measured unassisted over one minute. Below one hundred and five predicts success.

Remember its character. Sensitive, not specific. A high value is a strong warning, but a low value doesn't promise success, because it can't see the heart, the airway or the secretions. [[The RSBI says try. The breathing trial itself decides.]]

So now, the trial.

steps.bridge: T-piece or PS 5–8 for 30 minutes, 120 in COPD; a large RCT now settles the method. Next: what that trial showed →

lesson.text:
A spontaneous breathing trial asks one question. Can this patient carry, on his own, the work he'll face once the tube is out? Think of it as a test drive on the road he'll actually use.

There are two ways to run it. A T-piece, where he breathes through the tube with no support at all. Or low pressure support, five to eight centimetres of water, with or without a PEEP of five.

Why was low pressure support ever used for a trial? The idea was that the tube adds resistance, an extra load he won't carry once it's out, and a little pressure support would cancel it. But here's the twist. After extubation, that resistance doesn't simply vanish. The larynx and upper airway are often swollen, and they add a resistance of their own. [[So the T-piece is the closer copy of life after extubation. It's the harder test.]]

How long? [[Thirty minutes is as good as one hundred and twenty for most patients.]] Most failures show early, in the first half hour. But patients with COPD, and other high-risk patients, may decompensate later. So for them, use the full one hundred and twenty minutes.

And if he fails? Put him back on a comfortable, non-fatiguing mode. Find the cause, because a failed trial means something is still wrong. And try again after twenty-four hours. Why not again in the afternoon? Because once-daily trials did as well as several a day. Esteban showed that in nineteen ninety-five. Rest the muscles, fix the problem, and retry tomorrow.

Now, which method is better? For a long time the evidence was weak. Then the ATS and CHEST guideline of two thousand seventeen made a conditional recommendation, on moderate-certainty evidence, to run the first trial on pressure support of five to eight rather than on a T-piece.

{{**SBT:** T-piece, or PS 5–8 cmH₂O ± PEEP 5
Duration: 30 min ≈ 120 min; **120 min in COPD and high risk**
Failed → comfortable mode, find the cause, retry in 24 h
ATS/CHEST 2017: first SBT on PS 5–8 rather than T-piece (conditional, moderate certainty; extubation success 75% vs 69%)}}

And then a large trial put the question to the test.

steps.bridge: PSV 8 for 30 minutes got more patients extubated than a 2-hour T-piece. Next: when to call a trial failed →

lesson.text:
Subirà and colleagues published it in JAMA in two thousand nineteen. One thousand one hundred and fifty-three patients. One group had a thirty-minute trial on a pressure support of eight with zero PEEP. The other had a two-hour T-piece trial.

The result. [[Successful extubation was eighty-two point three percent with pressure support, against seventy-four percent with the T-piece. Reintubation was the same.]]

Now think about what that second sentence means. The fear about an easier test was that it would let through patients who'd fail afterwards. It didn't. More patients passed, and they stayed extubated just as often. So the harder test had been holding back patients who were ready. Ninety-day mortality was also lower with pressure support, but that was a secondary outcome, so treat it as support, not proof.

{{**Subirà** (JAMA 2019, n = 1,153): PSV 8 / ZEEP × 30 min vs T-piece × 2 h
Successful extubation **82.3 vs 74.0%** · reintubation same · 90-day mortality lower with PSV (secondary)}}

[[So for most patients, the answer is pressure support of eight with no PEEP, for thirty minutes.]]

But keep one exception. The T-piece mimics the effort after extubation most closely. So when you suspect the heart will fail on weaning, the T-piece is the more honest stress test. Say both sentences in the viva, and you've answered which is better.

Now, during the trial, how do you know he's failing?

steps.bridge: Stop for poor gas exchange, fast breathing, unstable circulation or distress. Next: when the harder T-piece test is better →

lesson.text:
The failure criteria look like a long list. Don't learn them as one. Sort them into four groups, and start with the ones you can see from the door.

The breathing pattern usually changes first. The rate climbs above thirty-five, or rises by half. The RSBI climbs above one hundred and five. Then the circulation answers, with an adrenergic surge. A heart rate above one hundred and forty, or up by a fifth. A systolic pressure above one hundred and eighty, or up by a fifth, or below ninety. An arrhythmia. And the clinical signs. Agitation, sweating, cyanosis, the accessory muscles working, the abdomen moving in as he breathes in.

Gas exchange often changes later. An SaO2 below ninety percent, or a PaO2 of fifty to sixty or less on an FiO2 of at least zero point five. A PaCO2 above fifty, or a rise of more than eight. A pH below seven point three two, or a fall of zero point zero seven or more.

{{**SBT failure**
Gas exchange: SaO₂ <90% or PaO₂ ≤50–60 on FiO₂ ≥0.5; PaCO₂ >50 or ↑ >8 mmHg; pH <7.32 or ↓ ≥0.07
Pattern: RR >35 or ↑50%; RSBI >105
Circulation: HR >140 or ↑20%; SBP >180 or ↑20%, or <90; arrhythmia
Clinical: agitation, sweating, cyanosis, accessory muscles, abdominal paradox}}

[[Don't wait for the gases. A rising rate, a racing heart and sweating already mean failure.]]

And one pattern to notice. Early distress with a rise in both blood pressure and heart rate is the clue that the heart is failing on weaning. We'll come back to it.

Now, two kinds of patient need their own plan. First, the obese.

steps.bridge: In obesity, a T-piece mimics post-extubation work; extubate to NIV. Next: the COPD extubation standard →

lesson.text:
In obesity, the heavy chest wall and abdomen push the diaphragm up and collapse the lung at the bases, more so when he lies flat. On the ventilator, positive pressure hides this, because it holds that lung open. Take the pressure away, and the bases collapse, and the work of breathing rises.

So which trial tells the truth? In morbidly obese patients, Mahul and colleagues, in two thousand sixteen, compared the work of breathing during each kind of trial with the work measured after extubation. [[Only a T-piece, or a pressure support of zero with a PEEP of zero, matched the work after extubation. Any added support underestimated it.]]

Notice that this goes against the general answer you've just learned. For most patients, pressure support of eight. For the obese patient, the support itself hides the problem, so you take it all away.

Then the extubation. Stop the sedation, and extubate straight onto NIV or CPAP. It keeps the bases open, prevents atelectasis, and prevents reintubation. His pre-operative settings can be used.

One more point from the same card, because the panel may wander there. Proning is feasible and safe in the obese with a trained team. It improves the P to F ratio, and it may reduce mortality. The precautions are careful positioning, so the abdomen hangs free, and reverse Trendelenburg, which lets the abdominal contents fall away from the diaphragm.

As an anaesthetist, you know this patient well. He's the one whose saturation drops in recovery once the PEEP has gone.

[[Remove all support to test him. Then give support back the moment the tube comes out.]]

And the other patient with his own rule is the one with COPD.

In COPD, the standard is simple. [[Extubate him to NIV.]]

Why does he need it? After extubation, his airways still empty slowly. Gas is trapped at the end of each breath, and that trapped pressure, the auto-PEEP, loads his inspiratory muscles before any air moves. NIV answers both halves of the problem. Its external PEEP offsets the auto-PEEP, so each breath is easier to start. Its pressure support shares the work. So the muscles don't tire into hypercapnic failure.

[[NIV straight after extubation prevents post-extubation respiratory failure. It lowers reintubation and ICU mortality.]]

But notice the word prevents. It works as prevention, not as rescue. Once failure has set in after extubation, NIV mainly delays the tube, and that delay was linked to higher mortality. We'll meet that trial when we reach post-extubation failure.

Two links to the trial you've just learned. In COPD, run the full one hundred and twenty minutes, because these patients may tire late. And pressure support is easier for him than a T-piece.

The panel may then widen the question to outcome. Asthma has the better prognosis, and ventilation doesn't worsen it, because its bronchospasm reverses and the lung returns to normal. COPD has fixed obstruction and a flattened, weak diaphragm, so failure tends to recur. Six-month survival in ventilated COPD is forty to seventy percent. Prognosis depends on functional and nutritional status, how often he exacerbates, and his other illnesses. Markers of a poor outcome are dyspnoea at rest, cor pulmonale, obstruction that doesn't reverse with a beta-agonist, cachexia, frequent exacerbations, and a cardiomyopathy or nephropathy.

spine: Who: daily screen. Cause improving, P/F ≥150 on FiO2 ≤0.4 and PEEP ≤8, stable without high-dose pressors, awake, can cough. RSBI <105 supports trying.
How: pressure support 5–8 cmH2O with zero or low PEEP for 30 minutes, or a T-piece for 30–120 minutes. Use 120 minutes in COPD and high-risk patients.
Fail if: RR >35, SpO2 <90%, heart rate >140 or up 20%, systolic BP >180 or <90, agitation, sweating, accessory muscles. Then rest, find the cause, retry in 24 hours.
Evidence: Subirà (JAMA 2019, n = 1,153): PSV 8 with zero PEEP for 30 minutes vs a 2-hour T-piece: successful extubation 82.3% vs 74.0%, same reintubation.
Which is better: PSV for most. The T-piece is the harder test and mimics post-extubation effort: prefer it if cardiac failure on weaning is suspected, and in obesity.
After: extubate COPD to NIV; it lowers reintubation and ICU mortality.

open.text:
Let me start with two ways of asking the same question.

Patient A is put on a T-piece. No support at all, just humidified oxygen flowing past the tube, for two hours. Patient B stays on the ventilator, with a pressure support of eight and no PEEP, for thirty minutes. Both are being asked the same thing. Can you breathe on your own?

But they're not being asked equally hard. The T-piece is the tougher exam. So which should you use? The harder test, which might hold back a patient who could have come off? Or the easier one, which might let through a patient who'll fail?

For years the honest answer was that we didn't really know. Now we do.

What the professor is checking with this question is three things. Do you know who gets a trial and how to run it? Do you know when to stop it? And do you know the trial that compared the two methods, with its numbers, and the patients in whom you'd still choose the T-piece?

You already have the first part, the daily screen and the RSBI, from the last lesson, so we'll pass through those quickly. Then the method and the duration. Then the trial. Then the failure criteria. And finally two patients who need their own plan, the obese patient and the patient with COPD.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Who gets a trial? Everyone, screened daily. The cause improving, a P to F ratio of at least one hundred and fifty on an FiO2 of zero point four or less and a PEEP of eight or less, a stable circulation without high-dose pressors, awake, able to cough. An RSBI under one hundred and five supports trying.

How? [[Pressure support of five to eight with zero or low PEEP for thirty minutes, or a T-piece for thirty to one hundred and twenty. The full hundred and twenty in COPD and high-risk patients.]]

When to stop? A rate above thirty-five, an SpO2 below ninety, a heart rate above one hundred and forty or up by a fifth, a systolic above one hundred and eighty or below ninety, agitation, sweating, accessory muscles. Then rest him, find the cause, and retry in twenty-four hours.

The evidence. Subirà, two thousand nineteen, eleven hundred and fifty-three patients. Pressure support of eight with zero PEEP for thirty minutes, against a two-hour T-piece. Successful extubation eighty-two point three against seventy-four percent, with the same reintubation.

Which is better? [[Pressure support for most. The T-piece is the harder test and mimics the effort after extubation, so prefer it when you suspect the heart, and in obesity.]]

And afterwards, the COPD patient goes straight onto NIV.

That's your answer. Who, how, when to stop, the evidence, which is better, and what comes after.

But here's something to carry forward. Some patients fail, and fail again. A week passes, then ten days, and the tube is still in. At some point someone on the round asks, shall we do a tracheostomy? And should he have had it on day three? That's next.

questions.text: Early versus late tracheostomy.

steps.bridge: Tracheostomy is a tool for difficult and prolonged weaning. Next: does doing it early help →

lesson.text:
Go back to the classification. The difficult weaner needs up to three trials or up to seven days. The prolonged weaner needs more. Each needs a plan, and a tracheostomy is one tool in it, not the plan itself.

In difficult weaning, four things. First, optimal assistance. Pressure support rather than full control, because a diaphragm that does some of the work doesn't waste from disuse. Second, look for every reversible cause. The heart, fluid, muscle, secretions. A BNP helps here, because fluid overload and the heart are easy to miss. Third, mobilise early. And fourth, consider a tracheostomy.

In prolonged weaning, the goal changes. It's no longer about the next trial. It's rehabilitation. A multidisciplinary team, and aggressive physiotherapy. And the tracheostomy becomes a pathway. Downsizing the tube. Trials on a T-piece with the cuff down. A speaking valve, which gives him back his voice. And, for some, ventilation at home.

[[In difficult weaning, find the cause and give the right support. In prolonged weaning, rehabilitate, and use the tracheostomy as a route back to breathing and speaking.]]

Why does a tracheostomy help these patients? It's much shorter than an oral tube, so it usually adds less resistance and dead space. It's far more comfortable, so he needs less sedation. And he can be taken off the ventilator and put back on easily, which makes progressive trials off the ventilator possible.

So the tool is clear. The real question is when.

The big trial is TracMan, from the United Kingdom, published in JAMA in two thousand thirteen. Nine hundred and nine patients, all expected to need prolonged ventilation. Early tracheostomy, on day one to four, against late, on day ten or later.

The result. [[Thirty-day mortality was thirty point eight against thirty-one point five percent. No difference.]] Early tracheostomy did give fewer days of sedation.

But here's the surprise, the part you should always say. In the late group, only about half ever needed a tracheostomy at all. Think about what that means. These were patients picked as likely to need a long time on the ventilator, and for about half of them it never came to that. [[We can't predict on day three who will need prolonged ventilation. So an early policy gives tracheostomies to many patients who'd never have needed one.]]

Then stroke. SETPOINT two, in JAMA in two thousand twenty-two, in ventilated stroke patients. Early tracheostomy, within five days, against later. No better function at six months. And the meta-analyses agree. [[Early tracheostomy may cut sedation and ventilator days. It doesn't cut mortality.]]

{{**TracMan** (JAMA 2013, n = 909): early d1–4 vs late d≥10 → 30-day mortality **30.8 vs 31.5%**; fewer sedation days; only ~half of the late group ever needed one
**SETPOINT two** (JAMA 2022, stroke): ≤5 d vs later → no better 6-month function
**Meta-analyses:** fewer sedation and ventilator days, not lower mortality}}

So what do you do? Decide when weaning is clearly prolonged, often around day seven to ten. That gives the patient time to declare himself. But go earlier in high cervical cord injury, and in severe brain injury needing airway protection. In them, the need is plain from the start, so the prediction problem disappears.

Then the technique. Percutaneous against surgical. Mortality is similar. Percutaneous is done at the bedside, it's quicker, and it has fewer wound infections. Surgical is for the difficult neck. A short, fat neck, previous neck surgery, a coagulopathy, an unstable spine.

[[So decide around day seven to ten, earlier when the need is certain, and go percutaneous unless the neck is difficult.]]

One honest caution. TracMan was a trial of timing, not of tracheostomy itself. It doesn't say tracheostomy is useless. It says that doing it early, as a policy, doesn't save lives.

spine: What it is: the timing question for tracheostomy in difficult or prolonged weaning. TracMan defined early as day 1–4 and late as day 10 or later.
Evidence: TracMan (JAMA 2013, n = 909): 30-day mortality 30.8% vs 31.5%, no difference; fewer sedation days with early. Only about half of the late group ever needed one.
More evidence: SETPOINT2 (JAMA 2022, stroke): early (≤5 days) gave no better 6-month function. Meta-analyses: early may cut sedation and ventilator days, not mortality.
What I do: decide when weaning is clearly prolonged, around day 7–10. Go earlier in high cervical cord injury or severe brain injury needing airway protection.
Technique: percutaneous and surgical have similar mortality. Percutaneous is bedside, quicker, fewer wound infections. Surgical for difficult anatomy, coagulopathy, unstable spine.

open.text:
Let me start with a prediction.

It's day three. Your patient is sedated, ventilated, and not going anywhere soon. You're asked to predict, now, whether he'll still need the ventilator in ten days' time. If yes, the argument goes, give him a tracheostomy now. Less sedation, more comfort, easier mouth care, earlier mobilisation. Why wait?

The catch is the prediction. And that's what this question is really about.

What the professor is checking is whether you know the big trial, its numbers and its surprise. Whether you know what early tracheostomy does help, and what it doesn't. Whether you have a sensible timing rule of your own, with the patients in whom you'd go early. And whether you can compare percutaneous with surgical.

So here's the plan. First, where tracheostomy sits in difficult and prolonged weaning. Then the evidence on timing, and the technique.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

Tracheostomy is a tool in difficult and prolonged weaning, alongside optimal support, the search for reversible causes, and rehabilitation.

[[TracMan, two thousand thirteen, nine hundred and nine patients. Early on day one to four, against late on day ten or later. Thirty-day mortality thirty point eight against thirty-one point five percent. No difference.]] Fewer sedation days with early. And only about half of the late group ever needed one.

SETPOINT two, in stroke, found no better function at six months. The meta-analyses show fewer sedation and ventilator days, but not lower mortality.

What I do. Decide when weaning is clearly prolonged, around day seven to ten. Earlier in high cervical cord injury or severe brain injury needing airway protection. Percutaneous at the bedside, and surgical for the difficult neck or a coagulopathy.

That's your answer. Where it fits, the evidence, what you do, and the technique.

But here's something to carry forward. Most of your patients will never need a tracheostomy. They pass the trial, and the tube comes out. And then, over the next day or two, some of them fail anyway. Can you see that coming, and stop it? That's next.

questions.text: How do you prevent post-extubation failure?

steps.bridge: Prevention starts with a proper breathing trial; high-risk COPD gets NIV afterwards. Next: the airway and NIV checks around extubation →

lesson.text:
Prevention starts before extubation, by doing the sequence properly. Two tests, one after the other. A quick screen that misses few who would succeed, and then a real test of the load.

The screen is the RSBI, the rate divided by the tidal volume in litres, measured over one minute of unassisted breathing. On a T-piece, with no pressure support and no PEEP, because support lowers the value and flatters the patient. Below about one hundred to one hundred and five predicts success.

The confirmatory test is the breathing trial. Thirty to one hundred and twenty minutes, on pressure support of five to eight or on a T-piece, once a day. If he fails, back to full support for twenty-four hours.

[[A sieve first, then a test drive. The screen picks who to test. Only the trial says he can go.]]

The card asks two more things. Which mode weans worst? Intermittent mandatory ventilation. It gives the longest weaning, and the most fatigue. You'd think the machine's breaths would give the muscles a rest. They don't. The muscles work about as hard during the machine's breaths as during their own. So they never rest, and they tire.

And if you wean on pressure support, come down in steps of three to six centimetres of water, watching the rate. Why the rate? Because a rising rate is the first sign that the load is outgrowing his capacity.

Then the high-risk COPD patient. [[Prophylactic NIV straight after extubation means fewer reintubations and lower mortality.]] It offsets his auto-PEEP and unloads his tired muscles, so hypercapnic failure is prevented rather than treated.

So the sequence is done well. Now the airway, and the support.

steps.bridge: The cuff leak test flags stridor risk; NIV can be facilitative or prophylactic. Next: who gets high-flow and who gets NIV →

lesson.text:
You met these in the indices lesson. The cuff leak test: deflate the cuff and look for gas escaping around the tube. A small leak means a swollen larynx, and a risk of stridor after extubation. Steroids shrink that oedema, but slowly, so they're started hours before. And NIV around extubation comes in two forms. Facilitative, to extubate early the COPD patient who failed his trial. Prophylactic, straight after extubation in the high-risk patient.

[[Both kinds of NIV are prevention. Neither rescues a failure that has already set in.]] Hold on to that. It's the trap at the end of the next card.

So, which patient gets which support?

steps.bridge: Low risk gets high-flow; high risk gets NIV with high-flow. Next: why COPD goes straight to NIV →

lesson.text:
First, spot the patient at high risk. The list is long, but it tells a story. [[Age over sixty-five, heart failure, COPD, a BMI over thirty, an APACHE two over twelve, a weak cough or many secretions, a failed first trial, prolonged ventilation, and a high carbon dioxide.]] Each one either weakens the pump, adds to the load, or threatens the airway.

Then the airway. A cuff leak below one hundred and ten millilitres, or below twenty-four percent of the tidal volume, means a risk of stridor. In the at-risk patient, give methylprednisolone twenty milligrams every four hours, starting twelve hours before extubation. That regimen comes from François and colleagues, in the Lancet, in two thousand seven.

Now the support after extubation. There are two trials to know, and they divide the patients neatly.

The low-risk patient. Hernández and colleagues, JAMA, two thousand sixteen. High-flow nasal oxygen for twenty-four hours, against standard oxygen. [[Reintubation fell from twelve point two to four point nine percent.]] Why does high-flow help? It delivers warmed, humidified gas at a high flow. That washes carbon dioxide out of the dead space of the upper airway, gives a little positive pressure, meets his own inspiratory flow so he isn't pulling against the interface, and keeps his secretions moist.

The high-risk patient. HIGH-WEAN, Thille and colleagues, JAMA, two thousand nineteen. NIV alternating with high-flow, against high-flow alone. [[Reintubation was eleven point eight against eighteen point two percent.]] Why NIV in this group? Because it does more. A real PEEP, real pressure support to share the work, and positive pressure in the chest, which lowers the afterload of the left ventricle. Remember that last point. It matters in heart failure.

And the hypercapnic or COPD patient goes straight onto NIV after extubation.

{{**Low risk** → HFNO 24 h (Hernández, JAMA 2016): reintubation 4.9 vs 12.2%
**High risk** → NIV alternating with HFNO (HIGH-WEAN, JAMA 2019): 11.8 vs 18.2%
**COPD / hypercapnic** → NIV straight after extubation
**Established failure** → reintubate; NIV ↑ mortality (Esteban, NEJM 2004)
Cuff leak <110 mL or <24% VT → methylprednisolone 20 mg 4-hourly from 12 h before}}

Now the trap. Suppose he's on high-flow, and over the next day he fails anyway. Respiratory failure is established. Do you put him on NIV to try to avoid the tube? Esteban and colleagues tested exactly that, in the New England Journal in two thousand four. And mortality was higher with NIV. The likely reason is that NIV delayed a reintubation he needed. [[Once failure is established, don't use NIV to delay reintubation. Reintubate.]]

So the pattern is clear. NIV helps when it's given early, to prevent. It harms when it's used late, to postpone.

One honest caution. These trials each defined high risk in their own way. So in the viva, name the risk factors you use, and then name the trial.

steps.bridge: In COPD, extubation to NIV lowers reintubation and ICU mortality. Next: the obese patient, the other NIV group →

lesson.text:
You met this with the breathing trial. In COPD, extubate straight to NIV. After extubation his airways still empty slowly, so trapped gas, the auto-PEEP, loads his muscles before each breath. NIV's PEEP offsets it, and its pressure support shares the work.

[[It lowers reintubation and ICU mortality, because it prevents the failure rather than chasing it.]] That's the Esteban lesson the other way round. Early NIV helps. Late NIV harms.

And the other group who goes straight onto NIV is the obese patient.

You met him with the breathing trial too. In obesity, the heavy chest wall and abdomen collapse the lung bases once positive pressure is taken away. That's why he was tested on a T-piece, or on zero support, which matched his work after extubation.

And that same collapse is why he needs support back the moment the tube comes out. Stop the sedation, and give him back his PEEP at once. [[Extubate the obese patient straight onto NIV or CPAP. It keeps the bases open and prevents reintubation.]]

spine: What it is: spotting the high-risk patient first: age >65, heart failure, COPD, BMI >30, APACHE II >12, weak cough or many secretions, failed first trial, hypercapnia.
Airway: cuff leak test; a leak <110 mL means stridor risk. Give methylprednisolone 20 mg 4-hourly, starting 12 hours before extubation.
Low risk: high-flow nasal oxygen for 24 hours (Hernández 2016: reintubation 4.9% vs 12.2%).
High risk: NIV alternating with high-flow (HIGH-WEAN 2019: reintubation 11.8% vs 18.2%). COPD, hypercapnic or obese patients: NIV straight after extubation.
Caution: once respiratory failure is established, do not use NIV to delay reintubation (Esteban 2004: higher mortality).

open.text:
Let me start with the patient who passed.

He sailed through his breathing trial. Thirty minutes on pressure support, calm, a good rate, good gases. You extubated him in the morning. By the evening, he's breathing at forty, sweating, his SpO2 is falling, and the nurse is calling you to reintubate.

That's extubation failure, the tube needed back soon after it came out. Most trials count the first forty-eight to seventy-two hours, and some count a full week. And it matters, because the patient who fails extubation is far more likely to die than the one who doesn't.

So how do you prevent it? You can't prevent all of it. But you can do three things. Spot the patient at high risk before the tube comes out. Protect his airway. And choose the right support after extubation, high-flow or NIV, for the right patient.

What the professor is really checking is that last part. Who gets high-flow, who gets NIV, and the trials behind each. And one more thing, which is the trap. What do you do once the failure has already started?

So here's the plan. First, the sequence that comes before extubation. Then the airway, and the two kinds of NIV. Then the trials of high-flow and NIV. And finally, the two groups who go straight onto NIV, the COPD patient and the obese patient.

close.text:
So let's bring it together.

First, spot the high-risk patient. Over sixty-five, heart failure, COPD, a BMI over thirty, an APACHE two over twelve, a weak cough or many secretions, a failed first trial, a high carbon dioxide.

Then the airway. A cuff leak under one hundred and ten millilitres means stridor risk. Methylprednisolone twenty milligrams every four hours, starting twelve hours before extubation.

Then match the support to the risk. [[Low risk, high-flow for twenty-four hours. Hernández, reintubation four point nine against twelve point two percent.]] [[High risk, NIV alternating with high-flow. HIGH-WEAN, eleven point eight against eighteen point two.]] COPD, hypercapnic and obese patients, NIV straight after extubation.

And the caution. Once respiratory failure is established, don't use NIV to delay reintubation. Esteban showed higher mortality.

That's your answer. Who is at risk, the airway, who gets high-flow and who gets NIV, and the trap.

But here's something to carry forward. Some patients fail not because of the lung or the airway, but because the muscles themselves have gone. After weeks in the ICU, they can barely lift an arm off the bed. What has happened to them? That's ICU-acquired weakness, and it's next.

questions.text: What is ICU-acquired weakness?

steps.bridge: ICU-AW is symmetrical weakness, MRC <48/60; nerve studies split CIP from CIM. Next: where it sits among neuromuscular causes →

lesson.text:
Start with the definition, because the panel wants it exactly. [[ICU-acquired weakness is diffuse, symmetrical limb weakness arising in the ICU with no other cause, with an MRC sum score below forty-eight out of sixty, in an awake, cooperative patient.]]

Where does sixty come from? Twelve muscle groups, six on each side, each scored out of five. Below forty-eight means an average below four out of five. That's weakness against resistance. And notice the two conditions, awake and cooperative. A sedated or delirious patient can't be scored. At the bedside, handgrip is a quick screen.

Now the two types. To tell them apart, think of a motor and its wires.

In critical illness polyneuropathy, the wires are cut. It's an axonal disease of motor and sensory nerves. The axons die, so on nerve conduction studies, both the motor response, the CMAP, and the sensory response, the SNAP, are small. But the fibres that survive still conduct at normal speed. Clinically, there's sensory loss, distally. Why does the normal speed matter? Because it tells you the disease is axonal. A demyelinating disease, like Guillain-Barré, would slow the conduction.

In critical illness myopathy, the wires are fine, but the motor is broken. The nerve is healthy, so the sensory response is normal, and only the motor response is small. Sensation is intact. The CMAP lasts longer, because conduction along the sick muscle fibres slows, which spreads the response out. The CK may be high. And the key test. Stimulate the muscle directly, bypassing the nerve. If the muscle still answers weakly, the problem is in the muscle.

[[In polyneuropathy, motor and sensory amplitudes are both low. In myopathy, motor is low, sensory is normal, and the muscle answers weakly even when stimulated directly.]]

{{**ICU-AW:** MRC sum <48/60 (12 groups × 5), awake and cooperative
**CIP** | axonal; ↓CMAP and ↓SNAP, normal velocity; distal sensory loss
**CIM** | ↓CMAP, normal SNAP; longer CMAP; weak direct muscle stimulation; may have ↑CK
Often both: CIPNM}}

Often the patient has both. That's critical illness polyneuromyopathy.

What puts her at risk? Sepsis and multi-organ failure. Hyperglycaemia. Immobility and long ventilation. Corticosteroids. Neuromuscular blockers. And early parenteral nutrition, which is where the EPaNIC trial comes in.

So prevention follows the risks. Avoid hyperglycaemia. Keep sedation light. Mobilise early. Avoid early parenteral nutrition.

[[It explains weaning failure on the capacity side. The load may be normal, but the pump is too weak to carry it.]]

So where does it sit among all the neuromuscular causes of weaning failure?

steps.bridge: CIP is a conduction problem; CIM and diaphragm dysfunction are peripheral. Next: what happens to the diaphragm itself →

lesson.text:
To breathe, the pump needs three things. A signal from the brainstem, a wire to carry it, and a muscle to answer. Think of a doorbell. The button, the wire, and the bell. If any one fails, nothing rings.

So sort the neuromuscular causes of weaning failure by level.

First, the drive, the button. Sedatives and opioids. Uraemia, encephalitis, stroke, central hypoventilation. And one the panel loves, metabolic alkalosis. Why does an alkalosis turn down the drive? Because the respiratory centre defends the pH. Faced with alkaline blood, it breathes less and lets the carbon dioxide rise. So a patient diuresed into an alkalosis may hypoventilate on his trial.

Second, conduction, the wire. A cord lesion. Guillain-Barré. Motor neuron disease. Phrenic nerve injury. Myasthenia. Neuromuscular blockers, which belong here because they act at the junction, and their effect can outlast the infusion if the drug accumulates. And critical illness polyneuropathy.

Third, the muscle itself, the bell. Critical illness myopathy. Ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction. Low phosphate, magnesium, potassium or calcium. Malnutrition. Thyroid and adrenal disease. Why the electrolytes? Low phosphate drains the muscle of ATP, and low magnesium, potassium or calcium impair contraction. So they weaken the diaphragm directly. And they're among the easiest causes on this list to fix.

{{Level | Causes | Test
**Drive** | sedatives, opioids, **metabolic alkalosis**, uraemia, encephalitis, stroke | CO₂ response, P0.1
