More even stretch means fewer over-stretched regions. The survival benefit seems to come from less lung injury, not just higher PaO₂.
RESP01C|ARDS-31.cap: A, supine: baby lung aerated at the front, collapsed back lung where most blood flows. B, prone: back lung re-opened with its blood flow; front lung now lower, with some collapse.

ECMO01|ECMO-03.intro:
ECMO is a bridge: it buys time for the lung to heal, or for a transplant. So it makes sense only if there is somewhere to go. It also needs anticoagulation, because blood clots on the circuit. The contraindications, all relative, follow from those two facts: no recovery, no exit, or bleeding that heparin would make worse.
See it: a bridge is worth building only if there is land on the other side.
why: 7 days at high settings: by then injurious ventilation has often driven the lung into scarring (fibroproliferation), which recovers less. Days ventilated before ECMO are a risk factor in the RESP score.
CNS haemorrhage: heparin for the circuit can make a recent or expanding bleed grow. Severe neutropenia and terminal disease are associated with poor survival, so the bridge leads nowhere.
Pulmonary haemorrhage is still an indication: modern circuits can run for a time with little or no heparin, and ECMO lets the bleeding lung rest.

RESP03|RSC-13.intro:
Obesity shrinks the oxygen store and raises the need for it. The heavy abdomen pushes the diaphragm up, so FRC falls, and lying flat makes it worse; alveoli at the base close. Oxygen use is also higher. So during apnoea he desaturates within a couple of minutes, not the 6–8 of a lean adult. Sitting up, PEEP from CPAP or NIV and apnoeic oxygenation each add to the store or keep it open.
See it: a smaller oxygen tank, emptied faster.
why: a

Hypercapnic failure, sleep apnoea and obesity hypoventilation need extra ventilation and a splinted upper airway, which NIV gives; HFNC adds little ventilation. Set tidal volume by predicted weight; give enough PEEP against the abdominal weight. Starting CPAP weeks ahead allows mask adaptation.
b
After anaesthesia and opioids the obese patient's bases collapse and the upper airway obstructs; CPAP/NIV splints both, so fewer pulmonary complications and ICU admissions follow.
c

Semi-sitting lets the abdomen fall away and raises FRC. CPAP/NIV keeps basal alveoli open, so more lung holds oxygen. A video laryngoscope raises first-pass success, and each extra attempt costs desaturation.

RESP01B|ARDS-21.intro:
The lungs grow with the skeleton, so their size follows height, and for the same height a woman's chest and lungs are smaller. Fat and fluid add kilograms but no lung. So a breath sized to actual weight over-stretches the lung whenever actual weight is above predicted (obesity, oedema), and in women or short patients when weight is guessed; a breath sized to predicted weight matches the lung he really has.
See it: a tall thin man and a short heavy man can weigh the same, but the tall man's lungs are far bigger.
why: a
152.4 cm is 5 feet: the formula starts at 50 kg for a 5-foot man and adds 0.91 kg for every cm above it (2.3 kg per inch).
b
Same slope, 4.5 kg lower start, because for the same height a woman's lungs are smaller.
c
Height decides lung size; weight gained as fat or oedema does not. So actual weight would over-dose the breath in the obese.

RESP01B|ARDS-22.intro:
The aim is a small breath for a small lung, but a sudden cut in tidal volume drops minute ventilation and the CO₂ climbs fast. So the protocol starts at 8 mL/kg and steps down 1 mL/kg at a time, raising the rate to hold minute ventilation while the body adjusts. The CO₂ that is still left over is accepted, because a stretched lung does more harm than a moderate acidosis.
See it: lowering a heavy load one step at a time instead of dropping it.
why: a
Stepping down over hours lets the rate rise in step, so minute ventilation holds and the pH does not fall abruptly.
b

Each extra breath carries the same fixed dead space and shortens expiration, so above about 35 the CO₂ gained per extra breath falls while gas trapping (auto-PEEP) rises; 35 is the protocol's cap on that trade-off.
c

Plateau is the alveolar pressure at end-inspiration, a bedside proxy for lung stretch (a stiff chest wall can raise it too). Above 30 the breath is still too big for the open lung, so Vt comes down; 4 mL/kg is the floor because below it CO₂ cannot be cleared.
d

Rate first, because it adds CO₂ removal without adding stretch. Only if the pH is below 7.15 at rate 35 is tidal volume allowed back up. Note: the target is 7.30–7.45, but accepting pH ≥7.20 (permissive hypercapnia) is also standard; both are right.

V4-031.intro:
ARDS lung is full of oedema, so it is heavy. Each layer presses on the layers below it, so the pressure squeezing the lung rises from front to back in a supine patient. The top stays aerated, the middle is part-filled (ground glass) and the bottom is squeezed airless. The open part left on top is small, which is why its compliance is near normal: it is a small lung, not a stiff one, in early ARDS.
See it: a wet sponge on a table, dry on top and squashed flat at the bottom.
why: The gradient follows gravity: turn him prone and much of the dense area moves to the new lowest part within minutes. That shows most dorsal collapse is squeezed-shut lung under weight, not fixed damage; true consolidation stays put.
Proning helps because more lung sits in the back than the front, and the blood flow stays mostly dorsal, so re-opened dorsal lung meets blood.
V4-031.cap: Panel A, supine: aerated baby lung at the front, poorly aerated middle, collapsed back where most blood flows. Panel B, prone: the back re-opens, blood still there; some collapse moves to the front.

HY7|VNX-01.intro:
Compliance tells how much volume each cmH₂O buys. So the pressure a breath adds above PEEP equals tidal volume ÷ compliance. In ARDS compliance is low mostly because less lung is open, so a low compliance means the same breath is going into fewer alveoli. Driving pressure therefore measures the breath relative to the lung that is actually open, which tidal volume per kilogram cannot.
See it: the same glass of water poured into a small cup and into a large one. The small cup's level rises much higher.
why: a
ΔP = Vt ÷ compliance of the respiratory system, so it sizes the breath against the open lung: a bedside surrogate for strain, not just volume.
b
Below 15: in Amato's data, risk of death rose steadily above about 14–15 cmH₂O, so 15 is a practical ceiling, not a proven safe line.
c
Trapped gas (auto-PEEP) is already holding the alveoli open above set PEEP. Using set PEEP alone overstates ΔP, so subtract total PEEP from an end-expiratory hold.
d

Amato (2015) found ΔP the variable most strongly associated with survival, even when Vt and plateau were within limits. It is an association from re-analysis, not proof that lowering ΔP causes benefit.
HY7|VNX-01.cap: Airway pressure is three layers stacked: pushing through the tubes, stretching the lung, and PEEP; driving pressure is the stretch layer.

V4-032.intro:
Supine, the wet lung, heart and abdomen squash the back of the lung, where most of the lung tissue and most of the blood flow are. Turned prone, the back is on top, so it re-opens. Blood flow stays mostly dorsal, so the re-opened lung now meets blood: less shunt, better V/Q. The lung also fits the chest shape better, so the squeeze from top to bottom is more even and each breath stretches the lung more evenly.
See it: a stack of wet sponges turned over. The big squashed layer is now on top and springs open.
why: Why it saves lives even when PaO₂ barely changes: the benefit seems to come from more even stretch and less lung injury, not from oxygen alone.
RV afterload falls: re-opened lung relieves hypoxic vasoconstriction, and lower PaCO₂ and lower alveolar pressure (less squeeze on vessels) all lower pulmonary vascular resistance.

Start at P/F <150, early, for ≥16 h: earlier trials of short sessions in mixed-severity patients showed no survival gain; PROSEVA showed benefit only when severe patients were proned early and for long.
Stop only if P/F stays ≥150 at least 4 h after turning supine on PEEP ≤10 and FiO₂ ≤0.6, because the gain often fades back supine.
Contraindications are the conditions that cannot stand the turn or face-down pressure: unstable spine, raised ICP, open abdomen or fresh sternotomy, massive haemoptysis.
V4-032.cap: Panel A, supine: aerated baby lung at the front, poorly aerated middle, collapsed back where most blood flows. Panel B, prone: the back re-opens, blood still there; some collapse moves to the front.

V4-033.intro:
Current passes easily through salty tissue and fluid but poorly through air. So as a region fills with gas its impedance rises, and as it empties it falls. Electrodes round the chest measure these changes from many angles and rebuild a picture of which part of the slice took the breath. Watching that while PEEP is lowered shows where the lung stops taking volume (collapse) and where it took too little because it was already full (over-distension).
See it: a stadium crowd seen from above, with lights coming on where people stand up as the breath arrives.
why: Decremental trial: at high PEEP the front is over-full and takes little volume per cmH₂O; at low PEEP the back collapses and stops ventilating. The crossing point is the best compromise between the two.
Pneumothorax shows as a sudden loss of ventilation on one side, because that lung no longer fills.
Limits: it sees one slice, and outcome benefit is not proven, so it guides PEEP rather than proving the PEEP is right.

RESP01C|ARDS-39.intro:
In ARDS the capillaries leak, so how much water crosses into the lung depends on the pressure pushing it out. Raising filling pressures with fluid pushes more water into the lung, which shrinks the aerated lung and stiffens it. Keeping filling pressures low, once the circulation no longer needs fluid, keeps the lung drier and gets the patient off the ventilator sooner.
See it: a leaking hose. The higher you turn the tap, the faster the leak.
why: a
Only after shock had resolved. Giving too little fluid during shock harms organs, so the strategy starts when the circulation is stable.
c
Mortality was not different, so the benefit is on lung function, not survival. Saying conservative fluids lower mortality is wrong.
d
More ventilator-free days fits the mechanism: less lung water, more aerated lung, faster weaning. The kidneys were not harmed (no more dialysis).
e
A PA catheter gave the same result as a CVC, with more complications, so it is not needed to guide the fluid plan.

RESP01C|ARDS-40.intro:
ARDS goes through phases. In the first week inflammation drives the leak, so steroids, which damp inflammation, can help. After about two weeks the lung is in a repair and fibrosis phase: steroids no longer target the main driver but still cause muscle weakness and may impair repair, so late starts showed harm (in a LaSRS subgroup).
See it: an extinguisher helps while the fire burns; sprayed on the wall being rebuilt, it only does damage.
why: a
Meduri started within 72 h, in the inflammatory phase, so the drug met its target: ICU mortality 21% vs 43% (small trial).
b
LaSRS started steroids in persistent ARDS (day 7–28): no survival gain and more neuromyopathy, which fits a phase where inflammation is no longer the main driver.
c
DEXA-ARDS enrolled P/F ≤200 on PEEP ≥10 and FiO₂ ≥0.5, early in the inflammatory phase, which is why it worked: 60-day mortality 21% vs 36%.
e
In LaSRS, those started ≥14 days after onset had 60-day mortality 35% vs 8% (post-hoc subgroup), so the rule is about when you start, not how long you give.

RESP07A|PLEU-08.intro:
Normally the visceral pleura slides against the parietal pleura with each breath, and ultrasound sees that shimmer. Air in the pleural space separates the two layers. Ultrasound cannot see through air, so it sees only the parietal layer, which does not move. Every sign that needs the lung to touch the chest wall, sliding or B-lines, therefore rules pneumothorax out at that spot.
See it: two panes of wet glass sliding on each other; slip a sheet of air between them and only the front pane is seen, still.
why: a
Sliding is the visceral pleura moving, so the lung must be touching the chest wall there.
b
B-lines start at the visceral pleura and reach the screen edge. They can only form if the lung touches the wall, so they exclude pneumothorax at that spot.
c

At the lung point the edge of the collapsed lung touches the wall on inspiration and leaves on expiration. Nothing else gives that switch, so it is 100% specific; a large pneumothorax may have no lung point.
d
On M-mode, moving lung gives grainy 'sand' below the pleural line (seashore). No movement gives straight lines all the way down (barcode).
e
Sliding also stops when that lung is not being ventilated or is stuck to the wall: the other lung intubated, blocked bronchus, adhesions, paralysed diaphragm. So absent sliding alone is not proof.

RESP07A|PLEU-09.intro:
Lung ultrasound sees three states. Dry aerated lung reflects the beam, giving A-lines. Water in the interlobular septa gives B-lines. Airless lung looks like tissue (consolidation). BLUE reads these at standard points and adds a leg vein scan. Anterior A-lines with sliding mean the front lung is dry, so the cause is in the airways, vessels or pleura, or is posterior (check PLAPS).
See it: dry lung is a mirror, wet lung a set of comet tails, airless lung looks like liver.
why: Oedema: B-lines on both sides with sliding, because cardiogenic water fills the septa everywhere.
Pneumothorax: A' (no sliding) because the pleurae are separated; the lung point confirms it.
PE: the lung itself stays dry (A-profile), so the clue is a clot in the leg veins.
COPD or asthma: dry lung, clean veins, no posterior consolidation: the problem is in the airways.

Pneumonia: the process is local, so the profiles are asymmetric or focal: A + PLAPS (posterolateral consolidation/effusion), B' (B-lines but no sliding, from inflammatory adhesion), A/B (B-lines one side only), or C (anterior consolidation).

V4-002.intro:
Ultrasound bounces off air. Fully aerated lung reflects the beam at the pleura, so you see only echoes of the pleural line (A-lines). When water thickens the septa, each wet septum gives a vertical B-line; as water rises they merge into a white field; when air is gone the lung looks like tissue. Each region's score therefore tracks how much air it has lost, and the total tracks the whole lung.
See it: a frosted window that loses its clear patches as it fogs, until it is solid white.
why: 0 → 3 is a ladder of air loss: normal, a few wet septa, many merging, airless. So a falling score means re-aeration.
Over-distended lung is still full of air, so it looks normal (A-lines). That is why LUS cannot show over-stretch and driving pressure must be checked too.
A high score before extubation means poorly aerated lung that will lose more air without positive pressure, so it predicts failure (>17).

MV04B|WEAN-17.intro:
Coming off the ventilator puts three loads on the patient at once: the diaphragm must do the work, the lung must stay open without positive pressure, and the heart must cope with more negative chest pressure. Ultrasound looks at each. A weak diaphragm moves and thickens less; a poorly aerated lung loses more air; a failing LV turns the breathing trial into cardiogenic oedema.
See it: a spontaneous breathing trial is a stress test of the pump, the lung and the heart together.
why: Diaphragm: excursion is how far the dome moves; thickening fraction is how hard the muscle contracts. Low values mean the pump cannot carry the load.
Lung score: >17 means much lost aeration that worsens off positive pressure; <13 predicts success.

LV: low EF or E/e' >12 predict failure: negative chest pressure and adrenergic surge raise LV afterload and venous return. No rise in output with leg raising means a flat Starling curve, so the trial's extra venous return raises filling pressure, not output, and floods the lung.

MV04B|WEAN-26.intro:
Each stage asks a different question. Before the trial: who is at risk? During: is he coping? After a failure: why? The main hidden causes of failure are the heart and the lung. Removing positive pressure makes chest pressure more negative, which raises venous return and LV afterload; a weak or stiff LV then backs up into the lungs (weaning-induced pulmonary oedema). The lung also loses aeration without PEEP.
See it: taking the ventilator away is like handing a load back to the patient, and ultrasound watches what buckles.
why: a

Each of these fails the same test. The trial raises venous return and LV afterload. A weak or stiff LV, or a preload-independent heart (flat Starling curve), turns that into high filling pressure and oedema. Poorly aerated lung or a large effusion loses more air once PEEP is gone.
b
No new B-lines or consolidation (no derecruitment) and a diaphragm that moves and thickens well mean the pump and the lung are holding.
c
New B-lines with a raised E/e' point to cardiogenic oedema; more consolidation points to derecruitment. Each has a different fix (diuretic or vasodilator vs PEEP or physiotherapy).

RESP07B|PLEU-14.intro:
The chest wall springs outwards and is held in only by the lung's pull, so fluid entering the pleural space mostly makes room by pushing the chest wall and diaphragm out, not by squeezing the lung. So oxygenation often changes little. The pushed-down diaphragm is the problem: flattened or inverted, its fibres are too short to contract well, so breathing feels hard. Draining restores its dome and relieves breathlessness even if gas exchange barely moves.
See it: a bow that has been flattened can no longer be drawn.
why: a
At FRC the chest wall sits inside its own resting position, held in by lung recoil; fluid lets it spring out, so only about one-third of the fluid volume comes out of the lung (one-fifth at TLC).
b
Length–tension: a flat or inverted diaphragm starts from a short, weak fibre length and cannot generate much pressure.
c

Raised pleural pressure compresses lung and great vessels: collapse raises pulmonary vascular resistance, loading the RV, and a large effusion limits filling like tamponade, which reverses with drainage.
d
Pleural pressure is so high on one side that it shifts the mediastinum and kinks venous return; it is the fluid version of tension pneumothorax.

RESP07B|PLEU-16.intro:
Pure fluid has nothing to reflect sound, so it is black. Protein, fibrin, cells and debris give echoes, so a complex effusion means more than a transudate's water: an exudate. Ultrasound also sees thin fibrin strands moving in real time, which CT often misses. The volume formula works because, in a supine patient, the depth of fluid between lung and chest wall at the base rises roughly in step with volume.
See it: clear water in a glass is black on the scan; soup with strands shows up.
why: a
Balik formula: measured supine, at the base, at end-expiration, as the maximum distance between lung and chest wall. It is an estimate, not exact.
b
Anechoic can be transudate or exudate; complex (septated, non-septated, echogenic) means exudate. Echogenic homogeneous fluid suggests pus or blood.
c
Septations are thin and mobile; ultrasound sees them moving and sees the safest pocket to needle, so it beats CT for septa and guidance.
d
Contrast shows enhancing pleura (inflamed, so exudate or empyema) and separates fluid from thickened pleura or a mass, which ultrasound may not.

RESP07B|PLEU-21.intro:
As bacteria and neutrophils invade the pleural space they burn glucose and make lactate and CO₂. So glucose falls, pH falls and LDH rises from dying cells. These numbers show the space has become a closed, acidic, walled-off collection, like an abscess; fibrin splits it into pockets, so antibiotics alone will not clear it and it needs drainage.
See it: a sealed jar of milk going sour: sugar used up, acid rising.
why: b
pH <7.20, glucose <60 and LDH >1000 are markers of active bacterial metabolism in the fluid; pus or a positive Gram stain prove the infection directly.
c

Free fluid drains through a small catheter. Septations trap fluid in pockets; tPA/DNase breaks them, and trials show small-bore (12–14 Fr) drains work as well as large-bore with it. Larger bore is kept for thick pus that blocks small tubes.
d
The tube stays until the infection has settled and the output is low (<200 mL/day), so there is no collection left to re-form.

RESP07B|PLEU-24.intro:
Any blood in pleural fluid stains it red, so colour proves nothing. Measuring the haematocrit shows how much of the fluid is really blood: above half the blood's own haematocrit, the space is filling with blood, not serous fluid. Blood clots, so the drain must be wide enough not to block, and placed where it drains the whole space.
See it: a drop of blood turns a glass of water red; the haematocrit tells you whether it is a drop or half the glass.
why: a
Even 1–2 mL of blood colours an effusion. A fluid haematocrit >50% of blood means the fluid is mostly blood.
b
More than 1.5 L on drainage means major bleeding that may need thoracotomy.
c

28–30 Fr because clot blocks small tubes. Mid-axillary line (safe triangle: pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, 5th space) because it avoids the internal mammary vessels, breast and muscle, stays above the diaphragm, liver and spleen, and drains the whole space.
d
In aortic injury, the clot and pleural tamponade may be all that limits bleeding; draining it can release that pressure and cause exsanguination, so go to surgery.

RESP07B|PLEU-26.intro:
When a long-collapsed lung is opened suddenly, two things happen. Pleural pressure drops sharply, so capillary transmural pressure jumps and fluid is pulled out of the vessels. And the lung that was hypoxic and short of surfactant is reperfused, so its capillaries leak. Both put water into the alveoli of the re-expanded lung. Slow, limited drainage gives the lung time to adapt.
See it: a sponge that has been squeezed for days, released all at once, soaks up water.
why: a
Hydrostatic: a sudden more negative pleural pressure raises the pressure across the capillary wall. Leak: ischaemia–reperfusion and loss of surfactant damage the capillaries.
b
Longer collapse (>3 days) means more ischaemia and surfactant loss; large and rapid drainage means a steeper pressure fall.
c
Up to 1.5 L per session, no faster than 500 mL/h, keeps the pleural pressure fall slow and small. Stop early if chest pain or cough appears.
d
CPAP raises alveolar pressure, so flooded alveoli stay open and gas exchange recovers while the leak settles; it does not remove the water. It is the same support as for other permeability oedema.
e
Full expansion means the space is closed. Below about 100–200 mL/day is fluid the pleura can reabsorb itself, so nothing re-collects (thresholds vary: PLEU-21 uses 200).

MV03|ASYN-01.intro:
Each breath has three hand-overs between patient and machine: the start (trigger), the push in between (flow) and the stop (cycling). Asynchrony is a mismatch at one of them. Trigger faults dominate because many efforts are too weak to be sensed: auto-PEEP must be cancelled first, and high support makes this worse, since large breaths leave less time to empty and blunt the drive.
See it: a baton passed at the start, carried, then handed back; most drops happen at the first pass.
why: b
Flow starvation: the machine gives less flow than the patient demands, so the patient sucks against the circuit and the pressure curve scoops downwards.
c
Name it by whose breath ends first. Premature: the machine stops while the patient is still breathing in. Delayed: the machine keeps pushing after the patient has started to breathe out.
d
Ineffective effort leads because with, say, 5 cmH₂O of auto-PEEP the patient must lower alveolar pressure by 5 plus the trigger before the sensor sees any change.

MV03|ASYN-07.intro:
The machine's breath ends on a fixed time or volume, but the brain is still sending an inspiratory signal. The patient keeps pulling, airway pressure falls below the trigger, and the machine gives a second breath before the first has been breathed out. Both volumes end up in the lung.
See it: two breaths for one effort, with no exhalation between them.
why: c
Volume control fixes inspiratory time; a hungry patient (low P/F, high demand) has a long, strong neural inspiration that outruns it.
d
The fix lengthens the machine breath to match the effort: longer Ti or larger Vt, or pressure support, which ends on the patient's own flow. Sedation, which lowers the drive, comes last.
e
The second breath starts from end-inspiratory volume, so the lung gets close to double the set Vt, which defeats lung-protective ventilation.

MV03|ASYN-08.intro:
In a deeply sedated patient the respiratory centre can lock onto the rhythm of passive inflation: the machine breath is thought to set off a reflex diaphragm contraction late in that breath. The effort follows the machine, not the reverse. Because the machine sets the timing, the effort repeats in a fixed ratio.
See it: a listener who claps along to a song, once every bar or once every two.
why: b
Deep sedation removes the patient's own rhythm, leaving the passive one to take over; controlled modes give a regular beat to lock onto.
d
The effort shows as a negative swing in oesophageal pressure, or a burst of EAdi, that begins after the machine breath has started.
e
An effort that outlasts the machine breath triggers another (stacking). An effort during the inspiratory hold pulls the plateau down, so the plateau understates the real lung stress.

HY7|VNX-05.intro:
Each asynchrony is one setting out of step with the patient, so each has one knob. Trigger too sensitive: the machine fires on noise. Trapped gas: effort is spent cancelling auto-PEEP before the trigger sees it. Breath too short: the effort outlasts it. Breath too long: the patient breathes out against it. Flow too low: the patient sucks harder than the machine gives.
See it: a dance where you correct whoever is a step early or late.
why: **Ineffective triggering**: trapped gas must be cancelled before the trigger sees an effort. External PEEP up to about 80% of auto-PEEP narrows that gap in flow-limited airways (COPD) without adding much trapped gas. Lowering PS or Vt also helps, because smaller breaths leave more time to empty.
**Double triggering**: lowering the cycle-off % ends pressure support later (at a smaller share of peak flow), so the breath lasts as long as the effort.
**Delayed cycling**: raising the cycle-off % (40–50% in COPD) ends the breath sooner, because slowly emptying airways make inspiratory flow decay slowly.
HY7|VNX-05.cap: Expiratory flow over time. A, normal lung: flow returns to zero before the next breath. B, COPD or asthma: the next breath starts while gas is still flowing out, trapping it as auto-PEEP.

MV05|AMV-08.intro:
PAV solves the equation of motion live: pressure needed = flow × resistance + volume × elastance. It measures the patient's flow and volume at each instant and supplies a set share of that pressure, so a bigger effort gets more help and a smaller one less. To do this it must know resistance and elastance; if they are wrong, the share is wrong.
See it: power steering that adds a fixed share to however hard you turn the wheel.
why: c
Without true resistance and compliance the machine cannot turn flow and volume into the patient's effort; PAV+ measures them with brief end-inspiratory pauses.
d
Help follows effort breath by breath, so tidal volume varies naturally and the patient stays in charge of the pattern, with less over-assistance.
e

No effort means no flow and no help, so it cannot ventilate a passive patient. A leak looks like inspiratory flow, so the machine keeps pushing (runaway). Effort spent cancelling auto-PEEP makes no flow, so it gets no help.

MV05|AMV-09.intro:
The diaphragm's electrical activity (EAdi) is the earliest sign of the brain's intent to breathe, before any pressure or flow reaches the circuit. NAVA reads it from electrodes on a nasogastric tube and uses it to start, size and end each breath: pressure = NAVA level × EAdi. Because it does not wait for flow or pressure, leaks and auto-PEEP cannot fool it.
See it: the machine hears the order from the brain instead of waiting to feel the push.
why: c
Units are cmH₂O per µV: each microvolt of diaphragm activity buys that many cmH₂O, so support scales with the drive.
d
With auto-PEEP, flow starts only after trapped pressure is cancelled, delaying a pneumatic trigger; EAdi rises at the start of the effort regardless. A leak changes flow, not the electrical signal.
e
It needs an intact path from brain to diaphragm: deep sedation flattens EAdi, and phrenic injury or a paralysed diaphragm silences it.

MV03|ASYN-13.intro:
In pressure support the patient gets the same pressure whatever the effort. In PAV and NAVA the pressure follows the effort, which closes a feedback loop: as the lung fills, the drive tends to fall, so support falls too, and large over-distending breaths become less likely. The patient's own breath-to-breath variation returns.
See it: a partner who matches your pace rather than pulling at a fixed speed.
why: c
Over-distension is limited because a large breath lowers the drive and lower drive means less pressure; in pressure support the set pressure arrives whatever the drive, so high levels overshoot.
d
NAVA ends the breath when EAdi falls to about 70% of its peak, so a dip within one effort can end a breath and start another.

MV05|AMV-11.intro:
For a given minute ventilation, fast shallow breathing wastes work on dead space, while slow deep breathing wastes work stretching the lung. Otis showed that one rate in between costs least. ASV calculates that rate from the target minute ventilation, the dead space it estimates from ideal body weight and the lung's time constant, then sets the tidal volume to match. It keeps a guaranteed rate, so it can ventilate a passive patient too.
See it: a cyclist's best cadence, neither spinning nor grinding.
why: a
%MinVol is the target as a share of normal minute ventilation (about 100 mL/kg/min of ideal body weight, worked out from height and sex); raise it when CO₂ production is high.
c
Time constant = resistance × compliance. A long one (COPD) needs a long expiration, so ASV picks a slower rate and bigger breaths; a short one (ARDS) gets a faster rate and smaller breaths.
d
It fills whatever the patient leaves: no effort gets mandatory pressure-control breaths, some effort a mix, and enough spontaneous breathing gets only pressure support, which is how it weans.
MV05|AMV-11.cap: Expiratory flow over time. A, normal lung: flow reaches zero before the next breath. B, long time constant (COPD, asthma): the next breath starts before emptying ends, leaving auto-PEEP.

NEURO06A|PADIS-07.intro:
Delirium is a disorder of attention, so CAM-ICU will not call it without its two core features: an acute or fluctuating change (feature 1) and inattention (feature 2). It then needs one more sign that the brain is not working clearly: an abnormal arousal level (feature 3) or muddled thinking (feature 4). Each feature alone has other causes; the combination is what makes delirium.
See it: a lock that needs two fixed keys plus either of two others.
why: Feature 3 counts any RASS other than 0, because delirium can be hypoactive (drowsy) as well as hyperactive (agitated).
Score RASS first: at −4 or −5 the patient cannot be tested, so record 'unable to assess' (coma), not 'no delirium'.

NEURO06A|PADIS-13.intro:
Delirium is linked to too little acetylcholine, too much dopamine and too much GABA-type inhibition. Benzodiazepines push GABA further and blunt attention, so they worsen it, except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, where losing that GABA effect is the cause. Dexmedetomidine sedates through α2 receptors in the brainstem, not GABA, so patients stay rousable and can still be assessed.
See it: the brain's brake is already pressed; benzodiazepines press it harder.
why: a
Antipsychotics block dopamine: they calm agitation but do not fix the failure of attention, which fits trials (MIND-USA, AID-ICU) showing no shorter delirium.
c
Propofol is GABAergic too but wears off within minutes, so it is preferred over benzodiazepines, which accumulate.
d
Cholinesterase inhibitors follow the acetylcholine idea, but an ICU rivastigmine trial was stopped for higher mortality; statins and melatonin target inflammation and sleep without proven benefit.

NEURO06B|PADIS-17.intro:
Most problems here follow from how each drug is cleared. A drug with an active metabolite cleared by the kidney (midazolam, morphine) builds up in renal failure. A fat-soluble drug (fentanyl, diazepam) fills body fat during a long infusion and leaks back out after it stops, so its effect outlasts the infusion. Remifentanil is broken down by esterases in blood and tissue, so it never builds up.
See it: fat as a sponge that soaks up drug during the infusion and wrings it out later.
why: **Propofol** comes in a 10% lipid emulsion, so 1.1 kcal/mL counts as feeding and raises triglycerides. PRIS is failure of mitochondrial fat use at high doses for days: acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, heart failure.

**Dexmedetomidine** cuts sympathetic outflow (bradycardia, hypotension); a fast load first constricts vessels through peripheral α2B receptors, giving transient hypertension. It spares the respiratory drive.
**Lorazepam**: the IV form is dissolved in propylene glycol, which at high doses gives a lactic acidosis and a raised osmolar gap.
**Morphine** releases histamine (vasodilation, hypotension); its metabolite M6G is active and renally cleared, so it accumulates in AKI.

NEURO06B|PADIS-18.intro:
Deep sedation keeps patients on the ventilator longer, adds delirium and, in cohort studies, is linked to higher mortality. Pain drives much agitation, so treating it first lets the sedative dose fall. Benzodiazepines accumulate and worsen delirium, while propofol and dexmedetomidine wear off quickly, so light targets are easier to hold with them.
See it: a patient who opens his eyes to his name and can join in the day's plan.
why: BIS when scales fail: a paralysed patient cannot move or open his eyes, so RASS reads −5 whatever his awareness; an EEG-based monitor is then the only objective guide to depth, though it is an imperfect guard against awareness.
Restraints provoke agitation and delirium and cause injury, and restrained patients still self-extubate.

V4-008.intro:
Volatile agents leave the body through the lungs, not the liver or kidney, so they wash out within minutes and do not build up. The AnaConDa reflector catches most exhaled agent and returns it on the next breath, which makes ICU use affordable. But it sits between the Y-piece and the patient, so it adds dead space: with small ARDS tidal volumes a bigger share of each breath is wasted and CO₂ rises.
See it: a sponge in the airway that soaks up exhaled agent and gives it back.
why: **Fluoride**: sevoflurane metabolism releases fluoride, which over days can blunt the kidney's response to ADH, giving dilute polyuria and high sodium (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus).
**SESAR**: more hypercapnic acidosis with sevoflurane is consistent with the dead space problem; with worse outcomes in ARDS, it is a rescue, not a routine sedative.
**Bronchodilation**: volatiles relax airway smooth muscle directly, which is why refractory status asthmaticus is their clearest use.

MV04B|WEAN-15.intro:
A failing respiratory pump keeps minute ventilation up by breathing faster and shallower, because small breaths need less effort each. Dividing rate by tidal volume magnifies that pattern: a rising rate and a falling volume both push the number up. Above 105, the pattern of a pump that cannot cope is already present.
See it: 35 breaths of 300 mL gives about 117; 20 breaths of 500 mL gives 40.
why: a
Tidal volume goes in litres: 30 breaths/min at 285 mL gives about 105.
c
Unassisted, because pressure support or CPAP enlarges the breath and slows the rate, lowering RSBI and making the patient look ready.
d

High sensitivity, low specificity: nearly all who will succeed have a low RSBI, but many with a low RSBI still fail from causes it cannot see (heart, airway, secretions). So it screens; the SBT decides.
e

Fever and sepsis raise the rate and a narrow tube adds load, so RSBI rises. Read off a ventilator, efforts that fail to trigger go uncounted, so the rate looks lower while each delivered breath is full-sized: RSBI reads falsely low. Another reason to measure it unassisted, counting every breath.

HY7|VNX-06.intro:
Weaning is two tests in sequence: a quick screen that misses few who would succeed (RSBI), then a trial of the load the patient must carry alone (SBT). A failed trial means a cause is still present, so full support until the next day's trial. IMV weans worst because the muscles work about as hard during the machine's breaths as during their own, so they never rest.
See it: a sieve first, then a test drive.
why: d
Small steps while watching the rate: a rising rate is the first sign that the load is outgrowing the patient's capacity.
e
In high-risk COPD, NIV straight after extubation offsets auto-PEEP and unloads tired muscles, so hypercapnic failure is prevented rather than treated.

MV04A|WEAN-05.intro:
The groups count the trials and days needed after the first breathing trial, because each further failure points to a deeper problem and a worse outcome. Simple weaners mostly needed only the trial; difficult ones have a reversible cause to find (often heart, fluid or muscle); prolonged ones often have chronic heart, lung or muscle failure.
See it: three exits after the first trial: out at once, out within a week, or a long road.
why: Its gap: patients who never had a trial are left out. **WIND (Béduneau 2017)** counts from the first separation attempt and so covers everyone.
Mortality is clearly higher only in prolonged weaning; difficult weaners did about as well as simple ones in later cohorts (Peñuelas 2011).

MV04B|WEAN-18.intro:
A breathing trial asks whether the patient can carry the work he will face after extubation. Low pressure support was meant to cancel the tube's extra resistance, but after extubation that resistance is replaced by a swollen upper airway, so the T-piece is the closer copy and the harder test. Most failures show early, so 30 minutes is enough for most patients.
See it: a test drive on the road you will actually use.
why: b
Most failures appear within the first 30 minutes; COPD and high-risk patients may decompensate later, so the longer trial catches them.
c
A failed trial means a cause is still present. Once-daily trials did as well as several a day (Esteban 1995), so rest, find the cause and retry in 24 h.

RESP03|RSC-15.intro:
In obesity the heavy chest wall and abdomen push the diaphragm up and collapse the dependent lung, more so when lying flat. On the ventilator, positive pressure hides this; once it is removed, the lung collapses and the work of breathing rises. So the trial must remove all support to show the true load, and extubation goes straight onto CPAP or NIV to keep the lung open.
See it: a heavy lid on the lung, held up only by the ventilator's pressure.
why: a
Proning takes weight off the dorsal lung and evens out ventilation, so oxygenation improves; the abdomen must hang free or its weight is passed to the chest.
b
Reverse Trendelenburg lets the abdominal contents fall away from the diaphragm.
c
In morbidly obese patients (Mahul 2016), only PS 0 with PEEP 0 or a T-piece matched the work of breathing measured after extubation; any added support underestimated it.

RESP02B|COPD-28.intro:
After extubation the COPD patient still has airways that empty slowly, so gas is trapped and auto-PEEP loads the inspiratory muscles. NIV adds external PEEP to offset that load and pressure support to share the work, so the muscles do not tire into hypercapnic failure. It works by preventing failure, not by rescuing it.
See it: a crutch handed over the moment the cast comes off.
why: b
It prevents rather than rescues: once respiratory failure has set in after extubation, NIV mainly delays reintubation, and the delay was linked to higher mortality (Esteban 2004).
c
Asthmatic bronchospasm is reversible, so the lung returns to normal; COPD has fixed obstruction and a flattened, weak diaphragm, so failure tends to recur.

MV04B|WEAN-21.intro:
With the cuff deflated, gas escapes around the tube only if there is room between tube and larynx. A small leak means the larynx is swollen tight around the tube, so after extubation the airway may narrow and cause stridor. Steroids shrink that oedema but take hours to act, so they are started well before extubation in those with a low leak.
See it: a ring so tight on the finger that no air slips past.
why: a

A good leak does not rule out stridor, and a small leak can come from secretions or a large tube, so it flags risk rather than decides. Steroids work best started 12–24 h before extubation, and at least 4 h before.
b
Facilitative NIV in COPD takes over the work at once, cutting days with a tube (and VAP) while still unloading the muscles.
c
Prophylactic NIV aims to stop failure in those likely to fail; it is not a rescue for failure that has already set in.

V4-013.intro:
Nerve studies show where the signal fails. In polyneuropathy the axons die, so both motor (CMAP) and sensory (SNAP) responses are small, but surviving fibres still conduct at normal speed. In myopathy the nerve is healthy, so sensory responses are normal; the muscle itself answers weakly, even when stimulated directly.
See it: in CIP the wires are cut; in CIM the wires work but the motor is broken.
why: Low amplitude with normal speed marks an axonal disorder; demyelination, as in Guillain–Barré, would slow conduction.
CMAP lasts longer in CIM because conduction along the sick muscle fibres slows, spreading out the response.
Direct muscle stimulation bypasses the nerve: a weak response points to the muscle (CIM); a normal one points to the nerve (CIP).
MRC sum: 12 muscle groups (6 a side) × 5 points = 60; below 48 means an average below 4/5, weakness against resistance.

MV04A|WEAN-10.intro:
The respiratory pump needs a signal from the brainstem, a wire to carry it and a muscle to answer. Breathing fails if any link breaks, so sorting causes by level points to the next test: drive by CO₂ response or P0.1, conduction by nerve studies, muscle by MIP or diaphragm ultrasound.
See it: a doorbell: the button, the wire and the bell.
why: a
Metabolic alkalosis: the respiratory centre defends pH by breathing less and retaining CO₂, so the drive is turned down.
b
Neuromuscular blockers act at the junction, so they belong with conduction; their effect can outlast the infusion with accumulation or in myasthenia.
c
Low phosphate depletes muscle ATP, and low magnesium, potassium or calcium impairs contraction, so they weaken the diaphragm directly.

MV04A|WEAN-11.intro:
Fully controlled ventilation leaves the diaphragm idle. An idle muscle starts breaking down its own proteins within hours, and oxidative stress damages what remains, so strength falls measurably by 48 hours. That is why partial support, which keeps the diaphragm working, is preferred once the patient can trigger.
See it: a leg in a cast that wastes within days.
why: c

Diaphragm and limb weakness overlap but are separate: the diaphragm can be weak with fair limbs and vice versa, so a normal limb MRC score does not rule out diaphragm dysfunction; test the diaphragm directly (ultrasound, MIP).
d
Too much support silences the diaphragm (disuse); too little overloads and injures it, so aim for moderate effort. Training then strengthens a muscle that has been rested too long.

MV04A|WEAN-08.intro:
On the ventilator, positive pleural pressure squeezes the chest: it slows venous return and helps the left ventricle eject. Remove it, and the patient's own efforts make pleural pressure negative. More blood returns (more preload), and the LV must eject against the negative pressure around it (more afterload). A weak heart cannot handle both, so LVEDP rises and the lungs flood.
See it: a weak pump given more to fill and harder to empty at the same moment.
why: a
LV afterload is the pressure across its wall: arterial pressure minus pleural pressure. A negative pleural pressure widens that gap.
b
Breathing work and stress hormones raise myocardial oxygen demand, so ischaemia can stiffen the LV. Hypoxaemia raises PVR; the RV dilates and pushes the septum left, shrinking the LV's filling space.
c
COPD gives the biggest pleural swings (high resistance, auto-PEEP), and left heart disease has the least reserve to meet them.

MV04A|WEAN-09.intro:
Weaning-induced oedema is a rise in left filling pressure during the trial, so the tests look for that rise or for its footprints. Echo E/A and E/e′ estimate left atrial pressure. Higher filling pressure pushes fluid, but not protein, out of the vessels into the lung, so the plasma left behind concentrates its protein and haemoglobin.
See it: water seeps out of a pipe and leaves the protein behind.
why: b
A tall E wave reflects high left atrial pressure; dividing E by e′ corrects for slow relaxation, so E/e′ tracks filling pressure.
c
If output does not rise with leg raising, the heart is on the flat part of the Starling curve, so the extra venous return of the trial will raise filling pressure, not output.
e
Diuretics remove the excess volume, so the preload rise of the trial meets a less full heart; BNP-guided fluid removal works the same way.
